claims.claim: Section 7 of the Aadhaar Act, 2016 permits the Central or a State Government, to establish identity as a condition for receipt of a subsidy, benefit or service paid from the Consolidated Fund of India, to require authentication or proof of an Aadhaar number (or an application for enrolment), and provides that a person not assigned an Aadhaar number shall be offered alternate and viable means of identification.
claims.source: The Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016 (No. 18 of 2016), s.7; text hosted by UIDAI, https://uidai.gov.in/images/targeted_delivery_of_financial_and_other_subsidies_benefits_and_services_13072016.pdf
claims.notes: Section 7 read verbatim in the UIDAI-hosted PDF of the Act on 2026-09-25. The power is permissive ('may ... require that such individual undergo authentication, or furnish proof of possession of Aadhaar number'), and its proviso requires that a person not assigned a number 'shall be offered alternate and viable means of identification for delivery of the subsidy, benefit or service'. The entry's earlier wording, that s.7 'makes proof of identity a condition for subsidies', overstated the section: the condition is one a government may impose. Later amendments were not checked. Part V's Aadhaar/PDS chain sits beside dreze-2017-cancelled-cards and the muralidharan-2025 entries; the UIDAI dashboard figures once cited here are not part of this entry.

claims.claim: Henry Shue argues that subsistence rights, together with security and liberty rights, are basic rights, and that each basic right correlates with duties to avoid depriving, to protect from deprivation, and to aid the deprived.
claims.source: Henry Shue, Basic Rights: Subsistence, Affluence, and U.S. Foreign Policy (Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press, 1980; 2nd ed. 1996; 40th anniversary ed. 2020, ISBN 9780691202280), ch. 1 'Security and Subsistence' (p. 13) and ch. 2 'Correlative Duties' (p. 35), 40th anniversary edition pagination; https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691202280/basic-rights
claims.notes: Checked the Princeton University Press page for the 40th anniversary edition: its description says Shue 'argues that subsistence rights, along with security rights and liberty rights, serve as the ground of all other human rights'. Checked the publisher's sample PDF (table of contents and index) for that edition: ch. 1 'Security and Subsistence' starts p. 13; ch. 2 'Correlative Duties' starts p. 35; the index has 'correlative duties (of avoidance, protection and aid)', with 'tripartite analysis of, 54-55'. The Oxford Academic listing gives the same chapter list. The page numbers belong to the 2020 edition and may differ from the 1980 and 1996 editions. I did not read the chapter text, so the three duties rest on the index headings and the publisher description, not on a quotation. The plan called the right 'unconditional', and I could not verify that: the third duty is aid to 'the deprived', which secondary accounts describe as owed to people unable to provide for themselves. The book should not say Shue argues for a floor with no conditions. Shue's triad of duties comes before Eide's respect/protect/fulfil framework (see the Eide entry). Whether Eide drew on it is not stated in the documents I checked.

claims.claim: In his 1987 UN study, Special Rapporteur Asbjørn Eide analysed State obligations for the right to food on three levels (respect, protect and fulfil). His 1999 update restated the framework with a separate obligation to facilitate and recorded that CESCR General Comment 12 had adopted the three levels, splitting fulfil into facilitate and provide.
claims.source: Asbjørn Eide, 'Report on the right to adequate food as a human right', UN Doc. E/CN.4/Sub.2/1987/23 (7 July 1987), paras. 66-69 and 112-115 (also 169-180); and Asbjørn Eide, 'The right to adequate food and to be free from hunger: Updated study on the right to food', UN Doc. E/CN.4/Sub.2/1999/12 (28 June 1999), paras. 52-53; https://documents.un.org/api/symbol/access?s=E/CN.4/Sub.2/1987/23&l=en&t=pdf and https://documents.un.org/api/symbol/access?s=E/CN.4/Sub.2/1999/12&l=en&t=pdf
claims.notes: Full text of both documents read from the official UN ODS PDFs. 1987 report (Sub-Commission on Prevention of Discrimination and Protection of Minorities, 39th session): para. 66 'State responsibility for human rights can be examined at three levels: The obligation to respect, the obligation to protect, and the obligation to fulfil human rights'. Paras. 67-69 define each level. Paras. 112-114 set them out as primary, secondary and tertiary levels, the last 'as a last resource'. Para. 115 rejects the idea that economic and social rights sit only at the fulfil level. Paras. 169-180 apply the three levels to food security. 1999 update: para. 52 says the 1987 framework had three levels, 'respect', 'protect' and 'assist and fulfil', then restates it as four ('facilitate' at the tertiary level, 'fulfil' at the fourth). Para. 53 says the Committee 'has now generally endorsed this approach in its general comment 12 (para. 15)', keeping three levels and subdividing the third into facilitate and provide. The 1999 update reproduces General Comment 12 as an annex. General Comment 12 fn. 1 cites the 1987 study's later publication as UN Human Rights Study Series No. 1 (1989), Sales No. E.89.XIV.2. The plan's pairing of the 1987 report with its 1999 update is correct. Note that fulfil/provide is framed as a last-resort obligation toward people whose needs cannot be met by their own efforts (1987 para. 69).

claims.claim: In General Comment 3 (1990), the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights held that every State party has a minimum core obligation to ensure at least minimum essential levels of each Covenant right. A State where any significant number of people lack essential foodstuffs, primary health care, basic shelter and housing, or basic education is prima facie failing its obligations.
claims.source: UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, General Comment No. 3: The nature of States parties' obligations (art. 2, para. 1, of the Covenant), fifth session (1990), contained in UN Doc. E/1991/23, annex III, para. 10; https://tbinternet.ohchr.org/_layouts/15/treatybodyexternal/Download.aspx?symbolno=INT%2FCESCR%2FGEC%2F4758&Lang=en
claims.notes: Read the English Word text on the OHCHR treaty-body database landing page (INT/CESCR/GEC/4758). Its header reads 'Fifth session (1990)' and its note reads 'Contained in document E/1991/23'. Cross-checked para. 10 against the University of Minnesota Human Rights Library copy (a mirror, not official), which cites E/1991/23, annex III at 86 (1991). Para. 10 verified verbatim, including 'a minimum core obligation to ensure the satisfaction of, at the very least, minimum essential levels of each of the rights is incumbent upon every State party' and the 'prima facie' sentence. The same paragraph limits the claim, and the book should keep those limits. Any assessment 'must also take account of resource constraints'. A State that blames a lack of resources 'must demonstrate that every effort has been made to use all resources that are at its disposition in an effort to satisfy, as a matter of priority, those minimum obligations'. The obligation is the State's. It is judged by whether a significant number of people are deprived, and it is not stated as an individual entitlement. I did not find the frequently cited adoption date of 14 December 1990 in the official text I read.

claims.claim: CESCR General Comment 12 (1999) holds that the right to adequate food imposes obligations to respect, to protect and to fulfil. Fulfil includes facilitating and, where people cannot enjoy the right by the means at their disposal for reasons beyond their control, providing food directly. States also have a core obligation to take the necessary action to mitigate and alleviate hunger.
claims.source: UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, General Comment 12: The right to adequate food (art. 11), twentieth session (1999), UN Doc. E/C.12/1999/5 (12 May 1999), paras. 6, 15 and 17 (and fn. 1); https://documents.un.org/api/symbol/access?s=E/C.12/1999/5&l=en&t=pdf
claims.notes: Full text read from the official OHCHR/ODS PDF (E/C.12/1999/5, 12 May 1999, twentieth session, Geneva 26 April-14 May 1999). Para. 15 verified: 'three types or levels of obligations on States parties: the obligations to respect, to protect and to fulfil. In turn, the obligation to fulfil incorporates both an obligation to facilitate and an obligation to provide.' Para. 15 says the provide obligation arises 'whenever an individual or group is unable, for reasons beyond their control, to enjoy the right to adequate food by the means at their disposal'. That condition differs from an unconditional floor, and the book should not present General Comment 12 as requiring unconditional provision. Para. 6: the right is realised through physical and economic access 'at all times'. It is not a minimum package of calories. It is realised progressively, but there is a 'core obligation to take the necessary action to mitigate and alleviate hunger'. Para. 17: a violation occurs when a State fails to ensure 'the minimum essential level required to be free from hunger'. A State claiming resource constraints bears the burden of proof and cross-refers to General Comment 3, para. 10. Fn. 1 credits the three levels to the Right to Food study (UN Study Series No. 1, 1989), the published form of Eide's 1987 report.

claims.claim: Amartya Sen argues that starvation concerns people's ability to command food through the legal means available to them (their entitlements), not the food supply as such. His case study of the 1943 Bengal famine rejects an explanation based on a decline in food availability.
claims.source: Amartya Sen, Poverty and Famines: An Essay on Entitlement and Deprivation (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1981), ch. 1 'Poverty and Entitlements' (pp. 1-8), ch. 5 'The Entitlement Approach' (pp. 45-51), ch. 6 'The Great Bengal Famine' (pp. 52-85), ch. 10 'Entitlements and Deprivation' (pp. 154-166); Oxford Scholarship Online, doi:10.1093/0198284632.001.0001
claims.notes: Checked the publisher's chapter abstracts and page ranges on Oxford Scholarship Online, through the Crossref metadata for DOIs 10.1093/0198284632.003.0001-0010. I did not read the full text. Ch. 1 abstract: starvation statements 'are about the relationship of persons to the commodity of food, rather than about the food supply per se'. Ch. 5 abstract: the approach 'concentrates on the ability of people to command food through the use of the legal means available in society'. Ch. 6 abstract: for the Bengal famine of 1943, an explanation by food availability decline (FAD) 'is rejected for various reasons'. The other case studies differ, so the book should not generalise to 'every famine'. Ethiopia 1972-4 rejects FAD 'except for the situation in the province of Wollo'. Bangladesh 1974: FAD 'offer[s] very little by way of explanation'. The online edition's metadata carries a 1983 date (a later printing), and page ranges are from that edition. The book was first published by Clarendon Press in 1981. Sen's 'entitlement' is a descriptive, legal-economic command over goods, not a normative right. The book should not blur the two senses.

claims.claim: Drèze and Sen argue that eliminating hunger needs public action in a broad sense. They treat famine prevention as a problem of protecting entitlements, including through employment provision and cash support. They distinguish growth-mediated security from support-led security, in which public support such as health care, education and food subsidies raises living standards without first waiting for prosperity.
claims.source: Jean Drèze and Amartya Sen, Hunger and Public Action (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1989), ch. 2 'Entitlement and Deprivation' (pp. 20-34), ch. 5 'Famines and Social Response' (pp. 65-84), ch. 6 'Famines, Markets and Intervention' (pp. 85-103), ch. 7 'Strategies of Entitlement Protection' (pp. 104-121), ch. 10 'Economic Growth and Public Support' (pp. 179-203), ch. 12 'Experiences of Direct Support' (pp. 226-254), ch. 13 'The Economy, the State and the Public' (pp. 257-280); Oxford Scholarship Online, doi:10.1093/0198283652.001.0001
claims.notes: Checked the publisher's chapter abstracts and page ranges on Oxford Scholarship Online, through Crossref metadata for DOIs 10.1093/0198283652.003.0001-0013. I did not read the full text. Ch. 5: famine prevention thought of 'in terms of an entitlement protection problem'. Ch. 6: discusses 'deficiencies of direct delivery strategies' and 'recommends [the] greater use' of cash support. Ch. 7: employment provision as entitlement protection; 'the limits of nutritional status as a basic selection criterion'. Ch. 10: 'growth-mediated security' against 'support-led security'. Ch. 12: support-led security in Sri Lanka, Chile and Costa Rica. Ch. 13: 'public action (in a broad sense)'. The plan's framing 'entitlement versus delivery' is not the book's own contrast. The book discusses entitlement protection and, within it, direct food delivery against cash and employment support, so the book should use the book's own terms. The online edition's metadata carries a 1991 date (a later printing). First publication 1989, Clarendon Press, as the book reviews listed in Crossref record. I did not verify the name of its WIDER series. Page ranges are from the online edition.

claims.claim: Philip Pettit defends freedom as non-domination, the republican alternative to freedom as non-interference and as self-mastery: a person is unfree to the extent that another has the capacity to interfere in their choices on an arbitrary basis, even if the other never actually interferes.
claims.source: Philip Pettit, Republicanism: A Theory of Freedom and Government (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1997; Oxford Political Theory; ISBN 0198290837), ch. 1 'Before Negative and Positive Liberty' and ch. 2 'Liberty as Non-Domination' (pp. 51-79 in the 1999 paperback/online edition); Oxford Scholarship Online doi:10.1093/0198296428.001.0001
claims.notes: Checked the publisher's chapter abstracts on Oxford Scholarship Online through Crossref, not the full text. Ch. 1 abstract: non-domination 'requires that no one is able to interfere on an arbitrary basis ... in the choices of the free person'. Those subject to another's arbitrary will are unfree 'even if the other does not actually interfere with them'. Ch. 2 abstract: 'Domination in the sense defined may occur without actual interference ... and interference may occur without any domination'. Ch. 4 abstract: non-domination as a primary good. First publication (Clarendon Press, 1997, ISBN 0198290837, Oxford Political Theory) is confirmed by a Utilitas review header and a bookseller record. The Oxford Scholarship Online version is the 1999 paperback, which adds 'Republicanism: Once More With Hindsight'. The chapter page ranges above come from that version and may differ from the 1997 hardback.

claims.claim: In On the People's Terms, Pettit argues that state coercion need not dominate citizens so long as they share equally in a form of control over those in power. He develops a model of democratic influence and control to secure this.
claims.source: Philip Pettit, On the People's Terms: A Republican Theory and Model of Democracy (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2012; The Seeley Lectures), ch. 1 'Freedom as non-domination' (pp. 26-74), ch. 3 'Political legitimacy' (pp. 130-186), ch. 4 'Democratic influence' (pp. 187-238), ch. 5 'Democratic control' (pp. 239-292); doi:10.1017/CBO9781139017428
claims.notes: Checked the publisher's book abstract and chapter page ranges through Crossref for DOI 10.1017/CBO9781139017428. I did not read the full text. The abstract says Pettit 'argues that state coercion will not involve individual subjection or domination insofar as we enjoy an equally shared form of control over those in power', 'supported by a realistic model of the institutions that might establish such democratic control'. Online publication date 6 December 2012. ISBNs 9781107005112 (hb), 9780521182126 (pb). The Seeley Lectures series is confirmed by retailer listings, not by the publisher page, which I did not open. No page-level pinpoint was verified beyond the chapter ranges.

claims.claim: Elizabeth Anderson's 'democratic equality' holds that people are entitled to the capabilities needed to avoid or escape oppressive social relationships and to the capabilities needed to function as an equal citizen in a democratic state.
claims.source: Elizabeth S. Anderson, 'What Is the Point of Equality?', Ethics 109, no. 2 (January 1999): 287-337, at 316 (see also 289, 318); https://doi.org/10.1086/233897
claims.notes: Bibliographic data from Crossref (Ethics 109(2), 287-337, DOI 10.1086/233897). Full text read from a JSTOR-generated PDF hosted on a Rutgers philosophy course page (third-party copy, used only to check wording and pages). Verbatim at p. 316: 'Negatively, people are entitled to whatever capabilities are necessary to enable them to avoid or escape entanglement in oppressive social relationships. Positively, they are entitled to the capabilities necessary for functioning as an equal citizen in a democratic state.' The plan's framing matches. Anderson's guarantee is conditioned in ways the book's unconditional floor is not. At p. 289, democratic equality 'guarantees all law-abiding citizens effective access to the social conditions of their freedom'. At p. 318, it guarantees effective access rather than actual functioning, and it 'can make access to certain functionings - those requiring an income - conditional upon working for them', provided people can work and find a job. The book should cite Anderson for relational, democratic equality, not as support for an unconditional or non-citizen floor.

claims.claim: Elizabeth Anderson argues that most modern workplaces are private governments: employers hold authority to issue orders backed by sanctions over workers' lives, while workers have no say in how that authority operates. She defines private government as 'government that has arbitrary, unaccountable power over those it governs'.
claims.source: Elizabeth Anderson, Private Government: How Employers Rule Our Lives (and Why We Don't Talk about It), ed. Stephen Macedo (Princeton, NJ: Princeton University Press, 2017; The University Center for Human Values Series; ISBN 9780691176512), Lecture 2 'Private Government' (pp. 37-72), at 41, 42 and 45; doi:10.1515/9781400887781
claims.notes: Checked the Princeton University Press page (published 23 May 2017, 224 pp., University Center for Human Values Series). The page says the book is based on the Tanner Lectures at Princeton's Center for Human Values, edited and introduced by Stephen Macedo, with commentary by Bromwich, Cowen, Hughes and Kolodny. Chapter pages from Crossref: '2. Private Government', pp. 37-72. Chapter text read from a course-hosted scan of ch. 2 that carries the book's pagination (third-party copy, used only to check wording). p. 41: 'Most modern workplaces are private governments.' p. 42: 'government exists wherever some have the authority to issue orders to others, backed by sanctions, in one or more domains of life'. p. 45: 'Private government is government that has arbitrary, unaccountable power over those it governs. This of course is a matter of degree.' Anderson frames this with a republican, non-domination vocabulary. Her remedies are not verified here.

claims.claim: K. Sabeel Rahman argues that firms controlling 'infrastructural' goods and services that many others depend on, such as finance, broadband and online platforms, are a form of private power that should be regulated through a revived public-utility framework: firewalling, public obligations and public options.
claims.source: K. Sabeel Rahman, 'The New Utilities: Private Power, Social Infrastructure, and the Revival of the Public Utility Concept', Cardozo Law Review 39, no. 5 (2018): 1621-1689, at 1626 and 1659-1661; https://larc.cardozo.yu.edu/clr/vol39/iss5/3/
claims.notes: Checked the official repository landing page (Cardozo Law Review, vol. 39, iss. 5, 2018) with its abstract. Read the full text in the PDF on the Cardozo Law Review website (http://cardozolawreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/07/RAHMAN.39.5.2.pdf): first page 1621, last page 1689. The abstract names 'three key elements of a twenty-first century framework for public utility regulation ...: firewalling; imposing public obligations; and creating public options'. The introduction at p. 1626 sets out the same three. The table of contents places 'Firewalls' at p. 1659 and 'Public Obligations and Public Options' at p. 1661. The intro at p. 1626 says 'four key elements' but then lists three; the abstract's three is the safer statement. The law review article has no DOI; the landing page is the official locator.

claims.claim: Kate Raworth's 'Doughnut' frames the economic goal as meeting everyone's needs within the means of the planet. The space lies between a social foundation, whose twelve dimensions are derived from the 2015 Sustainable Development Goals, and an ecological ceiling of nine planetary boundaries taken from Rockström et al.
claims.source: Kate Raworth, Doughnut Economics: Seven Ways to Think Like a 21st-Century Economist (London: Random House Business; White River Junction, VT: Chelsea Green, 2017; Chelsea Green ISBN 9781603586740); author's summary of the 2017 Doughnut at https://www.kateraworth.com/doughnut/
claims.notes: The description of the model was checked on the author's own page ('The Doughnut of social and planetary boundaries (2017)'). It says the 'environmental ceiling consists of nine planetary boundaries, as set out by Rockstrom et al' and the 'twelve dimensions of the social foundation are derived from internationally agreed minimum social standards, as identified by the world's governments in the Sustainable Development Goals in 2015'. Bibliographic facts: the Penguin (Random House Business imprint) page lists a 2017 ebook and a 2022 paperback (ISBN 9781847941398). The Chelsea Green 2017 edition (ISBN 9781603586740, 320 pp.) is confirmed by a published review header and bookseller records, not the publisher page, which did not load. I did not see a chapter or page in the book for the diagram, so no page pinpoint is given. The plan's framing (social foundation plus ecological ceiling) is accurate. The book should not attribute the planetary boundaries themselves to Raworth; see the Rockström entry.

claims.claim: Rockström and colleagues proposed nine planetary boundaries defining a 'safe operating space for humanity', quantified seven of them, and estimated that three (climate change, the rate of biodiversity loss and the nitrogen cycle) had already been transgressed.
claims.source: Johan Rockström et al., 'A safe operating space for humanity', Nature 461, no. 7263 (24 September 2009): 472-475, https://doi.org/10.1038/461472a; full version: Johan Rockström et al., 'Planetary Boundaries: Exploring the Safe Operating Space for Humanity', Ecology and Society 14, no. 2 (2009): art. 32, https://www.ecologyandsociety.org/vol14/iss2/art32/
claims.notes: Nature bibliographic data from Crossref (vol. 461, issue 7263, pp. 472-475, 29 authors) and the Nature article page. It is a Feature published online 23 September 2009, with the standfirst: 'Identifying and quantifying planetary boundaries that must not be transgressed could help prevent human activities from causing unacceptable environmental change'. The Nature full text is paywalled and was not read. The nine boundaries, the seven quantified, and the three transgressed were verified in the abstract of the open-access companion article in Ecology and Society 14(2):32. The boundaries are climate change, ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone, nitrogen and phosphorus cycles, global freshwater use, land-system change, biodiversity loss, chemical pollution and atmospheric aerosol loading; the last two were unquantified. These are 2009 estimates. The framework has since been revised by later papers not checked here, so the book should date any figure to 2009.

claims.claim: From comparative case studies of long-enduring, self-organised common-pool resource institutions, Elinor Ostrom distilled a set of 'design principles' those institutions tended to share and failed cases tended to lack. They include clear boundaries, rules fitted to local conditions, collective-choice arrangements, monitoring, graduated sanctions, accessible conflict resolution, recognition of users' right to organise, and nested enterprises.
claims.source: Elinor Ostrom, Governing the Commons: The Evolution of Institutions for Collective Action (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1990), ch. 3 'Analyzing long-enduring, self-organized, and self-governed CPRs' (pp. 58-102); doi:10.1017/CBO9780511807763; see also Ostrom's Nobel Prize lecture (2009), https://www.nobelprize.org/uploads/2018/06/ostrom_lecture.pdf
claims.notes: Book bibliographic data and chapter page ranges checked through Crossref (CUP, 1990; ISBNs 9780521371018, 9780521405997). I did not read the book's text, and I did not see the widely cited 'Table 3.1, p. 90' design-principles table, so no page is given for it. Ostrom's Nobel lecture (full text, nobelprize.org PDF) confirms she coined the 'design principles' to describe regularities 'among the systems that were sustained over a long period of time and were absent in the failed systems (E. Ostrom 1990)'. It says she 'did not mean that ... [users] overtly had these principles in their minds' and in a footnote that 'Perhaps I should have used the term "best practices"'. The lecture gives an updated list (after Cox, Arnold and Villamayor-Tomás 2009) that splits principles 1, 2 and 4. The book should cite the principles as empirical regularities associated with durable self-governance, not as sufficient conditions or guarantees, and should say whether it uses the 1990 wording or the later revision. The Ostrom Workshop page also describes them as characterising robust institutions.

claims.claim: Helen Nissenbaum proposes 'contextual integrity' as a benchmark for privacy: information gathering and dissemination must be appropriate to their context and obey that context's governing norms of distribution.
claims.source: Helen Nissenbaum, 'Privacy as Contextual Integrity', Washington Law Review 79, no. 1 (2004): 119 (symposium); https://digitalcommons.law.uw.edu/wlr/vol79/iss1/10
claims.notes: Checked the official University of Washington Law repository landing page and abstract. Recommended citation there: 'Helen Nissenbaum, Symposium, Privacy as Contextual Integrity, 79 Wash. L. Rev. 119 (2004)'. First page 119 verified. The end page is given as 157 in secondary listings but was not verified: the PDF was behind a bot check, so the full text was not read. Abstract: 'Contextual integrity ties adequate protection for privacy to norms of specific contexts, demanding that information gathering and dissemination be appropriate to that context and obey the governing norms of distribution within it.' The article's focus is public surveillance, and it builds on Walzer's 'spheres of justice'. No DOI exists for this law review article.

claims.claim: In Privacy in Context, Nissenbaum develops contextual integrity into a framework in which information flows are assessed against context-relative informational norms, specified in terms of actors, information attributes and transmission principles.
claims.source: Helen Nissenbaum, Privacy in Context: Technology, Policy, and the Integrity of Social Life (Stanford, CA: Stanford University Press, 2010), ch. 7 'Contexts, Informational Norms, Actors, Attributes, and Transmission Principles' (pp. 129-157); doi:10.1515/9780804772891
claims.notes: Checked chapter titles and page ranges through Crossref (De Gruyter/Stanford University Press). Ch. 7 pp. 129-157, ch. 8 'Breaking Rules for Good' pp. 158-185, ch. 9 'Privacy Rights in Context: Applying the Framework' pp. 186-230. I did not read the text; the claim rests on the chapter 7 title, which names the framework's parameters, and on the 2004 article's abstract. Crossref gives the monograph an issued date of 2009. The book is commonly cited as 2010, its copyright year; the publisher's own page (sup.org) did not load, so that date was not confirmed there. Print ISBN 9780804752367 appears in retailer listings only. The PDF on crypto.stanford.edu is an image scan of the table of contents and introduction and was not text-searchable.

claims.claim: Under the GDPR's purpose-limitation principle, personal data must be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes. Further processing for archiving in the public interest, scientific or historical research, or statistics is, under Article 89(1), not considered incompatible.
claims.source: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1, Article 5(1)(b); https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj
claims.notes: Full text read from EUR-Lex (CELEX 32016R0679, HTML). The header confirms 'Official Journal of the European Union L 119/1', 4.5.2016, Regulation of 27 April 2016. Article 5(1)(b) verified verbatim: '(b) collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes; further processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes shall, in accordance with Article 89(1), not be considered to be incompatible with the initial purposes ("purpose limitation");'. The principle bars incompatible further use, not all further use, and compatibility is assessed under Article 6(4), which was not checked here. The book should not describe it as a strict single-use rule.

claims.claim: Russell and Burch set out the 'three R's' of humane experimental technique. Replacement is the substitution of insentient material for conscious living higher animals. Reduction is reducing the number of animals used to obtain information of a given amount and precision. Refinement is any decrease in the incidence or severity of inhumane procedures applied to animals that still have to be used.
claims.source: W. M. S. Russell and R. L. Burch, The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique (London: Methuen, 1959), ch. 4 'The Sources, Incidence, and Removal of Inhumanity', section 'The Removal of Inhumanity: The Three R's'; online special edition hosted by the Johns Hopkins Center for Alternatives to Animal Testing, https://caat.publichealth.jhu.edu/the-principles-of-humane-experimental-technique-2/
claims.notes: Text read from the chapter PDF of the online special edition at Johns Hopkins CAAT ('17.-The-Removal-of-Inhumanity.pdf'). The definitions were verified verbatim: 'Replacement means the substitution for conscious living higher animals of insentient material. Reduction means reduction in the numbers of animals used to obtain information of a given amount and precision. Refinement means any decrease in the incidence or severity of inhumane procedures applied to those animals which still have to be used.' The authors add that 'There are clearly areas of overlap between these categories.' The CAAT online edition has no original page numbers, so no page is given; the often-cited p. 64 was not seen. The publisher (Methuen, 1959), the 1960 Charles C. Thomas reprint and the 1992 UFAW reissue were confirmed only by NORECOPA's description, a secondary source. The three R's are principles for reducing inhumanity in experiments. They do not themselves prohibit animal use.

claims.claim: Article 12 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities requires States to recognise that persons with disabilities enjoy legal capacity on an equal basis with others in all aspects of life. It requires access to the support they may require in exercising that capacity, and safeguards ensuring that such measures respect the person's rights, will and preferences, are free of conflict of interest and undue influence, are proportional, apply for the shortest time possible and are regularly reviewed.
claims.source: Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (New York, 13 December 2006; adopted by UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/61/106; entry into force 3 May 2008), United Nations Treaty Series, vol. 2515, p. 3, Article 12; https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetails.aspx?src=IND&mtdsg_no=IV-15&chapter=4&clang=_en
claims.notes: The article text was read in full on the UN DESA Division for Inclusive Social Development page for Article 12 (UN site). Treaty facts were checked on the UN Treaty Collection status page (chapter IV.15): New York, 13 December 2006; entry into force 3 May 2008; registration No. 44910; UNTS vol. 2515, p. 3; adopted by A/RES/61/106. Paras. 2-4 verified: 'enjoy legal capacity on an equal basis with others in all aspects of life'; 'access ... to the support they may require in exercising their legal capacity'; safeguards that 'respect the rights, will and preferences of the person, are free of conflict of interest and undue influence, are proportional and tailored ..., apply for the shortest time possible and are subject to regular review by a competent, independent and impartial authority or judicial body'. The phrase 'supported decision-making' does not appear in the treaty text. It is the Committee's interpretation in General Comment No. 1 (separate entry), and the book should attribute it there.

claims.claim: The CRPD Committee reads Article 12 as requiring States to replace substitute decision-making regimes with supported decision-making that respects the person's autonomy, will and preferences. Where, after significant efforts, a person's will and preferences cannot be determined, the 'best interpretation of will and preferences' must replace 'best interests' determinations.
claims.source: UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, General comment No. 1 (2014): Article 12: Equal recognition before the law, eleventh session (31 March-11 April 2014), UN Doc. CRPD/C/GC/1 (19 May 2014), paras. 3, 16-17, 21, 26-29; https://documents.un.org/api/symbol/access?s=CRPD/C/GC/1&l=en&t=pdf
claims.notes: Full text read from the official ODS PDF (Distr. 19 May 2014). Para. 3: the human rights model 'implies a shift from the substitute decision-making paradigm to one that is based on supported decision-making'. Para. 17: support 'should never amount to substitute decision-making'. Para. 21: 'Where, after significant efforts have been made, it is not practicable to determine the will and preferences of an individual, the "best interpretation of will and preferences" must replace the "best interests" determinations', and 'best interests' 'is not a safeguard which complies with article 12 in relation to adults'. Para. 27 defines substitute regimes, including plenary and partial guardianship. Para. 28: compliance requires 'both the abolition of substitute decision-making regimes and the development of supported decision-making alternatives'; running them in parallel 'is not sufficient'. This is the treaty body's interpretation, not treaty text, and the book should present it as such. Para. 21's rule is stated for adults.

claims.claim: Article 12 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child guarantees every child capable of forming views the right to express them freely in all matters affecting the child, with due weight according to age and maturity, and the opportunity to be heard in judicial and administrative proceedings. The Committee on the Rights of the Child reads it as imposing no age limit and requiring States to presume a child's capacity to form views.
claims.source: Convention on the Rights of the Child (New York, 20 November 1989; entry into force 2 September 1990), United Nations Treaty Series, vol. 1577, p. 3, Article 12; read with Committee on the Rights of the Child, General Comment No. 12 (2009): The right of the child to be heard, UN Doc. CRC/C/GC/12 (20 July 2009), paras. 20-21; https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetails.aspx?src=IND&mtdsg_no=IV-11&chapter=4&clang=_en and https://documents.un.org/api/symbol/access?s=CRC/C/GC/12&l=en&t=pdf
claims.notes: Treaty facts checked on the UN Treaty Collection status page (chapter IV.11): New York, 20 November 1989; entry into force 2 September 1990; registration No. 27531; UNTS vol. 1577, p. 3. The Article 12 text was read on UNICEF's convention-text page, a secondary host; the OHCHR page was behind a bot check. It was verified verbatim: '1. States Parties shall assure to the child who is capable of forming his or her own views the right to express those views freely in all matters affecting the child, the views of the child being given due weight in accordance with the age and maturity of the child. 2. ... the opportunity to be heard in any judicial and administrative proceedings affecting the child, either directly, or through a representative or an appropriate body ...'. The treaty text itself sets no minimum age. The 'no minimum age' point comes from the Committee: General Comment 12 (official ODS PDF, read in full) para. 21: 'article 12 imposes no age limit on the right of the child to express her or his views', and it discourages age limits in law or practice. Para. 20: 'States parties should presume that a child has the capacity to form her or his own views'. Para. 21 also calls for respect for non-verbal communication. The weight given to views still varies with age and maturity.

claims.claim: Will Kymlicka distinguishes two meanings of group or collective rights. 'Internal restrictions' are a group's claims to limit its own members' liberties for the sake of group solidarity. 'External protections' are claims to limit the power of the wider society over the group. He argues that external protections need not conflict with individual rights.
claims.source: Will Kymlicka, Multicultural Citizenship: A Liberal Theory of Minority Rights (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1995; Oxford Political Theory; ISBN 0198279493), ch. 3 'Individual Rights and Collective Rights' (pp. 34-48); Oxford Scholarship Online doi:10.1093/0198290918.001.0001
claims.notes: Checked the publisher's chapter abstract and page range on Oxford Scholarship Online through Crossref (DOI 10.1093/0198290918.003.0003, pp. 34-48). I did not read the full text. Abstract: 'collective rights ... can refer either to the right of a group to limit the liberties of members in the interest of group solidarity or purity (internal restrictions), or the right of a group to limit the powers of a majority to curtail the interests of minorities (external protections). It argues that the latter need not conflict with individual [rights]'. Ch. 8 'Toleration and Its Limits' (pp. 152-172) addresses minorities seeking to restrict members' civil liberties. The online version is the 1996 paperback (ISBN 0198290918). The 1995 Clarendon hardback (ISBN 0198279493) is confirmed by Open Library and bookseller records, not the publisher. Page numbers are from the online/paperback edition; no page within ch. 3 was verified.

claims.claim: Ayelet Shachar identifies a 'paradox of multicultural vulnerability': accommodating a cultural or religious group can expose its vulnerable members, especially women, to sanctioned rights violations within the group. She proposes 'joint governance', dividing jurisdiction between the group and the state so as to reduce injustice between groups and within them.
claims.source: Ayelet Shachar, Multicultural Jurisdictions: Cultural Differences and Women's Rights (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2001), esp. ch. 6 'Transformative accommodation: utilizing external protections to reduce internal restrictions' (pp. 117-145); doi:10.1017/CBO9780511490330
claims.notes: Checked the publisher's book abstract and chapter list through Crossref (CUP, online 6 September 2001; ISBNs 9780521772099, 9780521776745). I did not read the full text. Abstract: the book rejects prevalent solutions to 'this "paradox of multicultural vulnerability"' and argues for enhancing 'the jurisdictional autonomy of religious and cultural minorities while ... providing viable legal-institutional solutions to the problem of sanctioned intra-group rights violation'. The 'new "joint governance" approach' 'strives for the reduction of injustice between minority groups and the wider society, together with the enhancement of justice within them'. Chapters include 'The perils of multicultural accommodation' (pp. 17-44), 'Sharing the pieces of jurisdictional authority' (pp. 88-116) and 'Transformative accommodation' (pp. 117-145), whose title engages Kymlicka's terms. No page for the 'paradox' phrase itself was verified.

claims.claim: Crépeau and Hastie argue for 'firewalls': a separation between immigration enforcement and public service provision, so that irregular migrants can access fundamental rights and basic public services without fear of enforcement.
claims.source: François Crépeau and Bethany Hastie, 'The Case for "Firewall" Protections for Irregular Migrants: Safeguarding Fundamental Rights', European Journal of Migration and Law 17, no. 2-3 (2015): 157-183; https://doi.org/10.1163/15718166-12342076
claims.notes: Bibliographic data from Crossref (European Journal of Migration and Law 17(2-3), 157-183, published online 24 June 2015, DOI 10.1163/15718166-12342076). Crossref records the subtitle 'Safeguarding Fundamental Rights'. Abstract checked (the full text is paywalled and was not read): the article argues 'for the establishment of firewalls - a separation between immigration enforcement activities and public service provision'. It surveys trends that have eroded firewalls and practices that have built and maintained them. The plan's framing is accurate. The phrase 'without fear of enforcement' is a paraphrase of the firewall's purpose; the abstract speaks of the ability to access fundamental rights and basic public services.

claims.claim: The Supreme Court of Canada held that Quebec cannot secede unilaterally, meaning without principled negotiation, under either the Constitution or international law. It also held that a clear expression by a clear majority of Quebecers of a wish to secede would give rise to a reciprocal obligation on all parties to Confederation to negotiate constitutional changes in response.
claims.source: Reference re Secession of Quebec, [1998] 2 S.C.R. 217 (Supreme Court of Canada, decided 20 August 1998, file no. 25506), paras. 84, 86, 88, 90-92, 104, 151 and 155; https://decisions.scc-csc.ca/scc-csc/scc-csc/en/item/1643/index.do
claims.notes: Full text read on the Supreme Court of Canada's official decisions site. Decision information: date 1998-08-20; report [1998] 2 SCR 217; case number 25506; a reference by the Governor in Council under s. 53 of the Supreme Court Act. The opinion is by 'The Court'. Pinpoints verified. Para. 84: secession requires a constitutional amendment, 'which perforce requires negotiation'. Para. 86: 'unilateral' means secession 'without prior negotiations with the other provinces and the federal government'. Para. 88: 'the clear repudiation of the existing constitutional order and the clear expression of the desire to pursue secession by the population of a province would give rise to a reciprocal obligation on all parties to Confederation to negotiate constitutional changes to respond to that desire'. Paras. 90-92 reject both a duty to accede to secession and the claim that a clear vote imposes no obligations. Para. 104: secession 'cannot be accomplished by the National Assembly, the legislature or government of Quebec unilaterally'. Para. 151 summarises. Para. 155: 'there is no right, under the Constitution or at international law, to unilateral secession', though a de facto secession through international recognition is not ruled out. This is an advisory reference opinion, and the negotiation duty is triggered by a clear majority on a clear question. The Court did not define the threshold, and the book should not add one. The neutral CanLII citation was not verified and is omitted.

claims.claim: Article 13 TFEU requires the Union and the Member States, in formulating and implementing the Union's agriculture, fisheries, transport, internal market, research and technological development and space policies, to pay full regard to the welfare requirements of animals "since animals are sentient beings", while respecting Member States' legislative or administrative provisions and customs relating in particular to religious rites, cultural traditions and regional heritage.
claims.source: Consolidated version of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Article 13, OJ C 326, 26.10.2012, pp. 47-390; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:12012E/TXT
claims.notes: Read the consolidated TFEU on EUR-Lex (CELEX 12012E) and took Article 13 verbatim. The plan's 'full regard to their welfare' compresses the text: the duty is to pay full regard to 'the welfare requirements of animals', it applies only when formulating and implementing the listed Union policies, and it is expressly qualified by respect for Member States' provisions and customs on religious rites, cultural traditions and regional heritage. It is a policy-integration clause, not a free-standing right for animals. I did not verify the provision's origin in the Lisbon Treaty.

claims.claim: Article 20a of the German Basic Law obliges the state, mindful also of its responsibility towards future generations, to protect the natural foundations of life and animals by legislation and, in accordance with law and justice, by executive and judicial action, within the framework of the constitutional order; the words 'and animals' were added by an amending Act of 26 July 2002.
claims.source: Basic Law for the Federal Republic of Germany, Article 20a, official English translation (Tomuschat, Currie, Kommers, Kerr, with the Bundestag Language Service; version including amendments to 22 March 2025), https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/englisch_gg/englisch_gg.html; amending Act: Gesetz zur Änderung des Grundgesetzes (Staatsziel Tierschutz) of 26 July 2002, BGBl. I 2002 p. 2862, https://dejure.org/BGBl/2002/BGBl._I_S._2862
claims.notes: Article 20a text read on the official translation site (the German text is authoritative; the translation is not). History checked on verfassungen.de (https://www.verfassungen.de/gg/gg-a20a.htm): Article 20a was inserted by the Act of 27 October 1994 (BGBl. 1994 I p. 3146) covering the natural foundations of life only; 'und die Tiere' was added by the Act of 26 July 2002 (BGBl. 2002 I p. 2862). dejure.org gives publication on 31 July 2002 and entry into force on 1 August 2002, while verfassungen.de dates the version from 26 July 2002; I report the enactment date and leave the in-force date to dejure.org. The 2002 Act's title calls animal protection a state objective ('Staatsziel'). Limit worth stating beside it: in its 2021 climate order (see bverfg-2021-climate-order-intertemporal-freedom, para. 112) the Federal Constitutional Court held that Article 20a entails no subjective rights, though it is justiciable.

claims.claim: The Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022 requires the Secretary of State to establish an Animal Sentience Committee that may report on whether government, in formulating or implementing any policy, has had 'all due regard to the ways in which the policy might have an adverse effect on the welfare of animals as sentient beings', and defines 'animal' for the Act as any vertebrate other than Homo sapiens, any cephalopod mollusc and any decapod crustacean.
claims.source: Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022 (c. 22), ss. 1, 2 and 5(1); https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2022/22/contents
claims.notes: legislation.gov.uk returned a bot challenge (HTTP 202 with WAF challenge) to every fetch, so I could not read the official page. I read s. 2(1)-(2) and s. 5(1) verbatim, and the opening words of s. 1(1) ('The Secretary of State must establish and maintain a'), on LexisNexis's legislation pages (s. 1 is paywalled after those words). Royal Assent on 28 April 2022, the committee's composition and the s. 3 duty on the Secretary of State to respond to reports within three months come from J. Jowitt, 'Some Thoughts on the Animal Welfare (Sentience) Act 2022', UK Constitutional Law Association blog, 7 Sept 2022 (secondary); I did not see those provisions myself. The plan says the Act 'recognises sentience': it does not declare any animal sentient; it presupposes sentience ('as sentient beings') and creates a reporting committee whose views the government must answer but need not follow. A power to extend 'animal' to other invertebrates by regulations (s. 5(2)) was reported in search summaries only and is not verified.

claims.claim: A DEFRA-commissioned review by Birch, Burn, Schnell, Browning and Crump, drawing on over 300 scientific studies and eight evidential criteria, recommended that all cephalopod molluscs and decapod crustaceans be regarded as sentient animals for the purposes of UK animal welfare law.
claims.source: Jonathan Birch, Charlotte Burn, Alexandra Schnell, Heather Browning and Andrew Crump, Review of the Evidence of Sentience in Cephalopod Molluscs and Decapod Crustaceans (LSE Consulting, London School of Economics and Political Science, November 2021), Executive Summary pp. 7-8 ('Our central recommendation', p. 8); https://www.lse.ac.uk/News/News-Assets/PDFs/2021/Sentience-in-Cephalopod-Molluscs-and-Decapod-Crustaceans-Final-Report-November-2021.pdf ; landing page https://www.lse.ac.uk/business/consulting/reports/review-of-the-evidence-of-sentiences-in-cephalopod-molluscs-and-decapod-crustaceans
claims.notes: Downloaded the full 108-page report from LSE and extracted its text. Verified: title page and authors (p. 1); 'commissioned via LSE Consulting' (p. 2); 'Drawing on over 300 scientific studies' and the eight criteria (p. 7); the central recommendation (p. 8), which also says these animals should be counted as 'animals' for the Animal Welfare Act 2006. DEFRA as client is stated on the LSE landing page and the report refers to Defra throughout. The evidence is uneven by taxon: the report finds strong evidence for octopods and true crabs and less for squid, cuttlefish and other, less-studied groups, and recommends against restricting protection to the best-studied groups (pp. 6, 8-9); the foreword stresses that absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. It is a recommendation for the purposes of law, not a finding that every member of these taxa is sentient. The LSE page says DEFRA-selected external experts peer-reviewed it; it is a consultancy report, not a journal article, and has no DOI that I found.

claims.claim: Directive 2010/63/EU, which covers live non-human vertebrates (including independently feeding larval forms and foetal mammals in the last third of development) and live cephalopods, obliges Member States to ensure that a scientifically satisfactory method not using live animals is used wherever possible instead of a procedure, that animal numbers are reduced to a minimum without compromising a project's objectives, and that breeding, accommodation, care and procedural methods are refined to eliminate or reduce to the minimum any possible pain, suffering, distress or lasting harm (Article 4).
claims.source: Directive 2010/63/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 September 2010 on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes, OJ L 276, 20.10.2010, p. 33, Articles 1(3) and 4; consolidated text https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02010L0063-20190626 (original: CELEX 32010L0063)
claims.notes: EUR-Lex refused the original-text URLs (bot challenge), so I read the EUR-Lex consolidated version dated 26 June 2019, which gives the title, date and OJ L 276, 20.10.2010, p. 33. Article 4(1)-(3) and Article 1(3) quoted from it; I assume, but did not separately confirm against the 2010 OJ text, that Article 4 is unamended. Recitals do not appear in the consolidated text and are not verified. 'The 3Rs made binding' is fair as long as it is clear that a directive binds Member States, who must transpose it; replacement is qualified by 'wherever possible' and reduction by 'without compromising the objectives of the project'.

claims.claim: Donaldson and Kymlicka's Zoopolis moves animal rights into political theory: beyond universal basic rights for all animals, it argues that domesticated animals should be treated as co-citizens, wild animals as members of sovereign communities, and liminal animals living among people as denizens.
claims.source: Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka, Zoopolis: A Political Theory of Animal Rights (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2011), ISBN 978-0-19-959966-0 (hbk); ch. 2 'Universal Basic Rights for Animals', ch. 5 'Domesticated Animal Citizens', ch. 6 'Wild Animal Sovereignty', ch. 7 'Liminal Animal Denizens'; publisher page https://global.oup.com/academic/product/zoopolis-9780199599660
claims.notes: The OUP product page returned no content to my fetch. Publisher and year confirmed on the author's publications page (https://willkymlicka.ca/publications/books/zoopolis), whose summary gives the citizens/sovereignty/denizens framework; chapter numbers and titles confirmed from the Library of Congress table of contents (https://catdir.loc.gov/catdir/enhancements/fy1211/2011410664-t.html). The hardback ISBN comes from the OUP product URL; retailer listings give a paperback ISBN 978-0-19-967301-8. Page counts differ between sources (352 on the author's page, 329 in a journal review header), so none is given. I did not read the book and verified no page.

claims.claim: Martha Nussbaum's Justice for Animals extends her capabilities approach to non-human animals, arguing that humans share a collective responsibility for enabling animals to flourish in their own characteristic ways.
claims.source: Martha C. Nussbaum, Justice for Animals: Our Collective Responsibility (New York: Simon & Schuster, 2023), 400 pp., ISBN 978-1-982102-50-0 (hbk); paperback 2024, ISBN 978-1-982102-51-7; publisher page https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Justice-for-Animals/Martha-C-Nussbaum/9781982102517
claims.notes: Simon & Schuster's pages, PhilPapers and several reviews returned HTTP 403. Bibliographic details confirmed from the Leonardo/ISAST review (https://leonardo.info/review/2023/03/justice-for-animals-our-collective-responsibility: Simon and Schuster, New York, 2023, 400 pp., ISBN 978-1982102500), which describes the capabilities framework (bodily health and integrity, emotions, play, control over one's environment) and a chapter engaging Korsgaard. Google Books lists the 2024 paperback (ISBN 9781982102517, 400 pp.) with the publisher's description that 'all animals should have a shot at flourishing in their own way' (a blurb, not a quotation from the text). Bookstore listings put the hardcover in early January 2023; Chicago Unbound lists 2022; the exact day is not verified. No chapter or page verified, and I did not read the book. The publisher page link was found on 2026-09-25 by web search and names the paperback edition (ISBN 9781982102517).

claims.claim: In Fellow Creatures Christine Korsgaard argues on Kantian grounds that humans have direct obligations to the other animals and should treat sentient animals as ends in themselves, rejecting Kant's own view that duties regarding animals are only indirect.
claims.source: Christine M. Korsgaard, Fellow Creatures: Our Obligations to the Other Animals (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2018), ISBN 978-0-19-875385-8, Part Two; doi:10.1093/oso/9780198753858.001.0001
claims.notes: OUP's product and Oxford Academic pages returned no usable content. Crossref confirms the DOI, title, author, ISBN and online date (24 May 2018). The Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews review by Mark H. Bernstein (2019.05.02, https://ndpr.nd.edu/reviews/fellow-creatures-our-obligations-to-the-other-animals/) confirms the bibliographic line (OUP, 2018, 252 pp., ISBN 9780198753858), quotes the thesis that we are 'obligated to treat all sentient animals ... as what Kant called ends-in-themselves', and says Part 2 argues against Kant's indirect-duties view. A Philosophy Now review lists a paperback (ISBN 9780198854876, 272 pp.). Membership of OUP's Uehiro Series in Practical Ethics appears in retailer listings only. I did not read the book; no chapter or page is verified beyond 'Part Two' as described by the reviewer.

claims.claim: In Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja (7 May 2014) a two-judge bench of the Supreme Court of India held that jallikattu and bullock-cart races per se violate sections 3, 11(1)(a) and 11(1)(m)(ii) of the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1960, declared that the internationally recognised 'five freedoms' be read into sections 3 and 11, and held the Tamil Nadu Regulation of Jallikattu Act 2009 void for repugnancy.
claims.source: Animal Welfare Board of India v. A. Nagaraja & Ors., Civil Appeal No. 5387 of 2014 (with connected matters), Supreme Court of India (K.S. Radhakrishnan and Pinaki Chandra Ghose JJ.), judgment of 7 May 2014, (2014) 7 SCC 547, paras 54, 56 and 77; https://indiankanoon.org/doc/39696860/
claims.notes: Read the full judgment on Indian Kanoon (not an official reporter; the judgment's own paragraph numbers). Para 54 lists the five freedoms from the OIE guidelines (from hunger, thirst and malnutrition; fear and distress; physical and thermal discomfort; pain, injury and disease; and to express normal patterns of behaviour) and says they 'find a place in Sections 3 and 11' and are for animals 'like the rights guaranteed to the citizens' under Part III. Para 56 calls these 'only statutory rights' that 'have to be elevated' to fundamental rights. Para 77 contains the holding and the declarations: (1) rights under ss. 3 and 11 read with Arts. 51A(g) and (h); (2) the five freedoms read into ss. 3 and 11; (9) Parliament 'is expected' to make animal rights constitutional; (11) the TNRJ Act is void under Art. 254(1). The Court also upheld the MoEF notification of 11 July 2011. The SCC citation is confirmed by the 2023 Constitution Bench judgment (para 2), which cites Nagaraja as (2014) 7 SCC 547. Later history: in 2023 the Constitution Bench upheld the 2017 state amendments and rejected Nagaraja's view that jallikattu is not part of Tamil Nadu's cultural heritage (see awbi-v-union-of-india-2023); the 2014 holding concerned the Act as it then stood.

claims.claim: On 18 May 2023 a five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court of India upheld Tamil Nadu's 2017 amendment to the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act permitting jallikattu, holding that it is not colourable legislation, falls under Entry 17 of the Concurrent List, and does not violate Articles 14, 21 or 51-A(g)-(h), and held that this decision also governs the Maharashtra and Karnataka amendments, all three being valid.
claims.source: The Animal Welfare Board of India & Ors. v. Union of India & Anr., Writ Petition (Civil) No. 23 of 2016 with connected matters, Supreme Court of India, Constitution Bench (K.M. Joseph, Ajay Rastogi, Aniruddha Bose, Hrishikesh Roy and C.T. Ravikumar JJ.; opinion by Aniruddha Bose J.), judgment of 18 May 2023, 2023 INSC 548, paras 37 and 40-42; official copy https://api.sci.gov.in/pdfdate/index1.php?filename=supremecourt%2F2016%2F1216%2F1216_2016_3_1501_44624_Judgement_18-May-2023.pdf&dno=12162016&dt=2023-05-18 ; text also at https://indiankanoon.org/doc/124059674/
claims.notes: The plan's name and date are correct. Read the full text on Indian Kanoon and confirmed the official Supreme Court PDF, which carries the neutral citation 2023 INSC 548 and the same para 41. One judgment, signed by all five judges. Para 40 answers the five referred questions: (i) not colourable, Entry 17 of List III, minimises cruelty once implemented with its Rules; (ii) whether jallikattu is integral to Tamil culture is for the legislature and the Court 'would not disrupt this view of the legislature', expressly disagreeing with Nagaraja on cultural heritage, while adding that cultural tradition cannot justify activities that offend the law; (iv) no violation of Arts. 51-A(g)-(h), 14 or 21; (v) the amendment and Rules cure the defects identified in Nagaraja. Para 41 extends the decision to the Maharashtra and Karnataka Amendment Acts, which concern bullock-cart races and kambala rather than jallikattu. Para 37: the Court proceeds 'on the basis that the Constitution does not recognise any Fundamental Right for animals'. Para 42 directs strict enforcement by District Magistrates. Para 3 records that the AWBI changed its stance and supported the State.

claims.claim: In its climate order of 24 March 2021 the German Federal Constitutional Court held that fundamental rights, as 'intertemporal guarantees of freedom', protect against greenhouse-gas reduction burdens under Article 20a being unilaterally offloaded onto the future, found parts of the Federal Climate Change Act incompatible with fundamental rights for lacking reduction targets from 2031, and ordered the legislature to enact them by 31 December 2022; it also held that future generations hold no present fundamental rights, the duty to protect them being objective only.
claims.source: Bundesverfassungsgericht, Order of the First Senate of 24 March 2021, 1 BvR 2656/18, 1 BvR 78/20, 1 BvR 96/20, 1 BvR 288/20 (Climate Change), ECLI:DE:BVerfG:2021:rs20210324.1bvr265618, paras 183 and 192-194 (intertemporal freedom), 116-122 (standing), 109 and 146 (future generations), 112 (Art. 20a confers no subjective rights); official English translation https://www.bundesverfassungsgericht.de/SharedDocs/Entscheidungen/EN/2021/03/rs20210324_1bvr265618en.html
claims.notes: Read the Court's official English translation with its paragraph anchors. The translation omits some passages (for example para 191 appears as '[...]'); the German original is authoritative. The intertemporal-freedom holding is headnote 4 and para 183 ('As intertemporal guarantees of freedom, fundamental rights afford the complainants protection against the greenhouse gas reduction burdens imposed by Art. 20a GG being unilaterally offloaded onto the future'), developed at paras 192-194 (proportionality across generations; the 'radical abstinence' passage at 193). The operative part declares s. 3(1) second sentence and s. 4(1) third sentence KSG with Annex 2 incompatible with fundamental rights insofar as they lack provisions updating reduction targets for periods from 2031, and requires legislation by 31 December 2022. The plan's 'climate protection obligations to future generations' needs care: the complainants succeeded on their own fundamental rights; paras 109 and 146 hold that future generations, 'either as a whole or as the sum of individuals not yet born', carry no fundamental rights now, and that the duty of intergenerational protection is 'solely objective'. The Court found no violation of Article 20a itself (paras 183, 195-196). 'Neubauer' is the popular name after a complainant; the Court's page calls the case 'Climate Change'. I did not verify the BVerfGE reporter citation.

claims.claim: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (24 April 1973) a thirteen-judge bench of the Supreme Court of India held, by a narrow majority, that Parliament's power under Article 368 to amend the Constitution does not include power to alter its basic structure or framework.
claims.source: Kesavananda Bharati Sripadagalvaru & Ors. v. State of Kerala & Anr., Writ Petition (Civil) No. 135 of 1970, Supreme Court of India, judgment of 24 April 1973, (1973) 4 SCC 225, AIR 1973 SC 1461; Khanna J. para 1599(vii), Sikri C.J. paras 316-317 (paragraph numbers as in the Indian Kanoon text); https://indiankanoon.org/doc/257876/ ; Supreme Court of India case site https://judgments.ecourts.gov.in/KBJ/?p=home%2Fconclusion
claims.notes: Read the Indian Kanoon text, which gives the equivalent citations (1973) 4 SCC 225 and AIR 1973 SC 1461. Khanna J.'s conclusions at para 1599(vii): 'The power of amendment under Article 368 does not include power to abrogate the Constitution nor does it include the power to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution', and subject to that the power is 'plenary' and extends to fundamental rights; (viii) says the right to property is not part of the basic structure. Sikri C.J. (paras 316-317) lists supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic government, secularism, separation of powers and federalism, built on the dignity and freedom of the individual; that is one judge's list, not the Court's holding. The Supreme Court of India's own Kesavananda site describes the decision as 7-6 and names the seven majority judges (Sikri C.J., Shelat, Grover, Hegde, Mukherjea, Jaganmohan Reddy and Khanna JJ.). Limits: the Indian Kanoon copy lists only twelve judges in its header (omitting A.K. Mukherjea J.) and jumps from para 2253 to the order at para 2263, so the nine-judge 'View by the majority' summary is not in it and I did not see that summary's text. The paragraph numbers are Indian Kanoon's continuous numbering and were not checked against the printed SCC report.

claims.claim: Article 79(3) of the German Basic Law makes inadmissible any amendment of the Basic Law affecting the division of the Federation into Länder, their participation in principle in the legislative process, or the principles laid down in Articles 1 and 20.
claims.source: Basic Law for the Federal Republic of Germany, Article 79(3), official English translation (version including amendments to 22 March 2025), https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/englisch_gg/englisch_gg.html
claims.notes: Read Article 79(3) verbatim in the official translation (the German text is authoritative). 'Eternity clause' (Ewigkeitsklausel) is the common name, not a term in the text. The clause protects the principles laid down in Articles 1 (human dignity; human rights; basic rights binding the state) and 20 (democratic and social federal state; popular sovereignty; rule of law; right to resist), not those articles' full wording. verfassungen.de (https://www.verfassungen.de/gg/gg-a79.htm) shows paragraph 3 in the 1949 text and unchanged since; the 1954 amendment altered paragraph 1 only. The year in this id refers to that 1949 origin.

claims.claim: In judgment C-141 of 26 February 2010 Colombia's Constitutional Court declared unconstitutional in its entirety Law 1354 of 2009, which convened a referendum on permitting a second presidential re-election, finding both procedural defects and that a second re-election, and the third term it would bring, would substitute structural axes of the 1991 Constitution.
claims.source: Corte Constitucional de Colombia, Sentencia C-141 de 2010, 26 February 2010, expediente CRF-003, Magistrado Sustanciador Humberto Antonio Sierra Porto, Part V section 6 ('La sustitución de la Constitución') and Part VI ('Decisión'); https://www.corteconstitucional.gov.co/relatoria/2010/C-141-10.htm
claims.notes: Read the Court's official relatoria text (Spanish). Verified: the header (expediente CRF-003, review of Law 1354 of 2009, Magistrado Sustanciador Sierra Porto, Bogotá, 26 February 2010); the operative part ('Declarar INEXEQUIBLE en su totalidad la Ley 1354 de 2009'); and the conclusion of Part V section 6 that 'una segunda reelección presidencial sustituye ejes estructurales de la Constitución Política', reasoning from the principle of alternation, separation of powers and checks, pluralism and the republican model. The syllabus contrasts this with the 2004 amendment allowing one immediate re-election (Acto Legislativo 02 de 2004), which was not a substitution. The earlier sections of Part V find procedural defects, including in the financing of the citizen initiative and the congressional passage, as Landau (2013) at 202-203 also summarises. The plan's 'referendum on a third presidential term' is substantively right; the law spoke of a second re-election. The signature block records two dissents (salvamento de voto: González Cuervo, Pretelt Chaljub) and three concurrences (aclaración). This is a summary of a long Spanish judgment, not a systematic translation.

claims.claim: Yaniv Roznai's Unconstitutional Constitutional Amendments is a comparative and theoretical study of the explicit and implicit limits on constitutional amendment powers and of courts' role in enforcing them.
claims.source: Yaniv Roznai, Unconstitutional Constitutional Amendments: The Limits of Amendment Powers (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2017, Oxford Constitutional Theory), ISBN 978-0-19-876879-1 (hbk); doi:10.1093/law/9780198768791.001.0001
claims.notes: OUP's online pages returned HTTP 403. Crossref confirms the DOI, title, author, ISBN and an online date of 16 February 2017. The series and a paperback (ISBN 978-0-19-884066-4) come from retailer and OUP product URLs I could not open. The author interview on the IACL-AIDC blog (18 Aug 2017) and a review on constitutional-change.com describe the book's scope: explicit, implicit and supra-constitutional unamendability; the amendment power as a delegated, limited 'secondary constituent power'; and judicial enforcement. I did not read the book, and no chapter or page is verified; the review's p. 196 quotation was not checked.

claims.claim: Landau identifies 'abusive constitutionalism', the use of constitutional amendment and replacement by would-be autocrats to make themselves hard to dislodge and to disable courts and other accountability institutions, and argues that established defences such as militant democracy and the unconstitutional-constitutional-amendment doctrine are often hard to deploy against it or easy to avoid.
claims.source: David Landau, 'Abusive Constitutionalism' (2013) 47 U.C. Davis Law Review 189-260; abstract p. 189, Colombia pp. 200-203, unconstitutional-constitutional-amendments doctrine pp. 231-239; https://lawreview.law.ucdavis.edu/sites/g/files/dgvnsk15026/files/media/documents/47-1_Landau.pdf ; SSRN https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2244629
claims.notes: Downloaded the journal's own PDF (pp. 189-260) and extracted its text. Verified the abstract (p. 189), the table of contents (p. 190) and the Colombian discussion (pp. 200-203). At pp. 202-203 Landau says the Constitutional Court struck down the third-term referendum on procedural and substantive grounds (citing C-141/10), that the decision was complied with and Uribe did not run, and that while 'it is probably too much to say' the Court prevented competitive authoritarianism, it 'probably did prevent a significant erosion of democracy'. His later cases are Venezuela and Hungary. No DOI found (Crossref search); the journal has none that I found.

claims.claim: Waldron argues against strong judicial review of legislation, meaning courts' authority to decline to apply statutes or to strike them down, on outcome-related and democratic-legitimacy grounds, but only for societies meeting four assumptions: working democratic institutions, working judicial institutions, a general commitment to rights, and disagreement about rights.
claims.source: Jeremy Waldron, 'The Core of the Case Against Judicial Review' (2006) 115 Yale Law Journal 1346-1406, abstract p. 1346, strong and weak review p. 1354, four assumptions pp. 1359-1369, non-core cases p. 1401; doi:10.2307/20455656
claims.notes: Verified from a scan of the journal pages (ProQuest reproduction hosted at https://www.humanities.mcmaster.ca/~walucho/3Q3/Waldron.Core%20Case%20Judicial%20Review%20Yale%20LJ.pdf; images read directly): abstract (p. 1346); essay contents (p. 1347: Part II 'Four Assumptions' at 1359, with A Democratic Institutions, B Judicial Institutions, C A Commitment to Rights, D Disagreement About Rights; Parts IV and V outcome- and process-related reasons; Part VII non-core cases at 1401; Conclusion 1406); and p. 1354, 'My target is strong judicial review'. Crossref confirms the DOI, volume 115, issue 6 (April 2006) and first page 1346. The plan's 'for legislative primacy' paraphrases Waldron: the essay targets strong review only, and the abstract says the case 'is not absolute or unconditional' and ends by considering what follows when the conditions fail.

claims.claim: Robert Goodin argues that the principle of enfranchising all affected interests, read coherently, gives a say to everyone who might possibly be affected by any possible decision on any possible agenda, so that in principle virtually everyone would vote on virtually everything, and he discusses second-best institutional approximations of that ideal.
claims.source: Robert E. Goodin, "Enfranchising All Affected Interests, and Its Alternatives", Philosophy & Public Affairs 35(1) (Winter 2007): 40-68; doi:10.1111/j.1088-4963.2007.00098.x; https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1088-4963.2007.00098.x
claims.notes: Bibliographic data verified via Crossref and an archived copy (Wayback, 2021) of the Wiley landing page: vol. 35, issue 1, Winter 2007, pp. 40-68, first published online 23 January 2007; the ANU research portal gives the same. The article has no abstract and the full text is paywalled (Wiley and PhilPapers returned 403), so the argument was NOT read in the article itself. The summary above rests on Koenig-Archibugi, 'How to diagnose democratic deficits' (LSE Research Online, eprint 68641), which quotes Goodin 2007 at p. 64: 'good grounds for thinking that (at least in principle) we should give virtually everyone a vote on virtually everything virtually everywhere in the world', and reports Goodin's 'probably affected' amendment and his second-best (limited world appellate body) and third-best (international-law compensation) arrangements. Page 64 is as quoted there, not checked against the article. Caution for the book: Goodin's principle cuts against any territorially or residence-bounded demos; it does not support residence as the basis of the franchise, and should not be cited as if it did. The plan gave no specific claim for this source.

claims.claim: Claudio López-Guerra's 'Critical Suffrage Doctrine' holds that, in polities with universal suffrage, noncitizen residents should be allowed to vote, excluding nonresident citizens is permissible, blanket disenfranchisement of minors and the mentally impaired cannot be justified, and criminal offenders should not be disenfranchised.
claims.source: Claudio López-Guerra, Democracy and Disenfranchisement: The Morality of Electoral Exclusions (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014), 208 pp., ISBN 978-0-19-870578-9; ch. 4, 'Disenfranchisement on the Basis of Nonresidency and Noncitizenship', pp. 83-108; doi:10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198705789.001.0001; https://academic.oup.com/book/4419
claims.notes: Verified the book abstract (Oxford Academic abstract as reproduced by OpenAlex) and the chapter list with page ranges and DOIs via Crossref (ch. 4 DOI 10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198705789.003.0004, pp. 83-108). The Notre Dame Philosophical Reviews review (Chad Flanders, 2015.07.20) confirms the publisher, year, 208 pp., ISBN, and that ch. 4 argues resident noncitizens should vote and nonresident citizens need not. Oxford Academic returned 403 and the OUP product page could not be fetched, so the book text was not read. The plan's framing ('the vote for all subject to public power') is only partly checked: the abstract supports enfranchising resident noncitizens, but I did not verify that the book grounds this in subjection to public power. The book is not a straightforward defence of universal suffrage: its ch. 2 ('Disenfranchisement on the Basis of Ignorance', pp. 23-60) argues that in some realistic circumstances an alternative excluding most sane adults for being largely uninformed (an 'enfranchisement lottery') is morally acceptable, and the abstract says so. OUP's product URL spells the title 'disfranchisement'.

claims.claim: New Zealand's Electoral Act 1993, s 74(1), qualifies every adult who is either a New Zealand citizen or a permanent resident of New Zealand, and who has at some time resided continuously in New Zealand for at least one year, to be registered as an elector of an electoral district.
claims.source: Electoral Act 1993 (NZ), Public Act 1993 No 87, s 74 (Qualification of electors) and s 73 (Meaning of permanent resident of New Zealand), version as at 27 November 2025; https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/1993/0087/latest/whole.html
claims.notes: Full text of ss 73-74 read in the version as at 27 November 2025 (legislation.govt.nz whole-Act page, read through a Wayback Machine capture of 31 Dec 2025 because the live site returned 403 to automated fetches) and in the reprint as at 1 July 2014 (ILO NATLEX PDF); s 74 is identical in both. Section 73 defines a permanent resident as a person who resides in New Zealand and is not a person to whom s 15 or 16 of the Immigration Act 2009 applies, not obliged to leave New Zealand, and not treated as unlawfully in New Zealand; it does not itself say 'resident visa'. The Electoral Commission reportedly applies it to holders of resident and permanent resident visas, but I did not verify that against a Commission page. Section 74(1)(c) and (2) govern which electorate a person enrols in (one month's residence). I did not check s 60 (who may vote at an election) or the definition of 'adult' in s 3. The plan's description (non-citizen permanent residents voting in national elections, statutory basis) is consistent with s 74.

claims.claim: Article 14 of Chile's Constitution, as amended by Ley 21.773 of October 2025, lets foreigners vote in the cases and forms set by law if they have lived in Chile for more than ten uninterrupted years, counted from obtaining a permanent residence permit and without absences of more than ninety days in any twelve months, and meet the citizen requirements of age eighteen and no afflictive sentence; the change applies from 2026, replacing a five-year requirement.
claims.source: Constitución Política de la República de Chile, art. 14 (texto refundido, Decreto 100 de 2005), as replaced by Ley N° 21.773, 'Modifica la Carta Fundamental en materia de derecho de sufragio de personas extranjeras', Diario Oficial 7 October 2025, and transitional provision 54 (Quincuagésima cuarta); https://www.bcn.cl/leychile/navegar?idNorma=1217272 and https://www.bcn.cl/leychile/navegar?idNorma=242302
claims.notes: Read the full text of Ley 21.773 (promulgated 1 Oct 2025, published 7 Oct 2025) and the current consolidated Constitution (BCN XML, version dated 2026-04-16) through the Biblioteca del Congreso Nacional's official LeyChile services. The current art. 14 reads: foreigners 'avecindados en Chile por más de diez años ininterrumpidos', who meet art. 13(1) (18 years, no afflictive penalty), may vote in the cases and forms the law determines; they count as resident only from obtaining a 'permiso de residencia definitiva' and must not have left the country for more than 90 days in any 12-month period. Transitional provision 54 says the changes to arts. 14 and 15 apply from 2026. The plan's premise is out of date: the widely cited five-year period was the rule only until the 2025 presidential and parliamentary elections (BCN 'Ley Fácil: Cómo votar' guide states this).
