The same BCN guide says foreign voters are not fined for not voting and that the pre-2026 rule applied to presidential and parliamentary elections; the implementing organic law (Ley 18.556) was not read directly.

claims.claim: Article 22(1) TFEU gives every EU citizen residing in another member state the right to vote and to stand as a candidate in municipal elections there under the same conditions as that state's nationals, with the detailed arrangements, including limited derogations, laid down in Council Directive 94/80/EC.
claims.source: Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, art. 22(1) (ex art. 19 TEC), consolidated version OJ C 115, 9.5.2008, p. 57 (CELEX 12008E022); Council Directive 94/80/EC of 19 December 1994, OJ L 368, 31.12.1994, pp. 38-47 (CELEX 31994L0080), arts. 1, 3, 5(3), 12; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/1994/80/oj and https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:12008E022
claims.notes: Full texts read from the EU Publications Office cellar (EUR-Lex itself served a JavaScript challenge). Art. 22 read in the 2008 consolidated TFEU; the 2012/2016 consolidations were not separately fetched. Directive: art. 1(1) scope; art. 1(2) leaves member states' rules on third-country nationals and on their own nationals abroad untouched; art. 3 conditions (EU citizen, non-national, meets the conditions imposed on nationals); art. 5(3) lets member states reserve the office of elected head, deputy or member of the executive of a basic local government unit to their own nationals; art. 12(1) allows residence-period derogations where non-national EU citizens exceeded 20% of voting-age EU citizens on 1 January 1996 (with a specific Belgian provision). Limits: the right covers only EU citizens and only municipal (and, under art. 22(2), European Parliament) elections, not national elections or third-country nationals. Later amendments to the directive (annex updates for new member states) were not checked.

claims.claim: Switzerland's Federal Constitution vests executive authority in a seven-member Federal Council elected by the Federal Assembly for four-year terms that reaches its decisions as a collegial body, and composes the Council of States, a chamber of equal standing with the National Council, of 46 cantonal representatives: two from each canton and one from each of six named cantons.
claims.source: Federal Constitution of the Swiss Confederation of 18 April 1999 (SR 101), arts. 148(2), 150, 174, 175 and 177(1), status as of 3 March 2024 (English translation); https://www.fedlex.admin.ch/eli/cc/1999/404/en
claims.notes: Read the English text from the Fedlex filestore (latest English consolidation, status 3 March 2024, located via the Fedlex SPARQL endpoint). Art. 148(2): two chambers of equal standing. Art. 150: 46 representatives; Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden elect one each, other cantons two; cantons set the electoral rules. Art. 174: the Federal Council is the supreme governing and executive authority. Art. 175: seven members, elected by the Federal Assembly after each National Council general election for four years, with regard to appropriate representation of geographical and language regions. Art. 177(1): 'The Federal Council reaches its decisions as a collegial body.' Fedlex states that English is not an official language and the translation has no legal force; the German, French and Italian texts are authoritative. Nothing here was checked about the absence of a confidence procedure or about the Council's practical operation.

claims.claim: Uruguay was governed from 1952 to 1966 by a purely collegial nine-member National Council of Government (six seats for the leading party, three for the runner-up) under its 1952 Constitution, abandoned for a presidential system in the 1966 Constitution amid economic decline, inflation and social unrest; the colegiado was blamed, but historian Martin Weinstein argues the failure lay in political leadership rather than the collegial form.
claims.source: Martin Weinstein, "Uruguay, Colegiado", in Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture (Gale; edition not stated on the page), via Encyclopedia.com; https://www.encyclopedia.com/humanities/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/uruguay-colegiado
claims.notes: Read the full entry. It states: the 1952 Constitution created the National Council of Government of nine members, six for the majority party and three for the next; it was a 'Colegiado Integral' with no presidency; Uruguay was governed under it 'from 1952 until 1966'; the Blancos' 1958 win produced little policy change because of near-total power sharing; 'in the midst of a declining economy, growing inflation, and increased social unrest, Uruguay returned to a presidential system with the adoption of the 1966 Constitution'; and 'On both occasions the colegiado was blamed for the problem, but ... the problem rested in political leadership, not the colegiado.' The plan's '1952-1967' and 'abolished 1967' are not what this source says; the date the 1966 constitution took effect or the council left office (1967) was not verified. Weinstein is also author of Uruguay: The Politics of Failure (1975), cited in the entry's bibliography. The edition of the encyclopedia is inferred, not verified: the entry carries an 'Additional Bibliography' (a 1995 work), consistent with the 2nd edition (Gale, 2008). The 1952 constitutional text itself was not read; the entry's bibliography (e.g., Milton Vanger, APSR 48(2), 1954, 500-513) was not checked. Caution: this source supports calling the colegiado a contested cautionary case, but it expressly disputes that the collegial form caused the failure.

claims.claim: Angela Y. Davis argues for prison abolition through 'decarceration': not prison-like substitutes such as electronically monitored house arrest, but a constellation of alternative institutions—transformed schools, free physical and mental health care, and a justice system based on reparation and reconciliation—meant eventually to crowd the prison out.
claims.source: Angela Y. Davis, Are Prisons Obsolete? (New York: Seven Stories Press, 2003), 128 pp., ISBN 978-1-58322-581-3; publisher page https://www.sevenstories.com/books/2907-are-prisons-obsolete ; authorised excerpt 'Abolitionist Alternatives', Bookforum, 23 June 2020, https://www.bookforum.com/politics/an-excerpt-from-are-prisons-obsolete-24084
claims.notes: Publisher page checked: paperback ISBN 9781583225813, 128 pp., publish date listed 2003-08-05 (ebook ISBN 9781609801045); the description says Davis 'argues forthrightly for "decarceration," and argues for the transformation of the society as a whole'. The quoted argument was read in Bookforum's excerpt, marked 'Excerpted from Are Prisons Obsolete? by Angela Y. Davis (2003). Reprinted with permission from Seven Stories Press', which contains the 'constellation of alternative strategies and institutions' and 'positing decarceration as our overarching strategy' passage. The excerpt corresponds to the book's 'Abolitionist Alternatives' material, but the chapter number and page were not verified. The book is an argument, not empirical evidence that abolition works.

claims.claim: Ruth Wilson Gilmore argues that California's prison buildup, which proceeded while crime rates were falling, was produced by surpluses of finance capital, labor, land and state capacity arising from the state's economic crises.
claims.source: Ruth Wilson Gilmore, Golden Gulag: Prisons, Surplus, Crisis, and Opposition in Globalizing California (Berkeley: University of California Press, 2007; American Crossroads series), 412 pp., ISBN 978-0-520-24201-2 (paperback); https://www.ucpress.edu/books/golden-gulag/paper
claims.notes: Verified bibliographic data and the argument only from the UC Press book page: publication date Jan 2007, 1st edition, 412 pp., ISBN 9780520242012 (listed as paperback), American Crossroads; description says the book explains the buildup through 'surpluses of finance capital, labor, land, and state capacity', notes 'a crime rate that has been falling steadily for decades', and quotes a state analyst calling it 'the biggest prison building project in the history of the world'. Chapters: Prologue; 1 Introduction; 2 The California Political Economy; 3 The Prison Fix; 4 Crime, Croplands, and Capitalism; 5 Mothers Reclaiming Our Children; 6 What Is to Be Done?; Epilogue. The book text was not read (Google Books rate-limited; only unauthorised copies surfaced, which were not used). The commonly quoted figures (California prison population up nearly 500 percent 1982-2000; twenty-three major new prisons since 1984) appear in search snippets attributed to ch. 1 but are NOT verified here and should not be printed without checking an authorised copy. The 'more than 450%' US figure is the publisher's blurb, not checked in the book. The claim follows the publisher's description; check it against the introduction before printing.

claims.claim: The Dutch parliamentary inquiry committee on childcare benefits found that fundamental principles of the rule of law were violated in administering the benefit, faulting not only the tax administration's benefits service but also the legislature and the administrative courts, and found that a group-wise, all-or-nothing recovery approach wrongly branded parents as intentional fraudsters.
claims.source: Parlementaire ondervragingscommissie Kinderopvangtoeslag, Ongekend onrecht (Verslag), Kamerstukken II 2020/21, 35 510, nr. 2, 17 December 2020, pp. 7-8 ('Constateringen: De rechtsstaat in het geding'); https://zoek.officielebekendmakingen.nl/kst-35510-2.html ; PDF https://www.tweedekamer.nl/sites/default/files/atoms/files/20201217_eindverslag_parlementaire_ondervragingscommissie_kinderopvangtoeslag.pdf
claims.notes: Read the full report PDF from the Tweede Kamer (132 numbered pages) and confirmed the same text in the official publication (Kamerstuk 35510, nr. 2, officielebekendmakingen.nl). Covering letter dated 17 December 2020, chair Van Dam. p. 7: 'De commissie constateert dat bij de uitvoering van de kinderopvangtoeslag grondbeginselen van de rechtsstaat zijn geschonden. Dit verwijt treft niet alleen de uitvoering - specifiek de Belastingdienst/Toeslagen - maar ook de wetgever en de rechtspraak.' The same page says the legislature passed rigid law without a hardship clause and with too little attention to proportionality; that the group-wise approach, the 'alles-of-niets' approach and the use of 'opzet/grove schuld' seriously breached the principle of doing justice to individual situations; and that parents were 'ten onrechte gebrandmerkt als opzettelijke fraudeurs'. pp. 7-8: administrative jurisprudence for years sustained the rigid execution; p. 8: information to parliament was repeatedly late, incomplete and incorrect. Translations are mine. The body was formally a 'parlementaire ondervraging' with sworn hearings, which the plan calls an 'inquiry'. This check did not verify victim counts or compensation figures, which the report's conclusions do not state.

claims.claim: The Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme found that Robodebt, which raised welfare debts by averaging employer-reported income data from the Australian Taxation Office, was 'a crude and cruel mechanism, neither fair nor legal', and records that the government refunded $746 million to some 381,000 people and wrote off debts totalling $1.751 billion.
claims.source: Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme (Commissioner Catherine Holmes AC SC), Report, 7 July 2023, Vol. 1, 'Overview of Robodebt', pp. xxvi-xxix; ISBN 978-1-921241-58-1 (online); https://robodebt.royalcommission.gov.au/publications/report (archived PDF: https://web.archive.org/web/20230707033019/https://robodebt.royalcommission.gov.au/system/files/2023-07/report-volume-1.pdf)
claims.notes: Read Vol. 1 in full-text PDF (Wayback capture of 7 July 2023 of the Commission's own file; the Commission site timed out on live fetch). Letter of transmittal dated 7 July 2023, signed by Catherine Holmes AC SC; it also says a sealed additional chapter recommends referral of individuals for civil action or criminal prosecution. p. xxvi: the scheme 'was devised without regard to the social security law' and averaging was 'essentially unfair, treating many people as though they had received income at a time when they had not'. p. xxix: in September 2019 the Solicitor-General advised averaged PAYG data could not support a debt without further evidence; the Federal Court in Amato declared averaged PAYG income 'not capable of satisfying a decision-maker of the existence of a debt'; refunds of $746 million to some 381,000 individuals and write-offs of $1.751 billion; and 'Robodebt was a crude and cruel mechanism, neither fair nor legal, and it made many people feel like criminals.' Page placement is approximate because the PDF uses two-page spreads (the quote sits on the spread paginated xxviii-xxix). The number of volumes and recommendations was not verified here.

claims.claim: In ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (28 April 1976), a 4-1 majority of India's Supreme Court held that while the Presidential Order of 27 June 1975 under Article 359(1) was in force, no detainee had standing to seek habeas corpus under Article 226 to challenge a detention order, even as illegal or mala fide; Justice H. R. Khanna dissented, holding that Article 21 is not the sole repository of the right to life and liberty and that the State has no power to deprive anyone of life or liberty without the authority of law.
claims.source: Additional District Magistrate, Jabalpur v. S. S. Shukla, Supreme Court of India, 28 April 1976, (1976) 2 SCC 521; AIR 1976 SC 1207; 1976 SCR 172 (majority holding, headnote [477 E-F] and final order; Khanna J dissenting, headnote [266 F, 302 H], [268 C-D], [269 H-270 C]); https://indiankanoon.org/doc/1735815/
claims.notes: Read the full judgment as reproduced on Indian Kanoon, which carries the reported headnote with SCR page markers; the official Supreme Court PDF was not located (the JUDIS file surfaced by search was a different case). Bench: Ray CJ, Khanna, Beg, Chandrachud and Bhagwati JJ; the majority was Ray CJ, Beg, Chandrachud and Bhagwati JJ. The majority order: 'In view of the Presidential order dated 27 June 1975 no person has any locus standi to move any writ petition under Article 226 before a High Court for habeas corpus ... to challenge the legality of an order of detention on the ground that the order is not under or in compliance with the Act or is illegal or is vitiated by malafides'. It also upheld s. 16A(9) of the Maintenance of Internal Security Act. Khanna J's headnote includes 'Even in the absence of Art. 21 in the Constitution, the State has got no power to deprive a person of his life or liberty without the authority of law' and the 'appeal to the brooding spirit of the law' passage [304 G]. The SCR cite is given as Indian Kanoon lists it; it is often cited as [1976] Supp. SCR 172, but 'Supp.' was not verified. Plan wording 'habeas corpus suspended' is loose: the Court held the right to move courts to enforce Article 21 was suspended by the Presidential Order, so detainees lacked standing; the writ itself was not abolished. Its later overruling (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017) was not checked here.

claims.claim: India's Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, section 40, amended Article 359 so that a presidential order during an emergency can no longer suspend the right to move courts to enforce Articles 20 and 21, a change its Statement of Objects and Reasons says was meant 'to put the right to life and liberty on a secure footing'.
claims.source: The Constitution (Forty-fourth Amendment) Act, 1978 (assented 30 April 1979), s. 40 (amendment of art. 359), with Statement of Objects and Reasons para. 8; Legislative Department, Government of India, https://cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in/s380537a945c7aaa788ccfcdf1b99b5d8f/uploads/2023/03/2023030242-2.pdf ; current Constitution of India art. 359(1)-(1A)
claims.notes: Read the Act's full text and Statement of Objects and Reasons in the Legislative Department's PDF (hosted on the Government of India's s3waas CDN, the same bucket that hosts the Department's official Constitution text). s. 40(a): in art. 359(1) and (1A) 'the rights conferred by Part III' becomes 'the rights conferred by Part III (except articles 20 and 21)'; s. 40(b) inserts cl. (1B). The current art. 359(1) wording with '(except articles 20 and 21)' was confirmed on Indian Kanoon's Constitution text. SOR para. 8: 'to put the right to life and liberty on a secure footing, it would be provided that the power to suspend the right to move the court for the enforcement of a fundamental right cannot be exercised in respect of the fundamental right to life and liberty'. SOR para. 6 also records the narrowing of emergency grounds to war, external aggression or armed rebellion. The Act is titled 1978 but its date of assent is 30 April 1979; commencement was by notification with different dates for different provisions, and the commencement date of s. 40 was not verified. The SOR is appended to the Constitution (Forty-fifth Amendment) Bill, 1978 (Bill No. 88 of 1978), enacted as the Forty-fourth Amendment, as the document itself states.

claims.claim: In the first Hussainara Khatoon judgment (12 February 1979), India's Supreme Court, responding to reports of Bihar undertrials held for three to ten years without trial for offences that might carry only months' punishment, directed their release on personal bond without monetary obligation and held that speedy trial, though not enumerated, is implicit in Article 21's guarantee of a reasonable, fair and just procedure.
claims.source: Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar, Supreme Court of India, 12 February 1979, (1980) 1 SCC 81; AIR 1979 SC 1360; [1979] 3 SCR 169, at 173 and 179H-180F (Bhagwati J for himself and Koshal J; Pathak J separately); https://indiankanoon.org/doc/1007347/
claims.notes: Read the full judgment as reproduced on Indian Kanoon with its reported headnote and SCR page markers. Headnote holding 2: 'Though speedy trial is not specifically enumerated as a fundamental right, it is implicit in the broad sweep and content of Art. 21 ... an integral part of the fundamental right to life and liberty' [179 H, 180 C, F], relying on Maneka Gandhi. At SCR 173, Bhagwati J: offences 'which, even if proved, would not warrant punishment for more than a few months, perhaps for a year or two', yet undertrials were in jail 'for periods ranging from three to ten years'. The Court proceeded on Indian Express reports of 8-9 January 1979 because Bihar did not appear, and directed release on personal bond without monetary obligation as an exceptional interim measure because some had been held 'for offences for which the punishment would in all probability be less than the period of their detention'. The plan's 'detained longer than the maximum sentence' is only partly this judgment's wording; the express 'maximum period' finding appears in the later judgment of 4 May 1979, (1980) 1 SCC 115, AIR 1979 SC 1819 (headnote read). The series also includes the judgment of 9 March 1979, listed by Indian Kanoon as (1980) 1 SCC 98, AIR 1979 SC 1369 (free legal aid under arts. 21 and 39A).

claims.claim: The UN General Assembly adopted the revised Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Nelson Mandela Rules) on 17 December 2015; they require every prisoner to be treated with respect for their inherent dignity, state that imprisonment is afflictive in itself and that the prison system must not aggravate that suffering, and prohibit indefinite and prolonged solitary confinement, defined as more than 15 consecutive days of 22 or more hours a day without meaningful human contact.
claims.source: UN General Assembly, Resolution 70/175, 'United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (the Nelson Mandela Rules)', adopted 17 December 2015, A/RES/70/175 (distributed 8 January 2016), annex, rules 1, 3, 43(1), 44 (pp. 8, 16-17); https://documents.un.org/api/symbol/access?s=A/RES/70/175&l=en&t=pdf
claims.notes: Read the official UN document (33 pp.). Header: A/RES/70/175, distributed 8 January 2016; 'Resolution adopted by the General Assembly on 17 December 2015 [on the report of the Third Committee (A/70/490)]'. Rule 1 (p. 8): respect due to inherent dignity; no torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. Rule 3 (p. 8): imprisonment is 'afflictive by the very fact' of deprivation of liberty and the prison system shall not aggravate the suffering inherent in it. Rule 43(1) (p. 16): prohibits indefinite and prolonged solitary confinement, dark or constantly lit cells, corporal punishment or reduced diet or water, and collective punishment. Rule 44 (p. 17): definitions quoted in the claim. Rule 4(1) states the purposes of imprisonment as protecting society and reducing recidivism, achievable only through reintegration. Limits: a GA resolution; preliminary observation 1 (p. 7) says the rules set out 'what is generally accepted as being good principles and practice', not a model system, and they are not a treaty.

claims.claim: Gabriel 'Jack' Chin argues that the network of collateral consequences of conviction—restrictions on civil rights, employment, public benefits, residence and legal status—has practically revived the old punishment of civil death and should be treated as constitutional punishment rather than non-punitive civil regulation.
claims.source: Gabriel J. Chin, "The New Civil Death: Rethinking Punishment in the Era of Mass Conviction", University of Pennsylvania Law Review 160(6) (2012): 1789-1833; https://scholarship.law.upenn.edu/penn_law_review/vol160/iss6/6 ; SSRN abstract 2072736
claims.notes: Journal, volume, issue, pages (1789-1833) and year verified from repository metadata via OpenAlex, which also carries the abstract; no DOI exists. The abstract says collateral consequences are generally treated by courts as non-punitive civil regulation, that they 'have practically revived the traditional punishment of civil death', and that 'The new civil death ... should be understood as constitutional punishment'; it also notes most people convicted of felonies are not sentenced to prison. The full text was not read: the Penn Law repository now redirects to a JavaScript search page and SSRN returned 403. No page pinpoints are given for that reason. Related: Chin was the Reporter for the Uniform Law Commission's Collateral Consequences of Conviction Act (named in the Act's drafting-committee list).

claims.claim: The Uniform Law Commission's Collateral Consequences of Conviction Act (last amended 2010; redesignated a model act in 2022) would require states to collect and publish all collateral consequences, notify defendants of them at charge, plea, sentencing and release, construe ambiguous provisions as discretionary disqualifications rather than automatic sanctions, decide disqualifications by individualized assessment, and offer an 'order of limited relief' and a 'certificate of restoration of rights'.
claims.source: National Conference of Commissioners on Uniform State Laws (Uniform Law Commission), Uniform Collateral Consequences of Conviction Act (Last Amended or Revised in 2010), approved at the annual conference, Chicago, 9-16 July 2010, with prefatory note and comments (ULC copy dated 24 September 2024), ss. 4-8, 10-11; https://www.uniformlaws.org/HigherLogic/System/DownloadDocumentFile.ashx?DocumentFileKey=663b42c8-f9d1-f365-dd70-8f71ae3a3697 (enactment kit: https://www.uniformlaws.org/viewdocument/enactment-kit-84?CommunityKey=74d9914f-f15e-49aa-a5b0-f15f6e5f258a&tab=librarydocuments)
claims.notes: Read the ULC's own text with comments (42 pp.). Cover: 'Last Amended or Revised in 2010', approved July 9-16, 2010, and a note that 'The conference changed the designation of the Collateral Consequences of Conviction Act from Uniform to Model as approved by the Executive Committee on July 7, 2022'. The plan did not know of the redesignation; the ULC page now titles it 'Collateral Consequences of Conviction Act' and tags it #ModelAct. The 2009 original approval is reported by secondary sources but was not verified on a ULC page (an April 2009 committee draft exists). Sections: s. 4 identification, collection and publication (p. 10); s. 5 notice at charge and guilty plea (p. 13); s. 6 notice at sentencing and upon release (p. 18); s. 7 collateral sanctions only by statute, ordinance or authorised rule, ambiguity construed as disqualification (p. 20); s. 8 individualized assessment, conduct considered only if substantially related (p. 20); s. 10 order of limited relief, petitionable at or before sentencing (p. 27); s. 11 certificate of restoration of rights after a bracketed five years (p. 30); s. 12 lists sanctions not relievable. Reporter: Gabriel 'Jack' Chin. This is a proposal for state enactment, not law anywhere by itself; which states enacted it was not checked.

claims.claim: John Pratt argues that Finland, Norway and Sweden's penal exceptionalism—low imprisonment rates and humane prison conditions—grew from cultures of equality embedded through the universalism of the Scandinavian welfare state, and that declines in social solidarity, security and homogeneity put it at risk, Sweden most of all.
claims.source: John Pratt, "Scandinavian Exceptionalism in an Era of Penal Excess: Part I: The Nature and Roots of Scandinavian Exceptionalism", British Journal of Criminology 48(2) (2008): 119-137, doi:10.1093/bjc/azm072; and "... Part II: Does Scandinavian Exceptionalism Have a Future?", British Journal of Criminology 48(3) (2008): 275-292, doi:10.1093/bjc/azm073
claims.notes: Both parts verified via Crossref (titles, volume, issues, pages, DOIs; published online 6 and 24 December 2007, in the 2008 volume) and their abstracts via OpenAlex. Part I abstract: exceptionalism is 'low rates of imprisonment and humane prison conditions', rooted in 'the cultures of equality ... embedded in their social fabrics through the universalism of the Scandinavian welfare state'. Part II abstract: all three countries have experienced 'declines in earlier levels of social solidarity, security and homogeneity, jeopardizing the future' of low imprisonment and humane conditions; 'Sweden is now most at risk'. Full texts (OUP) were not read, so no page pinpoints. The papers cover Finland, Norway and Sweden, not Denmark. Pratt's thesis has been contested in later literature, which this check did not review.

claims.claim: Using random assignment of cases to judges in Norway, Bhuller, Dahl, Løken and Mogstad estimate that imprisonment cut the probability of reoffending within five years by 29 percentage points; the decline came from defendants who were not working before incarceration, whose job-training participation rose 35 points and five-year employment 36 points, while previously employed defendants saw no significant change in reoffending and an immediate, lasting employment drop of about 30 points.
claims.source: Manudeep Bhuller, Gordon B. Dahl, Katrine V. Løken and Magne Mogstad, "Incarceration, Recidivism, and Employment", Journal of Political Economy 128(4) (2020): 1269-1324, doi:10.1086/705330; figures from the authors' manuscript of 11 February 2019, pp. 1-3 (https://econweb.ucsd.edu/~gdahl/papers/incarceration-recidivism-employment.pdf)
claims.notes: Journal data verified via Crossref (vol. 128, no. 4, April 2020, pp. 1269-1324). The published abstract (via OpenAlex) confirms: random judge design and Norwegian panel data; reoffending probability down 29 percentage points and criminal charges down 11 over five years; OLS reaches the opposite conclusion; the decline is driven by individuals not working before incarceration, who increase participation in employment programs and raise future employment and earnings; previously employed individuals experience lasting negative employment effects. The exact subgroup figures come from the authors' manuscript dated 11 February 2019 (read in full via a Wayback capture of Dahl's UCSD page), not the typeset article, whose numbers may differ slightly: for the previously non-employed, job-training participation +35 points, employment within five years +36 points (the text elsewhere says 'nearly 40' for ever-employed by year five), reoffending within five years down 43 points (from 96 to 50 percent); for the previously employed (working in at least one of the past five years, roughly half the sample), no significant effect on reoffending and an immediate 30-point employment drop lasting to five years, mostly from losing the pre-prison job. Limits: IV estimates apply to 'compliers', defendants whose sentence depends on the judge's stringency; the sample is 33,548 randomly assigned non-confession cases (23,373 defendants, 500 judges); the setting is Norway's rehabilitation-oriented prisons, and the authors do not claim the result generalises to other systems.

claims.claim: Sustainable Development Goal target 16.9, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2015, reads: "By 2030, provide legal identity for all, including birth registration."
claims.source: United Nations General Assembly, Transforming our world: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, A/RES/70/1 (adopted 25 September 2015), Goal 16, target 16.9, p. 25 of 35; https://docs.un.org/en/A/RES/70/1
claims.notes: Read the official A/RES/70/1 PDF from the UN Official Document System (documents.un.org symbol access); document dated 21 October 2015, resolution adopted 25 September 2015; target 16.9 text verified verbatim on p. 25. The global indicator 16.9.1 ("Proportion of children under 5 years of age whose births have been registered with a civil authority, by age") was read on the UN DESA SDG page https://sdgs.un.org/goals/goal16; its adopting resolution (the global indicator framework) was not separately checked. The plan's description is accurate. A target is a political commitment with a 2030 horizon, not a binding obligation, and says nothing about whether birth registration is achieved or whether services are gated on it.

claims.claim: The 1954 Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons defines a stateless person as someone "not considered as a national by any State under the operation of its law" (Art. 1(1)) and requires contracting states to issue identity papers to any stateless person in their territory who lacks a valid travel document (Art. 27).
claims.source: Convention relating to the Status of Stateless Persons, New York, 28 September 1954, entered into force 6 June 1960, 360 UNTS 117 (No. 5158), Art. 1(1) at p. 136, Art. 27 at p. 150, Art. 32 at p. 154; https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetailsII.aspx?src=TREATY&mtdsg_no=V-3&chapter=5
claims.notes: Read the English treaty text in the UNTS volume 360 PDF from treaties.un.org (volume-360-I-5158-English.pdf) and the UN Treaty Collection status page. Verified verbatim: Art. 1(1) definition (p. 136), Art. 27 identity papers (p. 150), Art. 28 travel documents for those lawfully staying (p. 152), Art. 32 naturalization to be facilitated 'as far as possible' (p. 154). Art. 1(2) excludes some groups (e.g. persons receiving protection from other UN agencies). The UNTC status page listed 99 parties on the retrieval date; the count changes over time and should not be printed. The plan named the treaty without a pinpoint; the claim is limited to what the text states and binds only states parties.

claims.claim: The 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness requires a contracting state to grant its nationality to a person born in its territory who would otherwise be stateless (Art. 1(1), at birth or on application subject to permitted conditions), treats foundlings as born in the territory to nationals (Art. 2), and bars deprivation of nationality that would render a person stateless (Art. 8(1)), subject to listed exceptions and a fair-hearing requirement (Art. 8(2)-(4)).
claims.source: Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness, New York, 30 August 1961, entered into force 13 December 1975, 989 UNTS 175 (No. 14458), Art. 1 at p. 176, Art. 2 at p. 177, Arts. 8-9 at p. 179; https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetailsII.aspx?src=TREATY&mtdsg_no=V-4&chapter=5
claims.notes: Read the English text in the UNTS volume 989 PDF from treaties.un.org (volume-989-I-14458-English.pdf) and the UNTC status page. Verified verbatim: Art. 1(1) (p. 176), Art. 2 foundlings (p. 177), Art. 8(1)-(4) and Art. 9 ban on deprivation on racial, ethnic, religious or political grounds (p. 179). Important limit for the book: the Convention does NOT make statelessness-creating deprivation absolutely unlawful - Art. 8(2) permits it for nationality obtained by misrepresentation or fraud (and loss under Art. 7(4)-(5)), and Art. 8(3) lets states that declared it at signature/ratification retain grounds such as conduct seriously prejudicial to vital state interests. Art. 1(1)(b) also allows nationality on application subject to conditions (e.g. habitual residence up to five years before application, no conviction for certain offences). The UNTC listed 82 parties on the retrieval date; do not print the count.

claims.claim: The UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights' General Comment No. 4 (1991) says the right to housing should not be read narrowly as 'merely having a roof over one's head' but as the right to live somewhere in security, peace and dignity, and lists seven aspects of adequacy: legal security of tenure; availability of services, materials, facilities and infrastructure; affordability; habitability; accessibility; location; and cultural adequacy.
claims.source: UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, General Comment No. 4: The right to adequate housing (art. 11(1) of the Covenant), sixth session (1991), contained in E/1992/23; reproduced in Compilation of General Comments, HRI/GEN/1/Rev.9 (Vol. I), 27 May 2008, beginning at p. 11, paras 7-8 at pp. 12-13; https://docs.un.org/en/HRI/GEN/1/Rev.9(Vol.I)
claims.notes: Read the official UN compilation HRI/GEN/1/Rev.9 (Vol. I) (dated 27 May 2008) from the UN Official Document System; its footnote states GC4 is 'Contained in document E/1992/23'. Could not retrieve E/1992/23 itself (the ODS request failed and the OHCHR and Refworld copies returned 403). Verified verbatim para 7 (roof over one's head; security, peace and dignity) and para 8(a)-(g) (the seven aspects). The exact adoption day (often given as 13 December 1991) was not seen in a primary source and is omitted; the compilation gives 'Sixth session (1991)'. The plan's description ('adequacy of housing') is accurate. A general comment is the treaty body's authoritative interpretation, not a binding treaty text, and the Committee says adequacy is determined partly by social, economic, cultural, climatic and ecological factors.

claims.claim: CESCR General Comment No. 14 (2000) states that the right to health contains four interrelated and essential elements - availability, accessibility (non-discrimination, physical accessibility, economic accessibility or affordability, and information accessibility), acceptability and quality - whose precise application depends on conditions in each State party.
claims.source: UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, General Comment No. 14 (2000): The right to the highest attainable standard of health (article 12), E/C.12/2000/4, 11 August 2000, para 12, pp. 4-5; https://docs.un.org/en/E/C.12/2000/4
claims.notes: Read the official E/C.12/2000/4 PDF from the UN Official Document System (twenty-second session, Geneva, 25 April-12 May 2000). Para 12(a)-(d) verified verbatim, including the qualifier that 'the precise application of which will depend on the conditions prevailing in a particular State party' and that availability varies with the State's developmental level. Note some pages of the ODS PDF carry the running header 'E/CN.4/2000/4' (a typographical artefact in the document itself); the cover symbol is E/C.12/2000/4. The plan's 'AAAQ' shorthand is a common label, not the Comment's own acronym. Interpretive, not binding treaty text.

claims.claim: India's Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Audit of Schemes Rules, 2011 require a social audit of works in every Gram Panchayat at least once in six months, facilitated by a state Social Audit Unit that must be independent of the implementing agency, with resource persons who must not reside in the audited Panchayat and who, with primary stakeholders, verify muster rolls and payments by contacting the wage seekers named in them.
claims.source: Ministry of Rural Development (India), Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Audit of Schemes Rules, 2011, notification G.S.R. 495(E), 30 June 2011, Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, Sec. 3(i), pp. 6-9ff; rules 3(1), 4(1)-(2), 5(1)-(4), 6(2)(i), 6(4), 6(8)-(9); https://mnregaweb4.nic.in/netnrega/SocialAudit/guidelines/document/MGNREGS%20Audit%20of%20Scheme%20Rules,%202011.pdf
claims.notes: Read the scanned Gazette notification hosted on the Ministry's NREGA portal (image pages read directly; no text layer). Verified: made under s. 24(1) of the MGNREGA 2005 in consultation with the CAG; rule 1(2) audit of schemes includes social audit; rule 3(1) at least once in six months per Gram Panchayat; rule 4(1) independent Social Audit Unit; rule 4(2)(d) verification of records with primary stakeholders and work sites; rule 5(1)-(2) independence and no interference by the implementing agency; rule 5(4) resource persons not residents of the same Panchayat; rule 6(2)(i) verify muster rolls 'by contacting the wage seekers whose names are entered'; rule 6(8)-(9) reports displayed in the local language and action-taken reports read out. India Code's copy could not be reached (connection refused). The plan said these show 'recipient-side verification in practice': the Rules establish the legal design of recipient-side verification, not that audits are held, independent or effective anywhere; implementation evidence (e.g. CAG or state audit reports) was not checked. This entry covers half of plan item 6; MKSS is the separate entry goetz-jenkins-mkss-jan-sunwai-2007.

claims.claim: Goetz and Jenkins describe the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan's public hearings (jan sunwai), held periodically since 1994 around Rajsamand district in Rajasthan, at which official records of local public works are read aloud and the workers listed on employment registers testify whether they actually worked and were paid.
claims.source: Anne Marie Goetz and Rob Jenkins, 'Citizen activism and public accountability: lessons from case studies in India', ch. 4 in Alnoor Ebrahim and Edward Weisband (eds), Global Accountabilities: Participation, Pluralism, and Public Ethics (Cambridge University Press, 2007), pp. 65-86, doi:10.1017/CBO9780511490903.005; manuscript version read at https://accountabilityindia.in/sites/default/files/document-library/99_1237218572.pdf
claims.notes: Bibliographic details (chapter 4, pp. 65-86, CUP 2007, DOI) verified on the Cambridge Core chapter page. The text read is an unpaginated manuscript of the chapter hosted by Accountability Initiative (Centre for Policy Research); it states it is an updated and abridged version of Goetz & Jenkins, 'Hybrid Forms of Accountability', Public Management Review 3(3) (2001) 363-383 (doi:10.1080/14616670110051957, verified via Crossref, not read). The printed chapter's wording and page numbers were not checked, so no page pinpoint is given; the passages relied on are in the chapter's section on the Rajasthan public hearings (records procured, workers on daily registers contacted, details read aloud, residents testify whether their experience differs from the record). The better-known Jenkins & Goetz, 'Accounts and accountability', Third World Quarterly 20(3) (1999) 603-622, doi:10.1080/01436599913712, exists (Crossref) but its text was paywalled and not read. MKSS's own website was not used. This is an academic account by sympathetic observers of a non-state practice; it does not measure outcomes, and the chapter itself says hearings were 'dramatic, but infrequent'. Covers the MKSS half of plan item 6.

claims.claim: Persad, Wertheimer and Emanuel propose a 'complete lives system' for allocating very scarce medical interventions that combines youngest-first (modified to prioritise adolescents and young adults over infants), prognosis (saving the most life-years), saving the most lives, lottery and instrumental value.
claims.source: Govind Persad, Alan Wertheimer and Ezekiel J. Emanuel, 'Principles for allocation of scarce medical interventions', The Lancet 373(9661) (31 January 2009) 423-431, doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(09)60137-9
claims.notes: Abstract read on PubMed (PMID 19186274); full text read via an Internet Archive capture (6 October 2023) of the Lancet full-text page because thelancet.com is paywalled. Verified: eight simple principles in four categories; the section 'The complete lives system' names its five principles (youngest-first, prognosis, save the most lives, lottery, instrumental value) and the modification favouring adolescents and young adults over infants (with a figure); the 'Prognosis or life-years' section says prognosis allocation 'aims to save the most life-years'. Page pinpoints within 423-431 were not visible in the HTML. The plan's gloss that the system 'counts life-years' is only partly right: life-years enter through the prognosis principle, but the system's distinctive feature is age-based priority, and it expressly rejects QALY/DALY allocation. Relevant to the book because it uses age and prognosis, which touch the forbidden 'generalized lifespan' key.

claims.claim: Emanuel and colleagues recommended during Covid-19 that maximizing benefits - saving the most lives and, as a subordinate aim, maximizing post-treatment length of life - be the most important value, and that among patients with similar prognoses scarce resources be allocated by random selection such as a lottery rather than first-come, first-served.
claims.source: Ezekiel J. Emanuel, Govind Persad, Ross Upshur, Beatriz Thome, Michael Parker, Aaron Glickman, Cathy Zhang, Connor Boyle, M. Smith and J.P. Phillips, 'Fair Allocation of Scarce Medical Resources in the Time of Covid-19', New England Journal of Medicine 382(21) (21 May 2020; online 23 March 2020) 2049-2055, doi:10.1056/NEJMsb2005114, Recommendations 1-3
claims.notes: nejm.org returned 403; full text read via an Internet Archive capture of the NEJM full-text page dated 1 April 2020; bibliographic data checked on PubMed (PMID 32202722) and Crossref. Verified verbatim: Recommendation 1 (maximizing benefits most important; 'saving the most lives and ... maximizing improvements in individuals' post-treatment length of life'; lives prioritised, length of life 'a subordinate aim' relevant only between patients with similar survival likelihood; quality-adjusted life-years not to be used in the emergency; withdrawing a ventilator to give it to others is justifiable); Recommendation 2 (priority for front-line health workers for instrumental value); Recommendation 3 (random allocation among similar prognoses, not first-come, first-served). Page pinpoints within 2049-2055 were not visible in the HTML. The plan's phrase 'includes maximising life-years' is accurate but the article ranks life-years below number of lives saved. It is an ethics recommendation, not law.

claims.claim: Jon Elster argues that lotteries are a defensible way to allocate goods or burdens when there are no reasons to choose one candidate over another - when candidates are equally good, when finer screening would cost more than it gains, or when the claims are incommensurable.
claims.source: Jon Elster, Solomonic Judgements: Studies in the Limitations of Rationality (Cambridge University Press and Editions de la Maison des Sciences de l'Homme, 1989), ix + 232 pp., ISBN 0-521-37457-X (hb), 0-521-37608-4 (pb), ch. II 'Taming chance: randomization in individual and social decisions'; argument read in its lecture version: Elster, 'Taming Chance: Randomization in Individual and Social Decisions', The Tanner Lectures on Human Values IX (1988) 105-179, at 109 and 162-164; https://tannerlectures.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/Elster88.pdf
claims.notes: Book bibliography verified from Library of Congress/Internet Archive and Open Library catalogue metadata (LCCN 88033997; publishers; ix, 232 p.; ISBNs); the book text itself is a restricted lending copy and was not read, so no book page is given. The chapter title 'Taming chance' as chapter II comes from search-result summaries, not a first-party table of contents. The argument was verified in the full Tanner Lecture text (delivered at Brasenose College, Oxford, 6-7 May 1987; PDF from tannerlectures.org): p. 109 ('The use of lotteries is associated with uncertainty, indifference, indeterminacy, and incommensurability. In the absence of reasons for choosing ... we might as well select one at random') and pp. 162-164 (three forms of indeterminacy: equi-optimality, equi-optimality within the limits of what it pays to find out, incommensurability). Whether the book chapter reproduces the lecture wording was not checked. Subtitle varies between catalogues ('Limitations' in LoC/Internet Archive; 'Limitation' in some publisher listings).

claims.claim: On 8 April 2020 the US HHS Office for Civil Rights closed a compliance review of Alabama without a finding of liability after the state agreed to remove its 2010 ventilator-triage criteria - which allegedly allowed denying ventilators on the basis of intellectual disability and referenced age as an exclusion category - and not to use disability-singling provisions or categorical age cut-offs in future crisis standards of care.
claims.source: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, press release, 'OCR Reaches Early Case Resolution With Alabama After It Removes Discriminatory Ventilator Triaging Guidelines', 8 April 2020; https://www.hhs.gov/about/news/2020/04/08/ocr-reaches-early-case-resolution-alabama-after-it-removes-discriminatory-ventilator-triaging.html
claims.notes: hhs.gov returned 403 to direct requests; the full release was read via an Internet Archive capture of that URL dated 11 April 2020. Verified: the review originated from a complaint by the Alabama Disabilities Advocacy Program and The Arc of the United States; the 2010 'Criteria for Mechanical Ventilator Triage Following Proclamation of Mass-Casualty Respiratory Emergency' allegedly allowed denial based on 'profound mental retardation' and 'moderate to severe dementia'; OCR's review covered both disability and age; laws cited are Section 504, ADA Title II, ACA Section 1557 and the Age Discrimination Act; Alabama agreed to remove links, clarify the criteria are not in effect, and not include similar provisions; closed 'as satisfactorily resolved without a finding of liability'. The plan's description omits the age dimension and should not imply a finding of discrimination: the violations were alleged, and it is an agency press release, not an adjudication.

claims.claim: In Grootboom the South African Constitutional Court held that section 26(2) requires the state to adopt and implement reasonable measures within available resources, that a housing programme excluding a significant segment of society or making no provision for people in desperate need is not reasonable, and declined to define a minimum core for lack of information.
claims.source: Government of the Republic of South Africa and Others v Grootboom and Others (CCT 11/00) [2000] ZACC 19; 2001 (1) SA 46 (CC); 2000 (11) BCLR 1169 (CC), decided 4 October 2000, per Yacoob J (unanimous), paras 32-33, 41-44, 66, 69, 99; https://www.saflii.org/za/cases/ZACC/2000/19.html
claims.notes: saflii.org returned 403; read the judgment via Internet Archive captures of SAFLII's HTML page (for the citations and date) and its PDF (for the text). Verified: 'Decided on: 4 October 2000'; Yacoob J with the other ten members concurring; para 33 (the 'real question' is whether measures are reasonable; not enough information to determine a minimum core); para 41 (court will not ask whether more desirable measures could have been adopted); para 42 (reasonable in conception and implementation); para 43 (a programme excluding a significant segment of society is not reasonable); para 44 (measures must not ignore those whose needs are most urgent; statistical advance not enough); paras 66 and 69 (failure to provide for people in desperate need); para 99 (declaratory order; the Court ordered no individual housing). The plan's description 'reasonableness review of housing policy' is accurate. The Court did not reject a minimum core outright here; it declined to determine one on the record.

claims.claim: The Grootboom judgment records that the respondents, 510 children and 390 adults, had lived in the Wallacedene informal settlement, where many had waited as long as seven years for subsidised housing; that in September 1998 they moved onto vacant private land earmarked for low-cost housing; that on 18 May 1999, at the start of the Cape winter, they were forcibly evicted at the municipality's expense, their homes bulldozed and burnt and their possessions destroyed; that they then sheltered on the Wallacedene sports field under plastic sheeting; and that the Court held neither section 26 nor section 28 entitled them to claim shelter or housing immediately upon demand, making a declaratory order.
claims.source: Government of the Republic of South Africa and Others v Grootboom and Others (CCT 11/00) [2000] ZACC 19; 2001 (1) SA 46 (CC), decided 4 October 2000, per Yacoob J, paras 7-11 and fn 2 (the facts), para 95 (no claim immediately upon demand), para 99 (the order); https://www.saflii.org/za/cases/ZACC/2000/19.html
claims.notes: saflii.org returned 403 to a direct request; read the judgment's HTML through an Internet Archive capture of the SAFLII page (web.archive.org/web/2021id_/ of the source URL), retrieved with curl on 2026-09-25. Verified verbatim: para 7 (Wallacedene on the edge of Oostenberg; a quarter of households without income), the following paragraphs (about half the population children; no water, sewage or refuse removal; many on the waiting list for as long as seven years; moved out at the end of September 1998 onto privately owned vacant land earmarked for low-cost housing, called New Rust; ejectment order of 8 December 1998; eviction on 18 May 1999 'at the beginning of the cold, windy and rainy Cape winter', 'at the municipality's expense', 'prematurely and inhumanely', homes 'bulldozed and burnt and their possessions destroyed'), para 11 (sheltered on the Wallacedene sports field; plastic sheeting afforded scant protection), footnote 2 ('The respondents are 510 children and 390 adults'), para 95 ('Neither section 26 nor section 28 entitles the respondents to claim shelter or housing immediately upon demand'), para 96 (declaratory order) and para 99 (the order's text). The HTML interleaves footnote and paragraph markers, so the facts are cited as paras 7-11 rather than sentence by sentence. The judgment's outcome for the families after 2000 was not checked.

claims.claim: In Treatment Action Campaign (No 2) the South African Constitutional Court held that sections 26 and 27 do not give everyone a self-standing right to demand a minimum core, reviewed the government's mother-to-child HIV transmission policy for reasonableness, and ordered the government without delay to remove restrictions preventing nevirapine being made available at public hospitals and clinics beyond the research and training sites.
claims.source: Minister of Health and Others v Treatment Action Campaign and Others (No 2) (CCT 8/02) [2002] ZACC 15; 2002 (5) SA 721; 2002 (10) BCLR 1033, decided 5 July 2002, judgment of the Court, paras 34-39, 95, 135; https://www.saflii.org/za/cases/ZACC/2002/15.html
claims.notes: saflii.org returned 403; read via Internet Archive captures of SAFLII's HTML page (citations as SAFLII prints them, without '(CC)') and PDF (text). Verified: heard 2, 3 and 6 May 2002, decided 5 July 2002; judgment by 'THE COURT'; paras 34-35 (minimum core possibly relevant to reasonableness, not a self-standing right; impossible to give everyone even a 'core' service immediately); paras 37-38 (courts not institutionally equipped for minimum-core standards; restrained, focused role with budgetary implications not directed at rearranging budgets); para 39 (s 27(1) not a self-standing positive right); para 95 and order para 135 (declaration and mandatory orders on nevirapine, counselling and testing). The plan gave no specific point; the claim states what the judgment holds.

claims.claim: In Mazibuko the South African Constitutional Court refused to fix 50 litres per person per day as the content of the right of access to sufficient water, reasoning as it had in rejecting minimum-core claims that a quantified standard is rigid and institutionally inappropriate for a court, and upheld Johannesburg's Free Basic Water policy as reasonable.
claims.source: Mazibuko and Others v City of Johannesburg and Others (CCT 39/09) [2009] ZACC 28; 2010 (4) SA 1 (CC); 2010 (3) BCLR 239 (CC), decided 8 October 2009, per O'Regan J, paras 9, 56-62, 68-69; https://www.saflii.org/za/cases/ZACC/2009/28.html
claims.notes: saflii.org returned 403; read via Internet Archive captures of SAFLII's HTML page (citations, date) and PDF (text). Verified: heard 2 September 2009, decided 8 October 2009, O'Regan J; para 9 (Free Basic Water policy within the bounds of reasonableness); para 56 (applicants sought 50 litres per person per day and 'expressly reject[ed]' calling it a minimum core; the argument fails 'for the same reasons that the minimum core argument failed in Grootboom and Treatment Action Campaign No 2'); para 57 and fn 46 (the Court 'has declined to adopt a minimum core approach', citing Bilchitz); paras 60-62 (fixing a quantified content would be rigid; institutionally and democratically inappropriate for courts); para 68 (lower courts erred in quantifying); para 69 (the regulatory basic supply of 25 litres per person per day or 6 kilolitres per household per month). Precision correction to the plan: the Court rejected a judicially fixed quantity as the content of the right; it did not strictly face a 'minimum-core quantity', which the applicants disclaimed.

claims.claim: In the right-to-food case (PUCL v Union of India, W.P. (C) 196 of 2001), the Supreme Court of India's interim order of 28 November 2001 directed governments to implement eight food and social-security schemes, including a cooked mid-day meal of at least 300 calories and 8-12 grams of protein for every child in government and government-assisted primary schools for at least 200 days a year, and required Gram Panchayats to display lists of beneficiaries for public inspection.
claims.source: Supreme Court of India, People's Union for Civil Liberties v Union of India and Others, Writ Petition (Civil) No. 196 of 2001, interim order dated 28 November 2001, directions 1-11; text as reproduced in Right to Food Campaign, Supreme Court Orders on the Right to Food: A Tool for Action (October 2005), pp. 10 and 43-45; https://www.corteidh.or.cr/tablas/27433.pdf
claims.notes: No Supreme Court-hosted copy of this 2001 interim order was found; the text was read in the Right to Food Campaign's October 2005 compilation (a campaign publication, hosted in the Inter-American Court of Human Rights library), which reproduces the order at pp. 43-45. Verified there: direction 3(ii) (cooked mid-day meal, 300 calories, 8-12 g protein, 200 days), directions on TPDS, Antyodaya, old-age pensions, Annapurna, ICDS, maternity and family benefit schemes, direction 10 (beneficiary lists displayed and available for inspection), and direction 11 (compliance affidavits). The statement that the order 'converted the benefits of these eight schemes into legal entitlements' is the Campaign's characterisation (p. 10), not the order's words, and the order itself does not declare a right to food under Article 21; the order is interim and the petition remained pending. The same compilation reproduces the 8 May 2002 order, whose direction (f) says Gram Sabhas 'are entitled to conduct a social audit into all Food/Employment schemes' (p. 46) - relevant to item 6 but a different order. Date and case number match the plan.

claims.claim: In judgment T-025 of 2004 the Colombian Constitutional Court declared an unconstitutional state of affairs in the situation of the internally displaced population, because of the mismatch between the gravity of the rights violations and the resources and institutional capacity devoted to them, and ordered the national council for displaced people to design and implement an action plan with deadlines and to give displaced people's organisations effective participation.
claims.source: Corte Constitucional de Colombia, Sala Tercera de Revisión, Sentencia T-025 de 2004, 22 January 2004, M.P. Manuel José Cepeda Espinosa, expediente T-653010 y acumulados, section 7 and Resuelve PRIMERO-SEGUNDO; https://www.corteconstitucional.gov.co/relatoria/2004/t-025-04.htm
claims.notes: Read the full Spanish text on the Court's official relatoría page. Verified: dated 'veintidós (22) de enero de dos mil cuatro (2004)'; decided by the Third Review Chamber (Cepeda Espinosa, Córdoba Triviño, Escobar Gil), not the full court; 108 tutela files accumulated with T-653010, brought by 1,150 family units; section 7 sets out the factors for an unconstitutional state of affairs (massive violation of several rights, prolonged omission by authorities, structural problem requiring coordinated action and additional budget) and records that the Court had declared such a state seven times before; PRIMERO declares the state of affairs; SEGUNDO orders the Consejo Nacional para la Atención Integral a la Población Desplazada to set the budget effort and action plan by 31 March 2004 and to offer displaced organisations participation. The plan's description is accurate. Translations here are my own paraphrase; the judgment does not by itself show that the situation improved (the Court's later follow-up autos were not checked).

claims.claim: Sabel and Simon define a public-law 'destabilization right' as a right to disentrench a public institution that is failing minimum standards of adequate performance and is substantially immune from conventional political correction, and describe US structural remedies moving from command-and-control decrees toward 'experimentalist' regimes of stakeholder negotiation, rolling rules and transparency.
claims.source: Charles F. Sabel and William H. Simon, 'Destabilization Rights: How Public Law Litigation Succeeds', Harvard Law Review 117(4) (2004) 1016-1101, at 1016 (abstract) and 1062 (definition), JSTOR doi:10.2307/4093364; https://scholarship.law.columbia.edu/faculty_scholarship/737
claims.notes: Read the full article PDF from Columbia Law School's Scholarship Archive (retrieved through the scholar.archive.org mirror because the direct download returned 403); it is a scan of the printed pages. Verified: abstract at p. 1016; definition at p. 1062 ('A public law destabilization right is a right to disentrench or unsettle a public institution when, first, it is failing to satisfy minimum standards of adequate performance and, second, it is substantially immune from conventional political mechanisms of correction'); the conclusion (pp. 1100-1101) says 'No definite assessment of the efficacy of this experimentalist approach is possible yet'. The recommended citation is 117 Harv. L. Rev. 1016; the journal's running head reads 117:1015 and Crossref lists first page 1015, so 1015 is the volume start (title page). The article concerns US institutional-reform litigation (schools, mental health, prisons, police, public housing), not social-rights courts abroad.

claims.claim: Mark Tushnet argues that 'weak-form' judicial review, in which legislatures can respond to or reject courts' constitutional interpretations, may allow social welfare rights to be judicially enforced more effectively than US-style strong-form review.
claims.source: Mark Tushnet, Weak Courts, Strong Rights: Judicial Review and Social Welfare Rights in Comparative Constitutional Law (Princeton University Press, 2008; copyright 2007; paperback 2009), xvi + 272 pp., ISBN 978-0-691-13092-7 (hb), 978-0-691-14320-0 (pb), ch. 8 'Enforcing Social and Economic Rights', pp. 227-264; publisher page https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691143200/weak-courts-strong-rights; doi:10.1515/9781400828159
claims.notes: Verified from the Princeton University Press paperback page (description, ISBNs, 'copyright 2007', paperback published 9 August 2009), the Project MUSE record (full table of contents with page ranges: Part III 'Judicial Enforcement of Social and Economic Rights', chs 6-8, pp. 161-264) and the Internet Archive/LoC catalogue record (Princeton, 2008; xvi, 272 p.). The book text was not read; the claim rests on the publisher's description ('such rights can be judicially enforced - not by increasing the power of the courts but by decreasing it'). The plan's year 2008 matches the hardback imprint; Open Library lists an October 2007 hardback date, so cite '2008 (copyright 2007)'. No page pinpoint for any specific argument inside chapter 8 is claimed. The publisher page and the De Gruyter DOI were found on 2026-09-25 by web search.

claims.claim: David Bilchitz defends a minimum core approach to socio-economic rights and criticises the South African Constitutional Court's reasonableness approach, a position the Court itself cited in Mazibuko as academic urging it had declined to follow.
claims.source: David Bilchitz, Poverty and Fundamental Rights: The Justification and Enforcement of Socio-economic Rights (Oxford University Press, 2007; paperback 2008), ISBN 978-0-19-920491-5 (hb), 978-0-19-955216-0 (pb); chapters 'Judicial Review in Practice: The Reasonableness Approach and its Shortcomings' (pp. 135-177) and 'Political Philosophy in Action: Developing the Minimum Core Approach to Socio-Economic Rights' (pp. 178-235), Oxford Scholarship Online doi:10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199552160.001.0001
claims.notes: The book text and OUP pages were not accessible (OUP returned 403/blocked). Bibliographic facts verified from Open Library (hb, OUP, April 2007) and Crossref's Oxford Scholarship Online records, which give chapter titles and page ranges for the 2008 paperback-based online edition (hardback pagination not confirmed). The claim's content rests on the chapter titles and on primary judicial characterisation: Mazibuko [2009] ZACC 28, para 57 fn 46 ('The Court has declined to adopt a minimum core approach ... despite the urging of some academic commentators. See, for example, D Bilchitz Poverty and Fundamental Rights ...'). No specific page for any argument was read. The plan's description ('defending the minimum core') is consistent with these sources.

claims.claim: Katharine Young's Constituting Economic and Social Rights examines how economic and social rights are made effective in legal systems, with chapters on interpreting the minimum core and on typologies of judicial review and of courts, including the idea of a 'catalytic' court.
claims.source: Katharine G. Young, Constituting Economic and Social Rights (Oxford University Press, 2012), ISBN 978-0-19-964193-2; chapters 'Interpreting the Minimum' (pp. 66-98), 'A Typology of Judicial Review' (pp. 133-166), 'The Catalytic Court' (pp. 167-191), 'A Comparative Typology of Courts' (pp. 192-220), Oxford Scholarship Online doi:10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199641932.001.0001
claims.notes: The book text and OUP pages were not accessible. Bibliographic facts and chapter titles/page ranges verified from Crossref's Oxford Scholarship Online records (online 30 August 2012) and Open Library (OUP, 2012). The five-stance typology (deferential, conversational, experimentalist, managerial, peremptory review) and the 'catalytic' role conception were verified in Young's own earlier article, 'A Typology of Economic and Social Rights Adjudication: Exploring the Catalytic Function of Judicial Review', International Journal of Constitutional Law 8(3) (2010), doi:10.1093/icon/moq029 (author's preprint from Boston College's repository), not in the book; Jamal Greene's I-CONnect review (14 October 2013) describes the book as carrying the same typology plus detached (UK), engaged (India), supremacist (Colombia) and catalytic (South Africa) courts - a secondary source. The plan gave no specific point; keep any use at the level of chapter topics unless the book is read.

claims.claim: The Siracusa Principles, adopted at a 1984 expert conference and circulated as UN document E/CN.4/1985/4, state that a limitation of an ICCPR right that must be 'necessary' has to respond to a pressing public or social need, pursue a legitimate aim and be proportionate, use no more restrictive means than required, with the burden of justification on the State; and that emergency derogations must be strictly necessary, with economic difficulties per se not justifying derogation.
claims.source: Siracusa Principles on the Limitation and Derogation Provisions in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, annex to UN Commission on Human Rights, note verbale of 24 August 1984 from the Permanent Representative of the Netherlands, E/CN.4/1985/4, 28 September 1984, annex paras 10-12, 39-41, 51-57; https://docs.un.org/en/E/CN.4/1985/4
claims.notes: Read the official E/CN.4/1985/4 PDF from the UN Official Document System. Verified: the Principles came from a conference at Siracusa, Italy, 30 April-4 May 1984, sponsored by the International Commission of Jurists and four other organisations, and were circulated as an official document of the Commission's forty-first session at the Netherlands' request; annex paras 10 (meaning of 'necessary'), 11 (least restrictive means), 12 (burden on the State), 39-41 (threat to the life of the nation; internal unrest short of that and 'Economic difficulties per se' cannot justify derogation), 51-57 (strict necessity; ordinary limitation measures preferred; independent legislative review and effective remedies; national judgement not conclusive). The plan's '1984/1985' dating is explained by the 1984 conference and document date and the 1985 session symbol. Status limit: an expert text circulated by a UN body, not adopted as binding law or by a treaty body.

claims.claim: Aharon Barak treats proportionality as the main tool for limiting constitutional rights and analyses its four components: proper purpose, rational connection, necessity (no less restrictive means achieving the purpose) and proportionality stricto sensu (balancing).
claims.source: Aharon Barak, Proportionality: Constitutional Rights and their Limitations, trans. Doron Kalir (Cambridge University Press, 2012), xxvi + 611 pp., ISBN 978-1-107-00858-8 (hb), 978-1-107-40119-8 (pb), doi:10.1017/CBO9781139035293; Part III chapters 'Proper purpose' (pp. 245-302), 'Rational connection' (pp. 303-316), 'Necessity' (pp. 317-339), 'Proportionality stricto sensu (balancing)' (pp. 340-370)
claims.notes: Cambridge Core returned 403; bibliographic data, translator, pagination and table of contents verified from Open Library (LoC-derived record) and Crossref's Cambridge Core metadata (online 19 January 2012, chapter page ranges). The claim follows the publisher's abstract carried in Crossref ('explores its four components (proper purpose, rational connection, necessity and proportionality stricto sensu)'). The gloss of necessity in the claim is the standard meaning and the chapter title, not a quotation read from the book; the text itself was not read, so no page pinpoint for any argument is claimed. The book also has chapters on proportionality and positive constitutional rights (pp. 422-434) and the burden of proof (pp. 435-454). The plan gave no specific point for this citation.

claims.claim: ILO Convention No. 29 defines forced or compulsory labour as all work or service exacted from any person under the menace of any penalty and for which the person has not offered himself voluntarily, and binds ratifying states to suppress its use in all its forms.
claims.source: International Labour Organization, Forced Labour Convention, 1930 (No. 29), adopted Geneva 28 June 1930, in force 1 May 1932, 39 UNTS 55, arts 1(1), 2(1)-(2), 25; ILO text: https://www.ilo.org/media/21026/download
claims.notes: Full text read in the ILO's own PDF, which marks art. 1(2) and arts 3-24 as transitional provisions no longer applicable. Adoption date from the text; entry into force and UNTS citation from the University of Minnesota Human Rights Library copy (hrlibrary.umn.edu/instree/n0ilo29.htm). The NORMLEX landing page returned a bot challenge and was not read. Limits: art. 2(2) excludes compulsory military service of a purely military character, normal civic obligations, work exacted as a consequence of a court conviction under public supervision and not hired out to private parties, emergency work, and minor communal services, so the Convention does not prohibit every form of compelled work. The plan gave no framing beyond the title; the 2014 Protocol was not checked.

claims.claim: ILO Convention No. 105 obliges ratifying states to suppress and not to make use of forced or compulsory labour as a means of political coercion or education, for economic development, as a means of labour discipline, as a punishment for having participated in strikes, or as a means of racial, social, national or religious discrimination.
claims.source: International Labour Organization, Abolition of Forced Labour Convention, 1957 (No. 105), adopted Geneva 25 June 1957, in force 17 January 1959, 320 UNTS 291, arts 1-2; ILO text: https://www.ilo.org/media/21031/download
claims.notes: Full operative text read in the ILO's PDF; entry into force and UNTS citation from the University of Minnesota Human Rights Library copy (hrlibrary.umn.edu/instree/n2ilo105.htm). NORMLEX was blocked by a bot challenge. Limit: the Convention prohibits forced labour only for the five purposes listed in art. 1; it supplements Convention No. 29 and is not a general ban on all compulsory work.

claims.claim: The ILO Committee on Freedom of Association accepts minimum services during strikes only in essential services in the strict sense, in services where a strike's extent and duration could cause an acute national crisis, and in public services of fundamental importance, and holds that such services must be confined to what is strictly necessary, must not render the strike ineffective, and should be defined with workers' organisations, with disputes settled by an independent body rather than the ministry.
claims.source: International Labour Office, Freedom of Association: Compilation of decisions of the Committee on Freedom of Association, 6th edn (Geneva: ILO, 2018), ISBN 978-92-2-131205-5 (print), 978-92-2-131206-2 (pdf), paras 830, 836-837, 866-867, 873-874, 876, 881-883; https://www.ilo.org/sites/default/files/wcmsp5/groups/public/@ed_norm/@normes/documents/publication/wcms_632659.pdf
claims.notes: Full PDF read. Essential services in the strict sense are services whose interruption would endanger the life, personal safety or health of the whole or part of the population (para 830; criterion of a clear and imminent threat, para 836; the concept varies with circumstances, para 837). Minimum services: three permitted situations (866); an alternative to prohibition (867); confined to operations strictly necessary and not rendering the strike ineffective (873-874); disagreements settled by an independent body, not the ministry or the administrative authority (876, 882); workers' organisations to participate in determining the services and the minimum number of workers (881); unilateral employer determination not in conformity (883). Caveats: para 872 accepts the requisition of some striking workers in the petroleum sector to set up a temporary minimum service for public-order problems affecting life, health or security, so the Committee does not say that minimum-service rules can never bind named workers. The Compilation collects a supervisory committee's decisions; it is not a binding court judgment.

claims.claim: ILO Recommendation No. 198 advises that whether an employment relationship exists should be guided primarily by the facts relating to the performance of work and the remuneration of the worker, notwithstanding how the relationship is characterised in any contrary contractual or other arrangement.
claims.source: International Labour Conference, Employment Relationship Recommendation, 2006 (No. 198), adopted Geneva 15 June 2006 (95th Session), para 9 (indicators in para 13, presumption option in para 11(b)); ILO text: https://www.ilo.org/media/153276/download
claims.notes: Para 9 read verbatim in the ILO's short PDF, which reproduces the preamble and paras 9-14 and 17 only. The adoption date ('this fifteenth day of June of the year two thousand and six') and 95th session were read in the full text reproduced as Annex I of the ILO guide 'Regulating the employment relationship in Europe: A guide to Recommendation No. 198' (https://www.ilo.org/media/458201/download). NORMLEX was blocked by a bot challenge. Limit: a Recommendation is non-binding guidance to member states, not a ratifiable convention.

claims.claim: The UK Supreme Court held that Uber drivers were 'workers' entitled to statutory minimum wage and working-time protections, reasoning that worker status is a question of statutory interpretation applied to the facts viewed realistically, so the written agreement drafted by the putative employer is not the starting point.
claims.source: Uber BV and others v Aslam and others [2021] UKSC 5, judgment of 19 February 2021 (Lord Leggatt, with whom Lord Reed, Lord Hodge, Lady Arden, Lord Sales and Lord Hamblen agreed), paras 69-71, 76-78, 83, 87, 94-101, 119; https://supremecourt.uk/uploads/uksc_2019_0029_judgment_19c9de2253.pdf
claims.notes: Full judgment read on the Supreme Court's site. Key passages: the rights are statutory, so the question is statutory not contractual interpretation (69-70); protective purpose (71); treating the written contract as the starting point would 'reinstate the mischief which the legislation was enacted to prevent' (76), illustrated by Uber's standard terms (77); no substitute for applying the statute to the facts viewed realistically, with control as the touchstone of subordination and dependence (87); factors (94-101); the tribunal was entitled to find, and could only reasonably find, that the drivers were workers (119). Limits: the drivers were held to be limb (b) 'workers', not employees; the appeal reviewed an employment tribunal's finding of fact. Lord Kitchin fell ill and the court was constituted by the other six Justices (para 140). The plan's 'the facts, not the contract label, decide' is a fair paraphrase for statutory employment rights.

claims.claim: The UK National Audit Office reported in 2016 that the Department for Work and Pensions had not used its own data to evaluate the effects of benefit sanctions, that sanction use varied in ways not explained by changes in claimant compliance, and that it could not conclude the Department was achieving value for money.
claims.source: Comptroller and Auditor General (National Audit Office), Benefit sanctions, HC 628, Session 2016-17, 30 November 2016, Summary paras 4, 6, 10, 13-14, 18-19, 21-23 (pp. 6-10); https://www.nao.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/Benefit-sanctions.pdf
claims.notes: Full PDF read. Para 10: 24% of Jobseeker's Allowance claimants receive a sanction at some point. Para 13: monthly JSA referral rate rose to 10.7% in March 2011 and fell to 3.1% in December 2015. Para 18: international evidence suggests sanctions increase movement from benefits into employment, but the effect can be short-lived, lead to lower wages and increase moves into inactivity. Para 19: the Department had not used its own data to evaluate impacts. Para 22: use of sanctions linked as much to management priorities and local staff discretion as to claimants' behaviour. Para 23: cannot conclude value for money. Limits: the NAO says it does not consider what the correct level of sanctions should be (para 6), and its own impact analysis was preliminary (para 19). It must not be cited as showing that sanctions have no employment effect; para 4's reference to 'hardship, hunger and depression' is the NAO's summary statement, not a measurement.

claims.claim: The ESRC-funded Welfare Conditionality project's qualitative longitudinal study (2013-2018) concluded that conditionality within the social security system was largely ineffective in moving the people it interviewed into or up within paid work, and that benefit sanctions rarely prompted moves into work and were commonly followed by debt, poverty, reliance on charity and worsened ill health.
claims.source: Peter Dwyer (project lead), Final Findings Report: The Welfare Conditionality Project 2013-2018 (University of York, June 2018), executive summary p. 4, introduction p. 8, 'Benefit sanctions' p. 23; White Rose deposit (published version): https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/154305/1/1._FINAL_Welfare_Conditionality_Report_complete.pdf
claims.notes: Full report read in the White Rose Research Online deposit of the published version. Funded under the ESRC Centres and Large Grants Scheme, grant ES/K002163/2 (foreword, p. 7), with teams from six universities. Data: interviews with 52 policy stakeholders, 27 practitioner focus groups, and repeat qualitative longitudinal interviews with welfare service users in England and Scotland (481 at wave a) across nine policy areas (p. 8). Page numbers are the report's printed page numbers. Limits: qualitative and non-representative; the findings describe participants' reported experiences and are not causal estimates. The project website (welfareconditionality.ac.uk) was not read.

claims.claim: Germany's Federal Constitutional Court held in 2010 that Article 1(1) with Article 20(1) of the Basic Law gives each person in need a fundamental right to the material prerequisites indispensable for physical existence and for a minimum of participation in social, cultural and political life, and requires the legislature to assess that need realistically and transparently.
claims.source: Bundesverfassungsgericht (First Senate), judgment of 9 February 2010, 1 BvL 1/09, 1 BvL 3/09, 1 BvL 4/09, BVerfGE 125, 175, ECLI:DE:BVerfG:2010:ls20100209.1bvl000109, headnotes 1-4, operative part, paras 132-136, 151; English translation: https://www.bverfg.de/e/ls20100209_1bvl000109en
claims.notes: Court's English translation read (paras 1-220). The right is framed for a person who cannot obtain the means from gainful employment, property or third parties (para 134): a guarantee of a subsistence minimum for those in need, not an unconditional income. It covers food, clothing, household goods, housing, heating, hygiene and health, and a minimum of participation (para 135). The Court found the standard benefits of EUR 345, 311 and 207 not 'evidently insufficient' (para 151); what failed was the method of calculating them. The provisions stayed applicable until new legislation, ordered by 31 December 2010, and the Court ordered a direct claim for irrefutable recurrent special needs in the meantime (operative part).
