The reporter citation BVerfGE 125, 175 was confirmed from search listings (DFR and dejure), not from the Court's page.

claims.claim: Germany's Federal Constitutional Court held in 2019 that the jobseekers' basic-income rules were incompatible with the Basic Law insofar as they cut benefits by more than 30% of the standard rate, withdrew them entirely, imposed sanctions mandatorily even in cases of extreme hardship, or fixed a rigid three-month duration; a 30% reduction for breaching reasonable cooperation duties could be justified.
claims.source: Bundesverfassungsgericht (First Senate), judgment of 5 November 2019, 1 BvL 7/16, BVerfGE 152, 68, ECLI:DE:BVerfG:2019:ls20191105.1bvl000716, headnotes, operative part, paras 137, 150, 158-159, 189, 201, 210, 213-217; English translation: https://www.bundesverfassungsgericht.de/SharedDocs/Entscheidungen/EN/2019/11/ls20191105_1bvl000716en.html
claims.notes: Court's English translation read; it is abridged (omissions marked [...]); the suggested citation covers paras 1-225. The plan's 'partly unconstitutional' is accurate, but 'struck down' overstates: the provisions were declared incompatible, not void, and continued to apply under a transitional regime set by the Court (operative part; paras 210, 213). The 30% first-stage reduction was held justifiable only with a hardship exception and without a rigid duration (paras 158-159, 214); 60% reductions (189) and complete withdrawal (201) failed. Headnotes: human dignity cannot be lost through supposedly 'undignified' behaviour, but the legislature may apply the principle of last resort and enforce reasonable cooperation duties with proportionate sanctions. The Court found no breach of the constitutional prohibition of forced labour in the cooperation duties (para 150). The reporter citation BVerfGE 152, 68 was confirmed from search listings (DFR and dejure), not from the Court's page.

claims.claim: Stuart White argues that, against a background of institutions sufficiently just in other respects, citizens who share in the social product have an obligation to make a productive contribution in return, so linking welfare rights to work-related responsibilities is not necessarily unjust, though whether such a link is just depends on how far economic institutions meet other requirements of justice.
claims.source: Stuart White, The Civic Minimum: On the Rights and Obligations of Economic Citizenship (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2003, Oxford Political Theory), ISBN 978-0-19-829505-1, doi:10.1093/0198295057.001.0001
claims.notes: Verified from the publisher's abstract (OUP listing via RePEc, https://ideas.repec.org/b/oxp/obooks/9780198295051.html) and the Google Books record (287 pp.; parts 'The Politics of Economic Citizenship' from p. 2, 'Fair Reciprocity' from p. 24, 'The Civic Minimum' from p. 128). The DOI resolves to academic.oup.com/book/11894, which was behind a bot challenge. The book's text was not read and no page for its treatment of basic income was verified. The plan's 'reciprocity-based objection to unconditional income' is close but must be kept conditional: per the abstract, White makes the justice of work-related conditions depend on background justice and calls for a generous civic minimum that also prevents poverty and vulnerability. Do not cite White as rejecting every form of unconditional income without reading his basic-income discussion.

claims.claim: Philippe Van Parijs and Yannick Vanderborght defend an unconditional basic income paid to everyone, rich or poor, active or inactive, as the most realistic response to economic insecurity and social exclusion, and devote a chapter to the objection that it rewards free riding.
claims.source: Philippe Van Parijs and Yannick Vanderborght, Basic Income: A Radical Proposal for a Free Society and a Sane Economy (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2017), 384 pp., ISBN 978-0-674-05228-4 (hardcover; paperback 2019, ISBN 978-0-674-23746-9), ch. 5 'Ethically Justifiable? Free Riding versus Fair Shares'; https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674237469
claims.notes: Verified from the Harvard University Press page (the current page is for the 2019 paperback; the hardcover ISBN page returns 404) and from the Library of Congress-derived catalogue record on the Internet Archive (LCCN 2016045726; 384 pages; contents: Prologue, The instrument of freedom, Basic income and its cousins, Prehistory, History, Ethically justifiable? free riding versus fair shares, Economically sustainable?, Politically achievable?, Viable in the global era?, Epilogue). The chapter number 5 follows that order and matches De Gruyter's chapter listing seen in search results (e.g. '4. History'). The book's text was not read and no page is verified; its exact definition of basic income was not checked.

claims.claim: The EU Digital Markets Act designates as gatekeepers undertakings that have a significant impact on the internal market, provide a core platform service that is an important gateway for business users to reach end users, and enjoy an entrenched and durable position, using rebuttable size and user-number presumptions, and imposes ex ante obligations on them without requiring a finding of dominance under competition law.
claims.source: Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 14 September 2022 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector (Digital Markets Act), OJ L 265, 12.10.2022, p. 1, recital 5, art. 3(1)-(5), (8), (10), art. 54; ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/1925/oj
claims.notes: Official Journal text read through the EU Publications Office (Cellar) because EUR-Lex returned a bot challenge. Art. 3(2) presumptions: annual Union turnover of at least EUR 7.5 billion in each of the last three financial years, or average market capitalisation of at least EUR 75 billion in the last financial year, plus the same core platform service in at least three Member States; at least 45 million monthly active end users and 10,000 yearly active business users in the Union; the user thresholds met in each of the last three years. The presumptions can be rebutted (3(5)); the Commission can also designate on qualitative criteria including lock-in, network effects and data advantages (3(8)); obligations in arts 5-7 apply six months after designation (3(10)); the Regulation applies from 2 May 2023 (art. 54). 'Without a dominance finding' rests on recital 5, which says existing law does not effectively address gatekeepers 'not necessarily dominant in competition-law terms', and on art. 3, which contains no dominance test.

claims.claim: Germany's 2009 constitutional amendment (the debt brake) requires federal and Land budgets to be balanced in principle without borrowing, lets the Federation borrow up to 0.35% of GDP in structural terms, adjusts symmetrically for the economic cycle, and allows the limits to be exceeded in natural disasters or unusual emergencies beyond state control by a Bundestag majority decision combined with an amortisation plan.
claims.source: Gesetz zur Änderung des Grundgesetzes (Artikel 91c, 91d, 104b, 109, 109a, 115, 143d) of 29 July 2009, BGBl. I p. 2248, in force 1 August 2009; Basic Law arts 109(3), 115(2), 143d(1); official English translation: https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/englisch_gg/englisch_gg.html
claims.notes: Current official translation read (as amended by the Act of 22 March 2025, BGBl. 2025 I No. 94); the pre-2025 wording read in an archived copy of the same translation (Wayback Machine, 26 December 2020, as amended to 28 March 2019). Under the 2009 wording the Länder were allowed no structural borrowing (art. 109(3), last sentence). The 2025 amendment lets the Länder together borrow up to 0.35% of GDP and deducts defence, civil-protection, intelligence, IT-security and aid-to-attacked-states spending above 1% of GDP from the borrowing counted (arts 109(3), 115(2)). Phase-in: the Federation from the 2016 budget, the Länder from 2020 (art. 143d(1)). The amending act's date, BGBl page and entry into force are from the buzer.de consolidated-law record, not the Federal Law Gazette facsimile. The book must say 'as amended in 2009' and note the 2025 changes if it describes current law.

claims.claim: Germany's Federal Constitutional Court declared the Second Supplementary Budget Act 2021 void in November 2023, holding that moving EUR 60 billion of unused pandemic emergency borrowing authorisations into a climate fund for later years breached the debt brake: the link to the emergency was not substantiated, the authorisations were decoupled from the year of the emergency, and the Act was adopted after the fiscal year had ended.
claims.source: Bundesverfassungsgericht (Second Senate), judgment of 15 November 2023, 2 BvF 1/22 (Second Supplementary Budget Act 2021), ECLI:DE:BVerfG:2023:fs20231115.2bvf000122, headnotes 1-3, operative part, paras 133, 188-208, 222, 230; English translation: https://www.bundesverfassungsgericht.de/SharedDocs/Entscheidungen/EN/2023/11/fs20231115_2bvf000122en.html
claims.notes: Court's English translation read; it is abridged (omissions marked [...]); paras 1-231. The Act of 18 February 2022 (BGBl I p. 194) was held incompatible with arts 109(3), 110(2) first sentence and 115(2) of the Basic Law and void (operative part; para 230). The Court accepted the COVID-19 pandemic as an emergency beyond state control, and the Bundestag's declaration and amortisation plan as valid (paras 188-194). The failures: insufficient substantiation of the causal link between the emergency and the measures funded (195-205); breach of yearly budgeting and annuality by holding the authorisations as reserves for later years (206-208); adoption after the end of the fiscal year (222). The fund is called the Climate and Transformation Fund in the judgment. The applicants were 197 members of the Bundestag. The official digest (BVerfGE) citation was not checked. The plan's description ('void') is accurate.

claims.claim: In Griggs v. Duke Power Co. the US Supreme Court held that Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 prohibits employment practices that are fair in form but discriminatory in operation unless the employer shows they are related to job performance, and that good intent does not save such practices.
claims.source: Griggs v. Duke Power Co., 401 U.S. 424 (decided 8 March 1971), opinion of Burger, C.J., at 431-432; Library of Congress US Reports copy: https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/usrep/usrep401/usrep401424/usrep401424.pdf
claims.notes: US Reports text read in the Library of Congress PDF. At 431: 'The Act proscribes not only overt discrimination but also practices that are fair in form, but discriminatory in operation. The touchstone is business necessity.' At 432: absence of discriminatory intent 'does not redeem' procedures that operate as 'built-in headwinds'; Congress directed the Act 'to the consequences of employment practices, not simply the motivation'; the employer bears the burden of showing a 'manifest relationship to the employment in question'. Page numbers follow the PDF sequence from the first page, 424, because the running page numbers did not extract. The Court was unanimous; Brennan J took no part. Limit: this is a statutory (Title VII) holding, not a constitutional one.

claims.claim: Kimberlé Crenshaw argued that antidiscrimination law's single-axis framework, which treats race and sex as mutually exclusive categories, erases Black women's experience, and illustrated the point with DeGraffenreid v. General Motors, where a court refused to let Black women bring a claim as Black women.
claims.source: Kimberle Crenshaw, 'Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex: A Black Feminist Critique of Antidiscrimination Doctrine, Feminist Theory and Antiracist Politics', University of Chicago Legal Forum, vol. 1989, iss. 1, art. 8, pp. 139-167, at 139-141, 149; https://chicagounbound.uchicago.edu/uclf/vol1989/iss1/8
claims.notes: The Chicago Unbound landing page and metadata were read (ISSN 0892-5593). The direct PDF download was blocked, so the full text was read in an archived copy of the same Chicago Unbound PDF (Wayback Machine, 2 January 2025). Page numbers follow the printed running heads. Pp. 139-140: the single-axis framework and its erasure of Black women. P. 141: DeGraffenreid v General Motors, 413 F Supp 142 (ED Mo 1976), including the court's refusal to 'combine statutory remedies to create a new super-remedy'. P. 149: the traffic-intersection analogy. No DOI was found.

claims.claim: In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court of India, in its leading judgment, held that reservations under Article 16(4) should not exceed 50% save in extraordinary situations, that the 'creamy layer' must be excluded from the backward classes, and that a 10% reservation based on economic criteria alone was invalid, while letting the 27% reservation for Other Backward Classes be implemented subject to that exclusion.
claims.source: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India, Supreme Court of India, 16 November 1992, AIR 1993 SC 477, 1992 Supp (3) SCC 217, [1992] Supp 2 SCR 454; leading judgment of B.P. Jeevan Reddy J for Kania CJ, Venkatachaliah and Ahmadi JJ and himself, paras 86, 94A-95, 115, 121 (paragraph numbers of that judgment as reproduced by Indian Kanoon); https://indiankanoon.org/doc/1363234/
claims.notes: Full text read on Indian Kanoon, a secondary host; no official Supreme Court copy was located. Pinpoints use the internal numbering of Jeevan Reddy J's judgment; the SCC report numbers paragraphs continuously across all opinions, so check before quoting. Para 86: creamy layer to be excluded, with the Government to specify the basis within four months. Paras 94A-95: 50% rule, with relaxation for extraordinary situations such as far-flung and remote areas, 'extreme caution' and 'a special case made out'. Para 121: summary of holdings, including the 50% rule applied year by year, no reservation in promotions (prospectively), and the 10% economic reservation struck down (para 115). Limits: Pandian J's separate opinion disagreed with a fixed 50% maximum, and the precise majority on each point was not verified. Later constitutional amendments and cases have modified parts of this settlement; they were not checked here.

claims.claim: In Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard the US Supreme Court held that Harvard's and the University of North Carolina's race-conscious admissions programs could not be reconciled with the Equal Protection Clause (applied to Harvard through Title VI), while stating that universities may still consider an applicant's discussion of how race affected his or her life.
claims.source: Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. President and Fellows of Harvard College, 600 U.S. 181 (2023), decided 29 June 2023 together with No. 21-707 (SFFA v. University of North Carolina), opinion of Roberts, C.J., slip op. at 6 n. 2 and 39-40; https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/22pdf/20-1199_hgdj.pdf
claims.notes: Slip opinion read. Slip op. 39: the programs 'cannot be reconciled with the guarantees of the Equal Protection Clause' because they lack sufficiently focused and measurable objectives, use race in a negative manner, involve racial stereotyping and lack meaningful end points. Slip op. 39-40: nothing in the opinion prohibits considering an applicant's discussion of how race affected his or her life, but universities may not achieve through essays what the Court held unlawful. Slip op. 6 n. 2: Harvard's program is evaluated under Title VI using Equal Protection standards. Roberts CJ wrote for six Justices; Jackson J took no part in the Harvard case. The plan's 'race-conscious admissions held unlawful' is slightly broad: the holding concerns these two programs. US Reports pagination (secondary sources place the latter passage at 600 U.S. 230-231) was not checked against the bound volume.

claims.claim: The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities defines reasonable accommodation as necessary and appropriate modification and adjustments, not imposing a disproportionate or undue burden, needed in a particular case to ensure that persons with disabilities enjoy their rights on an equal basis with others; it counts denial of reasonable accommodation as disability discrimination and requires states parties to take all appropriate steps to ensure that it is provided.
claims.source: Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, adopted New York 13 December 2006 (UN General Assembly resolution A/RES/61/106), in force 3 May 2008, 2515 UNTS 3, arts 2 and 5(3); UN text: https://www.un.org/disabilities/documents/convention/convoptprot-e.pdf; status: https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetails.aspx?src=TREATY&mtdsg_no=IV-15&chapter=4&clang=_en
claims.notes: Articles 2, 3, 4 and 5 read in the UN's PDF of the Convention. Adoption, resolution number, entry into force (under art. 45(1)) and the UNTS citation read on the UN Treaty Collection status page. Art. 2 defines both 'discrimination on the basis of disability' (including denial of reasonable accommodation) and 'reasonable accommodation'; art. 5(3) states the duty; art. 5(4) says specific measures to achieve de facto equality are not discrimination. Limit: the duty is bounded by the 'disproportionate or undue burden' qualification in the definition, so the book must not describe accommodation as unlimited.

claims.claim: The Supreme Court of the Netherlands held that Articles 2 and 8 ECHR oblige the Dutch State to take appropriate measures, doing 'its part', against the real and immediate risk of dangerous climate change, and upheld an order to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from Dutch soil by at least 25% compared with 1990 by the end of 2020, while leaving the State free to choose the measures.
claims.source: Hoge Raad der Nederlanden (Supreme Court of the Netherlands), Civil Division, State of the Netherlands (Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy) v. Stichting Urgenda, No. 19/00135, judgment of 20 December 2019, ECLI:NL:HR:2019:2007 (unofficial English translation; the authentic Dutch text is ECLI:NL:HR:2019:2006), paras. 5.2.2-5.3.4, 5.6.2, 5.7.1-5.8, 5.9.1, 7.5.1, 8.2.7, 8.3.2-8.3.5 and 9; https://uitspraken.rechtspraak.nl/details?id=ECLI:NL:HR:2019:2007
claims.notes: Read the full English translation through the rechtspraak.nl open-data service (data.rechtspraak.nl/uitspraken/content?id=ECLI:NL:HR:2019:2007), whose metadata give Hoge Raad, 20-12-2019, case 19/00135 (Engels). The same service confirms ECLI:NL:HR:2019:2006 as the Dutch text of the same case. The translation carries a disclaimer that it is unofficial and that the Dutch text alone is authentic. Pinpoints verified: 5.2.2 (Art. 2 positive obligation; a 'real and immediate' risk includes risks that materialise only in the longer term); 5.2.3-5.2.4 (Art. 8 in environmental matters, treated together with Art. 2); 5.3.2 (precaution; states choose the measures, which must be reasonable and suitable); 5.3.4 (the obligation concerns measures, 'not the achievement, or guarantee of the achievement, of the envisaged result', and may not impose an impossible or disproportionate burden); 5.6.2 (the climate threat falls within Arts. 2 and 8); 5.7.1-5.7.9 and 5.8 (partial responsibility: each state must do 'its part'; a small share of global emissions or other states' failure is no defence); 5.9.1 (conclusion); 7.5.1 (the 25% reduction by 2020 is an 'absolute minimum' because the State did not substantiate that a lower target was responsible); 8.2.7 (the order does not prescribe legislation, and the State remains free to choose measures); 8.3.2 (government and parliament have a large degree of discretion, and courts decide whether they stayed within the law); 8.3.4-8.3.5 ('an exceptional situation'); 9 (appeal rejected). The plan's 'a duty to reduce emissions under ECHR Articles 2 and 8' is accurate but should be framed as a positive obligation of means to take appropriate measures for the State's share. The 25% figure rests on the lower courts' findings of scientific and international consensus for Annex I countries. The Supreme Court decided in cassation on those established facts. The judgment establishes the legal obligation, not that the target was met.

claims.claim: The Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 requires Welsh public bodies to carry out sustainable development by setting well-being objectives and taking all reasonable steps to meet them. It also creates a Future Generations Commissioner, appointed by the Welsh Ministers, to act as a guardian of future generations' ability to meet their needs and to review public bodies and make recommendations. A body must take all reasonable steps to follow a recommendation unless it has good reason not to or chooses an alternative course, and it must publish its response.
claims.source: Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act 2015 (anaw 2), Act of the National Assembly for Wales, Royal Assent 29 April 2015, ss. 3, 5, 17-20 and 22 (as enacted); https://www.legislation.gov.uk/anaw/2015/2/contents
claims.notes: legislation.gov.uk answered every request (curl and WebFetch) with a WAF challenge, so the enacted text was read in full from the PDF of the Act hosted by the Future Generations Commissioner (https://www.futuregenerations.wales/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/WFGAct-English.pdf). That PDF reproduces the official print, with the bilingual title, '2015 anaw 2' and '[29 April 2015]'. Verified: s. 3(1)-(2), the well-being duty; s. 5(1), the sustainable development principle ('the needs of the present are met without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs'); s. 17(1)-(3), a Commissioner 'appointed by the Welsh Ministers' after consulting the Assembly's responsible committee; s. 18, the general duty, including to 'act as a guardian of the ability of future generations to meet their needs'; s. 19, advisory and research functions, not including financial assistance; s. 20, reviews, recommendations, publication and the power to require information; s. 22(1) and (4), the duty to take all reasonable steps to follow a recommendation, with exceptions for 'good reason' or an alternative course, and a duty to publish the response with reasons. The Commissioner's powers are advice, review and recommendation; nothing I read gives a power to veto or quash decisions. The appointment by the executive matters to any comparison of independence. The gov.wales 'essentials' guidance summarises the same scheme. Amendments after 2015 were not checked.

claims.claim: Hungary's Parliament created a Parliamentary Commissioner for Future Generations by amending the Act on the Parliamentary Commissioner for Civil Rights in November 2007, and the first commissioner was elected on 26 May 2008. That office described its statements as not binding. Since the Fundamental Law entered into force on 1 January 2012, the function has been held by a deputy of the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights who, like the Commissioner, is elected by two-thirds of the National Assembly for six years and is charged with protecting the interests of future generations.
claims.source: The Fundamental Law of Hungary (25 April 2011; in force 1 January 2012), Article 30(3) and Closing and Miscellaneous Provisions points 1 and 16, Ministry of Justice English translation as in force on 19 July 2026, https://njt.jog.gov.hu/jogszabaly/en/2011-4301-02-00; and Office of the Parliamentary Commissioners of Hungary (Sándor Fülöp), Comprehensive Summary of the Report of the Parliamentary Commissioner for Future Generations of Hungary 2008-2009 (Budapest, 2010), printed pp. 6-8, https://www.theioi.org/downloads/5elqn/Europe_Hungary_Parliamentary%20Commissioner%20for%20Future%20Generations_Annual%20Report_2009_English.pdf
claims.notes: Read the Fundamental Law in full from the Ministry of Justice's consolidated English translation, served as a PDF by the National Legislation Database (njt.jog.gov.hu) and marked 'produced for informational purposes only'. Art. 30(3): the Commissioner and deputies are elected 'with the votes of two thirds of the Members of the National Assembly for a term of six years'; 'The deputies shall protect the interests of future generations and the rights of national minorities living in Hungary'; they may not be party members. Closing provisions point 16: the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights is the legal successor of the Parliamentary Commissioner for Future Generations, and the commissioner then in office became 'Deputy of the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights responsible for the protection of the interests of future generations'. Point 1: in force 1 January 2012. Art. P(1) separately makes natural resources a common heritage to be preserved for future generations. The history comes from the office's own 2008-2009 report (an institutional self-account). Printed p. 7: the Act was amended in November 2007 'with an almost unanimous vote', and Fülöp was nominated by President Sólyom and elected on 26 May 2008 for six years. p. 8: the office operated from December 2008. p. 6, foreword: 'The statements of the Commissioner are not binding'. The plan's 'from 2008' is right for the first commissioner; the legal institution dates from the end of 2007. Not verified directly: the Act's number (commonly given as Act LIX of 1993) and Act CXI of 2011 on the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights. The Commissioner's site (ajbh.hu) was unreachable.

claims.claim: New Zealand's Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act 2017 recognises Te Awa Tupua as an indivisible and living whole comprising the Whanganui River from the mountains to the sea, and declares it a legal person. Its rights, powers and duties are exercised by Te Pou Tupua, an office of two persons: one nominated by the iwi with interests in the river and one nominated on behalf of the Crown. The Act states that it does not limit existing private property rights or affect rights or interests in water.
claims.source: Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act 2017, Public Act 2017 No 7 (New Zealand), date of assent 20 March 2017, ss. 12-16 and 18-20; https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2017/0007/latest/whole.html
claims.notes: legislation.govt.nz returned 403. Read a browser printout of the official legislation.govt.nz page, 'Reprint as at 30 January 2021' (printed 3 July 2021), hosted by ecojurisprudence.org (https://ecojurisprudence.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/New-Zealand_Te-Awa-Tupua-Act-2017_127.pdf). That reprint notes that 'some amendments have not yet been incorporated', and the current text was not checked. Verified: s. 12 (indivisible and living whole, including physical and metaphysical elements); s. 13 (Tupua te Kawa, its intrinsic values); s. 14(1) ('Te Awa Tupua is a legal person and has all the rights, powers, duties, and liabilities of a legal person'); s. 14(2) (these are exercised by Te Pou Tupua); s. 15 (decision-makers under Schedule 2 Acts must recognise and provide for, or have particular regard to, the status); s. 16 (no limit on existing private property rights, and no effect on rights to water, wildlife, fish or plants or on the application of enactments); s. 18 (Te Pou Tupua is 'the human face of Te Awa Tupua'); s. 19 (functions); s. 20 (two persons, one nominated by the iwi and one by the Crown, jointly appointed). Text extraction separated section numbers from their text, so numbers were matched to headings through the Act's contents list. This supplies the sections the plan asked for.

claims.claim: In judgment T-622 of 2016 a review chamber of the Colombian Constitutional Court found a grave violation of the fundamental rights of the ethnic communities of the Atrato basin, attributable to state omission in the face of illegal mining. It recognised the Atrato River, its basin and tributaries as an entity subject to rights to protection, conservation, maintenance and restoration, to be represented jointly by a government delegate and a member of the claimant communities as guardians.
claims.source: Corte Constitucional de Colombia, Sala Sexta de Revisión, Sentencia T-622/16 (M.P. Jorge Iván Palacio Palacio), 10 November 2016, Expediente T-5.016.242, fundamentos 9.27-9.32 and resolutive paras. SEGUNDO-CUARTO; https://www.corteconstitucional.gov.co/relatoria/2016/t-622-16.htm
claims.notes: Read the full Spanish text on the Court's relatoría. Verified the date ('diez (10) de noviembre de dos mil dieciséis'), the chamber (Sala Sexta de Revisión: Aquiles Arrieta Gómez (e), Alberto Rojas Ríos and Jorge Iván Palacio Palacio, presiding), the rapporteur and the file number. Resolutive CUARTO: 'RECONOCER al río Atrato, su cuenca y afluentes como una entidad sujeto de derechos a la protección, conservación, mantenimiento y restauración a cargo del Estado y las comunidades étnicas', citing fundamentos 9.27-9.32. It orders the government to exercise legal guardianship and representation jointly with the communities, through one community member and one government delegate as guardians, plus a commission of guardians with an advisory team (Humboldt Institute, WWF Colombia). SEGUNDO grants the tutela for the rights to life, health, water, food security, a healthy environment, culture and territory. TERCERO declares a grave violation attributable by omission to named state entities. Fundamento 9.28 grounds the recognition in 'derechos bioculturales', and 9.32 states the declaration; part of 9.32 is garbled in the Court's own HTML. Nuance for the book: this is a tutela (fundamental-rights) judgment of a three-judge review chamber, not a plenary constitutional ruling, and the rights recognised are to protection, conservation, maintenance and restoration. The judgment does not show that its orders were carried out.

claims.claim: The Stern Review argued that the only sound ethical basis for placing less value on future generations' welfare is uncertainty about whether they will exist, and adopted a pure time discount rate of 0.1% a year, which it noted implies an almost 10% chance of human extinction within a century. It concluded that business-as-usual climate change would cost the equivalent of losing at least 5% of global GDP each year, now and forever, against costs of action of around 1% of GDP a year.
claims.source: Nicholas Stern, The Economics of Climate Change: The Stern Review (HM Treasury web edition, autumn 2006; Cambridge University Press, 2007, ISBN 9780521700801, doi:10.1017/CBO9780511817434): Summary of Conclusions (CUP pp. xv-xx); Executive Summary p. x and Chapter 2A technical annex pp. 45-47 incl. Table 2A.1 (2006 web edition); https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511817434
claims.notes: CUP bibliographic data from Cambridge Core: print publication 4 January 2007; ch. 2 is pp. 25-45 and ch. 2A pp. 46-62 in the CUP edition. The Summary of Conclusions text was checked on its Cambridge Core abstract page: 'at least 5% of global GDP each year, now and forever'; damages could rise to '20% of GDP or more'; costs of action 'around 1% of global GDP each year'. The HM Treasury 2006 web edition was read from the Internet Archive (index captured 14 November 2006). Executive Summary p. x: at least 5% of global per-capita consumption, 'now and forever', rising to 11% with non-market impacts. Ch. 2A p. 45: 'the only sound ethical basis for placing less value on the utility (as opposed to consumption) of future generations was the uncertainty over whether or not the world will exist'. p. 47, Table 2A.1: δ = 0.1 gives a 0.905 probability of surviving 100 years ('almost 10% chance of extinction'), and 'that is the case we shall focus on later in the review'. The Chapter 2A pages cited are from the 2006 web edition; CUP pagination for those passages was not checked. The preface says the report was due by autumn 2006; the exact release date was not verified from a primary source. The plan's '(2006/2007)' is correct. The figures are the Review's own contested model estimates (see nordhaus-2007-review-of-stern).

claims.claim: William Nordhaus argued that the Stern Review's case for sharp, immediate emission cuts depends decisively on a near-zero time discount rate combined with a specific utility function, and would not survive assumptions consistent with market real interest rates and savings rates.
claims.source: William D. Nordhaus, 'A Review of the Stern Review on the Economics of Climate Change', Journal of Economic Literature 45(3): 686-702, September 2007; doi:10.1257/jel.45.3.686
claims.notes: Bibliographic data and the abstract were read on the AEA article page (https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/jel.45.3.686). The full text is paywalled (the AEA PDF returned 403), so the claim rests on the abstract alone and no page pinpoint was verified. Figures often attributed to this article, such as a 1.4% real interest rate implied by Stern, were not checked in the article's text; Stern's 0.1% pure time preference is verified in stern-review-2006-economics-climate-change. The plan's 'discount-rate critique' is accurate, but the abstract ties the critique to the discount rate together with the utility function. Its benchmark is observed market interest and savings rates, whereas Stern chose the rate on ethical grounds.

claims.claim: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 (England and Wales) presumes capacity and forbids treating a person as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help them have failed. Once a person is found to lack capacity for a particular decision, acts done and decisions made on their behalf must be in their best interests. That determination is made by someone else, who must consider the person's past and present wishes and feelings, beliefs and values, encourage their participation and consult named people and carers.
claims.source: Mental Capacity Act 2005 (c. 9), Royal Assent 7 April 2005, ss. 1-4 (esp. ss. 1(3), 1(5), 1(6), 4(4), 4(6), 4(7), 4(9)); https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/9/section/4
claims.notes: legislation.gov.uk is blocked by a WAF challenge. Read the as-enacted Queen's Printer PDF through the Internet Archive (http://web.archive.org/web/20260910001510/https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2005/9/pdfs/ukpga_20050009_en.pdf). Verified: s. 1(2)-(6) principles, including 'all practicable steps to help him' (1(3)), unwise decisions (1(4)), best interests (1(5)) and the less restrictive alternative (1(6)); s. 2 (incapacity is judged 'in relation to a matter' at 'the material time', never merely by age, appearance or condition); s. 3 (the functional test, with explanation in an appropriate way under s. 3(2)); s. 4 (the best-interests checklist); s. 4(9) (for decision-makers other than the court, reasonable belief suffices). The plan's framing, 'best-interests model (section 4) as the alternative to support', overstates the contrast. The Act itself builds in support duties (ss. 1(3), 3(2), 4(4)). What separates it from supported decision-making is that, after a finding of incapacity, another person decides on an objective best-interests standard, with the person's wishes as a mandatory consideration but not decisive. A claim that this conflicts with the UN CRPD needs its own source, which was not checked here. The current amended text was not checked.

claims.claim: Article 33(1) of the 1951 Refugee Convention forbids a contracting state to expel or return a refugee 'in any manner whatsoever' to the frontiers of territories where their life or freedom would be threatened on account of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. Article 33(2) withdraws that protection from a refugee reasonably regarded as a danger to the security of the country, or who has been convicted by final judgment of a particularly serious crime and is a danger to the community. Article 42(1) bars reservations to Article 33.
claims.source: Convention relating to the Status of Refugees, signed at Geneva 28 July 1951, entered into force 22 April 1954, 189 UNTS 137 (No. 2545), Article 33 (at p. 176) and Article 42(1); https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20189/volume-189-I-2545-English.pdf
claims.notes: Read UNTS vol. 189 (No. 2545) from the UN Treaty Collection: the Final Act begins at p. 137, the Convention text at p. 150 (with a footnote giving entry into force on 22 April 1954), and Article 33 is at p. 176. Article 42(1) excludes reservations to articles 1, 3, 4, 16(1), 33 and 36-46. OHCHR and UNHCR pages returned 403. An important difference from the plan's use: Article 33 is not absolute, because 33(2) states exceptions. Any claim that non-refoulement is absolute must rest on other instruments, such as Article 3 of the Convention against Torture or ECHR Article 3 case law, which were not checked here. Article 33 protects refugees as defined in Article 1; the 1967 Protocol's removal of the dateline and geographic limits was not checked.

claims.claim: Article 32(2) of the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples says that states shall consult and cooperate in good faith with the indigenous peoples concerned, through their own representative institutions, in order to obtain their free and informed consent before approving any project affecting their lands, territories and other resources, particularly the development, use or exploitation of mineral, water or other resources.
claims.source: United Nations General Assembly, Resolution 61/295, United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted 13 September 2007 (107th plenary meeting), annex, Article 32; UN Doc. A/RES/61/295; https://docs.un.org/en/A/RES/61/295
claims.notes: Text read in the UN DESA publication that reproduces the resolution and annex (https://www.un.org/development/desa/indigenouspeoples/wp-content/uploads/sites/19/2018/11/UNDRIP_E_web.pdf); the docs.un.org symbol page was reachable. The exact wording is 'in order to obtain their free and informed consent prior to the approval of any project'. The plan's 'free, prior and informed consent' is a common paraphrase, and the article frames consent as the aim of consultation ('in order to obtain') rather than expressly as a veto. Art. 32(1) covers indigenous peoples' own development priorities, and 32(3) requires mechanisms for just and fair redress. Related provisions: Art. 10 forbids relocation without free, prior and informed consent, in stronger terms, and Art. 19 requires consultation to obtain such consent before legislative or administrative measures. This is a General Assembly declaration, not a treaty, and it is not binding as such. The vote record was not checked.

claims.claim: ILO Convention No. 169 requires governments to consult indigenous and tribal peoples in good faith, through their representative institutions, on measures that may affect them directly, with the objective of achieving agreement or consent. It requires consultation before exploration or exploitation of state-owned sub-surface resources on their lands. Relocation may take place only with their free and informed consent, except that where consent cannot be obtained it may follow appropriate procedures established by national law.
claims.source: International Labour Organization, Indigenous and Tribal Peoples Convention, 1989 (No. 169), adopted Geneva, 76th ILC session, 27 June 1989, in force 5 September 1991, Articles 6, 7(1), 15(2) and 16; https://normlex.ilo.org/dyn/nrmlx_en/f?p=NORMLEXPUB:12100:0::NO::P12100_INSTRUMENT_ID:312314
claims.notes: normlex.ilo.org returned 403. Read the NORMLEX text page as captured by the Internet Archive on 26 April 2024 (http://web.archive.org/web/20240426213905/https://ilo.org/dyn/normlex/en/f?p=NORMLEXPUB:12100:0::NO::P12100_ILO_CODE:C169), which also gives the adoption and entry-into-force data. Verified the exact text of Arts. 6(1)(a) and 6(2), 7(1), 15(2) and 16(1)-(5). The key nuance for the book is that C169 gives no general consent veto. Art. 6(2) makes agreement or consent the 'objective' of consultation. Art. 15(2) requires consultation, not consent, for resource projects. Art. 16(2) allows relocation without consent through national procedures, including public inquiries, while 16(3)-(5) add return, equivalent land and full compensation. The Convention binds only ratifying states; the ratification list was not checked. The current NORMLEX URL in 'source' could not be fetched today.

claims.claim: The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held that, for logging and mining concessions restricting the Saramaka people's communal property not to deny their survival as a tribal people, Suriname must ensure their effective participation, a reasonable benefit and a prior independent environmental and social impact assessment. For large-scale development or investment projects with a major impact within their territory, the State must also obtain their free, prior and informed consent according to their customs and traditions.
claims.source: Inter-American Court of Human Rights, Case of the Saramaka People v. Suriname, Judgment of November 28, 2007 (Preliminary Objections, Merits, Reparations, and Costs), Series C No. 172, paras. 127-137 (esp. 129, 133, 134, 137); https://www.corteidh.or.cr/docs/casos/articulos/seriec_172_ing.pdf
claims.notes: Read the full English judgment PDF on the Court's site and verified the title page and date. Para. 129 sets out the three safeguards: effective participation, reasonable benefit, and prior environmental and social impact assessment by independent, technically capable entities. Para. 133: consultation must be in good faith, culturally appropriate, begin at early stages and aim at reaching agreement. Para. 134: 'regarding large-scale development or investment projects that would have a major impact within Saramaka territory, the State has a duty, not only to consult with the Saramakas, but also to obtain their free, prior, and informed consent, according to their customs and traditions'. Para. 137: consent is additionally required for major plans with a profound impact on property rights over a large part of their territory. Paras. 127-128 place this within permissible restrictions of property under Article 21 of the American Convention: consultation is always required, and consent is required for large-scale projects. The Series C number is taken from the Court's document filename (seriec_172); it did not appear in the extracted text. The plan's 'consultation and consent for large-scale projects' is accurate.

claims.claim: The Supreme Court of Canada granted the Tsilhqot'in a declaration of Aboriginal title. It held that such title confers the right to decide how the land is used and to benefit from it, so that governments and others must obtain the title holders' consent or else justify an incursion under s. 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982. The title is collective and held for all succeeding generations, so it cannot be alienated except to the Crown or encumbered in ways that would prevent future generations from using and enjoying the land.
claims.source: Tsilhqot'in Nation v. British Columbia, 2014 SCC 44, [2014] 2 S.C.R. 256, judgment of 26 June 2014 (McLachlin C.J. for a unanimous Court), paras. 50, 73-76, 88, 90, 97 and 153; https://decisions.scc-csc.ca/scc-csc/scc-csc/en/item/14246/index.do
claims.notes: The live site returned 403. Read the Court's decision text as captured by the Internet Archive on 1 April 2026 (the page's '?iframe=true' text). Verified date 2014-06-26, docket 34986, the coram, and unanimous reasons at paras. 1-153. The judgment header prints '[2014] 2 S.C.R. 256', while the site's metadata field shows '[2014] 2 SCR 7'; the header citation is used. Pinpoints: 50 (the test of sufficient, continuous where relied on, and exclusive occupation, extending to regularly used tracts); 73 (ownership rights similar to fee simple); 74 ('collective title held not only for the present generation but for all succeeding generations', which cannot be alienated except to the Crown or encumbered so as to prevent future use); 76 (consent, or justification under s. 35); 88 (summary: incursions need consultation, a compelling and substantial public interest and consistency with the fiduciary duty); 90 (after title is established the Crown must seek consent); 97 (obtaining consent avoids infringement); 153 (declaration of title granted, and British Columbia breached its duty to consult). The plan's 'Aboriginal title' is correct. The consent requirement is not absolute, because justification under s. 35 remains available.

claims.claim: In the Niyamgiri case the Supreme Court of India directed that the gram sabhas decide, within three months, the community, individual, cultural and religious claims of the Dongria Kondh and other forest dwellers, including whether the proposed bauxite mine would affect their right to worship Niyam Raja. The environment ministry was then to take its final decision on forest clearance in the light of the gram sabhas' decisions, with a district judge observing the gram sabha proceedings.
claims.source: Supreme Court of India, Orissa Mining Corporation Ltd. v. Ministry of Environment & Forest & Others, Writ Petition (Civil) No. 180 of 2011, judgment of 18 April 2013 (Aftab Alam, K.S. Radhakrishnan and Ranjan Gogoi JJ.; opinion of Radhakrishnan J.), paras. 55-62; https://fra.org.in/upload/courtCasesFile/21979c9ce765e968e2f62dbf19368bb8.pdf
claims.notes: Read the full reportable judgment in a PDF hosted at fra.org.in (81 pages, dated 'April 18, 2013' at the end, with para. 60 on p. 80) and cross-checked it against the Indian Kanoon transcription (https://indiankanoon.org/doc/109648742/), which lists the bench. A copy on the Supreme Court's own site was not located, and the operator of fra.org.in was not confirmed. The report citation (2013) 6 SCC 476 appears only in secondary listings and was not verified. Pinpoints: 56 (the gram sabha's role under s. 6 of the Forest Rights Act and PESA); 57 (PESA s. 4(d)); 58 (the religious-rights question 'to be considered by the Gram Sabha', including whether the mining area would affect the abode of Niyam-Raja); 59 (fresh claims within six weeks); 60 (a decision within three months, after which the MoEF takes its final decision on Stage II clearance 'in the light of the decisions of the Gram Sabha'); 62 (a District Judge observes and certifies that the proceedings were independent). The plan says 'gram sabhas to decide'. The gram sabhas were to decide the rights claims, including whether mining would affect religious rights, but the Court did not say in terms that they held a veto over the project; the final clearance decision stayed with the ministry. The judgment does not record what the gram sabhas later decided, and that outcome needs another source.

claims.claim: Joseph Carens's The Ethics of Immigration first assesses citizenship, residents' rights, temporary workers, irregular migrants, family admission and refugees on the conventional assumption that states may control admissions, including a chapter on 'the theory of social membership'. It then argues that democratic values of freedom and equality ultimately entail a commitment to open borders.
claims.source: Joseph H. Carens, The Ethics of Immigration (Oxford Political Theory; New York: Oxford University Press, 2013), hardcover, 384 pp., ISBN 9780199933839; ch. 8 'The Theory of Social Membership'; ch. 11 'The Case for Open Borders'; https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-ethics-of-immigration-9780199933839
claims.notes: Verified from the OUP product page as captured by the Internet Archive on 30 May 2014 (the live page is blocked): author, title, series, hardcover publication 15 November 2013 (US listing), 384 pages, ISBN 9780199933839, the full table of contents (Part I 'Who belongs?', chs. 2-8; Part II 'Who should get in?', chs. 9-12) and the publisher's description ('democratic values of freedom and equality ultimately entail a commitment to open borders'; the earlier chapters work 'within the moral framework provided by liberal democratic values'). The book's text was not seen, so no page numbers were verified. That social membership grounds residents' rights reflects the chapter title and secondary reviews, not a page I read. The paperback ISBN 9780190246792 appears only in search results.

claims.claim: Christopher Heath Wellman argued that legitimate states enjoy a right to freedom of association, as part of their self-determination, that grounds a presumptive right to exclude outsiders, and he concluded that such states are entitled to reject all potential immigrants, even people seeking asylum.
claims.source: Christopher Heath Wellman, 'Immigration and Freedom of Association', Ethics 119(1): 109-141, October 2008; doi:10.1086/592311
claims.notes: Bibliographic data from Crossref and the publisher's article page (Internet Archive capture of 6 July 2022). The article text was not accessible: it is behind the publisher's paywall, and the author manuscript in a Charles Sturt University repository returned 403. The thesis and page numbers therefore rest on quotations in Sarah Fine, 'Freedom of Association Is Not the Answer', Ethics 120 (January 2010): 338-356, DOI 10.1086/649626, which I read in full from an MIT-hosted copy. p. 109: states may 'close [their] doors to all potential immigrants, even refugees desperately seeking asylum from incompetent or corrupt political regimes', and freedom of association includes 'the right not to associate and even, in many cases, the right to disassociate'. p. 119: freedom of association supplies 'a presumptive case in favor of each legitimate state's right to exclude others from its territory'. p. 141: 'legitimate states are entitled to reject all potential immigrants, even those desperately seeking asylum from corrupt governments'. Fine also reports (citing pp. 127-28) Wellman's view that duties of global justice might be met by exporting justice rather than admitting people. Treat these quotations as second-hand until they are checked against the article.

claims.claim: Under Article 21(5) of the EU Whistleblower Directive, once a reporting person establishes that they reported or publicly disclosed a breach and suffered a detriment, the detriment is presumed to be retaliation, and the person who took the detrimental measure must prove that it was based on duly justified grounds.
claims.source: Directive (EU) 2019/1937 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2019 on the protection of persons who report breaches of Union law, OJ L 305, 26.11.2019, p. 17, Article 21(5) (rationale in recital 93); https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/1937/oj
claims.notes: Full Official Journal text read from the EU Publications Office (cellar XHTML for CELEX 32019L1937) because EUR-Lex returned a bot challenge. Article 21 is headed 'Measures for protection against retaliation'; paragraph 5 was checked verbatim: 'In proceedings before a court or other authority relating to a detriment suffered by the reporting person, and subject to that person establishing that he or she reported or made a public disclosure and suffered a detriment, it shall be presumed that the detriment was made in retaliation ... it shall be for the person who has taken the detrimental measure to prove that that measure was based on duly justified grounds.' Recital 93 states the rationale (prima facie showing shifts the burden). The plan's 'reversal of the burden of proof' is a fair description, but the operative text is a rebuttable presumption, not automatic success. Limits: it applies only within the Directive's material scope (reports of breaches of Union law in the areas listed in Article 2) and to the persons in Article 4, and it takes effect through national transposition, which was not checked.

claims.claim: Lijphart's Patterns of Democracy (second edition) compares thirty-six democracies over 1945-2010 against a majoritarian (Westminster) model and a consensus model, places them on a two-dimensional map, and in its last substantive chapters asks whether consensus democracy performs differently, chapter 16 being titled 'Consensus Democracy Makes a Difference'.
claims.source: Arend Lijphart, Patterns of Democracy: Government Forms and Performance in Thirty-Six Countries, 2nd ed. (New Haven: Yale University Press, 2012), 368 pp., ISBN 978-0-300-17202-7 (pbk), 978-0-300-18912-4 (ebook); ch. 2 (pp. 9-29), ch. 3 (pp. 30-45), ch. 14 (pp. 239-254), chs. 15-16 (pp. 255-294); https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300172027/patterns-of-democracy/ ; ebook doi:10.12987/9780300189124
claims.notes: Checked the publisher's page (second edition, published 11 September 2012, 368 pages; 'Examining thirty-six democracies during the period from 1945 to 2010') and the chapter titles and page ranges registered with Crossref for the De Gruyter ebook (e.g. ch. 2 'The Westminster Model of Democracy', ch. 3 'The Consensus Model of Democracy', ch. 14 'The Two-Dimensional Conceptual Map of Democracy', ch. 15 'Effective Government and Policy-Making: Does Consensus Democracy Make a Difference?', ch. 16 'The Quality of Democracy and a “Kinder, Gentler” Democracy: Consensus Democracy Makes a Difference'). The ebook pagination is assumed, not confirmed, to match print. The book text was not read, and the plan named no specific point, so the claim is limited to scope and structure. Do not cite this entry for a particular empirical finding (for example on growth, inflation or welfare spending) without reading chapters 15-16.

claims.claim: Tsebelis and Money use cooperative game-theoretic models to argue that bicameral legislatures, compared with unicameral ones, increase the stability of the status quo, and non-cooperative models to analyse the devices used to resolve disagreement between chambers: where a bill starts, which chamber has the final word, how many times a bill can shuttle, and whether conference committees are called.
claims.source: George Tsebelis and Jeannette Money, Bicameralism, Political Economy of Institutions and Decisions (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1997), ISBN 978-0-521-58037-3 (hbk), 978-0-521-58972-7 (pbk); doi:10.1017/CBO9780511609350; https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/bicameralism/DA2C43248D9A36D8BE00AD15A4B4AAE6
claims.notes: Checked the Cambridge Core book page (print publication 13 June 1997; series Political Economy of Institutions and Decisions) and its book description, which says the book examines 'some fifty countries', uses cooperative models 'to establish that bicameral legislatures, when compared with unicameral legislatures, increase the stability of the status quo and reduce intercameral differences to one privileged dimension of conflict', and draws empirical evidence 'mainly from the French Republic'. Chapter titles and ranges from Crossref, e.g. 'The core and the uncovered set of bicameral legislatures' (pp. 80-97), 'A model of intercameral bargaining' (pp. 98-109), 'Conference committees' (pp. 176-208). The book text was not read; the claim rests on the publisher's description, and no page was verified for the status-quo result.

claims.claim: On 16 October 2015 a five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court of India, by a 4:1 majority, declared the Constitution (Ninety-ninth Amendment) Act, 2014 and the National Judicial Appointments Commission Act, 2014 unconstitutional and void and declared the prior 'collegium' system of judicial appointment operative, Khehar J holding that the Commission's composition, including the Union Law Minister ex officio and two 'eminent persons', breached the independence of the judiciary and the separation of powers.
claims.source: Supreme Court of India, Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association and Another v. Union of India, Writ Petition (Civil) No. 13 of 2015, judgment of 16 October 2015, [2015] 13 S.C.R. 1 (headnote per Khehar J at pp. 17-18; Order of the Court at pp. 1055-1056); also reported as (2016) 5 SCC 1; https://cdnbbsr.s3waas.gov.in/s3ec0490f1f4972d133619a60c30f3559e/documents/aor_notice_circular/36.pdf
claims.notes: Read the official Supreme Court Reports volume (1,060-page PDF on the Government of India S3WaaS host used by the Court). Bench: Khehar, Chelameswar, Lokur, Kurian Joseph and Goel JJ. The 'Order of the Court' (pp. 1055-1056) rejects the prayer for reference to a larger bench, declares the 99th Amendment Act and the NJAC Act 'unconstitutional and void', declares the pre-amendment collegium system operative, and lists the matter to consider improvements to the collegium. The reasons summarised in the claim come from the reporter's headnote of Khehar J's opinion (pp. 17-18: clauses (a)-(b) of Art. 124A(1) insufficient to preserve the primacy of the judiciary; clause (c), the Law Minister, impinges on independence of the judiciary and separation of powers; clause (d), eminent persons, ultra vires); Khehar J's own paragraphs were not located, so no paragraph number is given. Chelameswar J dissented and would have upheld the amendment (headnote p. 53). The SCC citation was seen only in secondary sources. The same case also produced separate orders (for example on recusal, and a later hearing on improving the collegium); those are different sources.

claims.claim: In Hirst v. United Kingdom (No. 2) the European Court of Human Rights' Grand Chamber held, by twelve votes to five, that the United Kingdom's ban on voting by all convicted prisoners in custody violated Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, describing it as a 'general, automatic and indiscriminate restriction on a vitally important Convention right' falling outside any acceptable margin of appreciation.
claims.source: European Court of Human Rights (Grand Chamber), Hirst v. the United Kingdom (No. 2), application no. 74025/01, judgment of 6 October 2005, § 82 and operative point 1; https://hudoc.echr.coe.int/eng?i=001-70442
claims.notes: Full judgment read from HUDOC (header 'GRAND CHAMBER ... JUDGMENT STRASBOURG 6 October 2005'). § 82 verified verbatim: the margin of appreciation 'is wide, it is not all-embracing'; section 3 of the Representation of the People Act 1983 'remains a blunt instrument' applying 'irrespective of the length of their sentence and irrespective of the nature or gravity of their offence'; 'Such a general, automatic and indiscriminate restriction ... must be seen as falling outside any acceptable margin of appreciation, however wide that margin might be'. Operative point 1: violation 'by twelve votes to five'. Limits: the Court did not hold that every restriction on prisoners' voting breaches the Convention and left the choice of means to the State (§§ 83-84).

claims.claim: In Sauvé v. Canada (Chief Electoral Officer) the Supreme Court of Canada held, 5-4, that s. 51(e) of the Canada Elections Act, which barred prisoners serving sentences of two years or more from voting in federal elections, unjustifiably infringed the right to vote in s. 3 of the Charter and was of no force or effect.
claims.source: Supreme Court of Canada, Sauvé v. Canada (Chief Electoral Officer), 2002 SCC 68, [2002] 3 S.C.R. 519, judgment of 31 October 2002, per McLachlin C.J., paras. 62 and 64; https://decisions.scc-csc.ca/scc-csc/scc-csc/en/item/2010/index.do
claims.notes: Full text read on the Supreme Court of Canada's decisions site (neutral citation, report citation, file 27677 and date 2002-10-31 checked). The Crown conceded the s. 3 infringement; the contest was justification under s. 1. Para. 62: 's. 51(e)'s disenfranchisement of prisoners sentenced to two years or more cannot be justified under s. 1'; para. 64: the provision 'is inconsistent with the Charter and is of no force or effect'. Majority: McLachlin C.J. with Iacobucci, Binnie, Arbour and LeBel JJ.; dissent: Gonthier J. with L'Heureux-Dubé, Major and Bastarache JJ. Para. 62 expressly leaves open whether other activities such as standing for office could be restricted. This is the 2002 decision (often called Sauvé No. 2), not the 1993 Sauvé decision.

claims.claim: In August v Electoral Commission the Constitutional Court of South Africa held that prisoners kept their constitutional right to vote because Parliament had not limited it, that 'Parliament cannot by its silence deprive any prisoner of the right to vote', and ordered the respondents to make all reasonable arrangements for eligible prisoners to register and vote in the 1999 general election.
claims.source: Constitutional Court of South Africa, August and Another v Electoral Commission and Others (CCT 8/99) [1999] ZACC 3; 1999 (3) SA 1 (CC); 1999 (4) BCLR 363 (CC), decided 1 April 1999, per Sachs J, paras. 17, 31, 33 and order at para. 42; https://collections.concourt.org.za/handle/20.500.12144/2071
claims.notes: Official full judgment read from the Court's own collections repository (SAFLII refused automated access). Heard 19 March 1999, decided 1 April 1999; Sachs J with eight judges concurring. Para. 17: 'The vote of each and every citizen is a badge of dignity and of personhood. Quite literally, it says that everybody counts.' Para. 33: 'Parliament cannot by its silence deprive any prisoner of the right to vote ... The Commission's duty is to manage the elections, not to determine the electorate'. Para. 42 (order): prisoners not excluded by s. 8(2) of the Electoral Act 73 of 1998 are entitled to register and vote; respondents to make all reasonable arrangements. Limit: para. 31 says whether legislation disqualifying prisoners could be justified under s. 36 'was not raised in these proceedings'; the case does not decide that prisoner disenfranchisement is unconstitutional as such.

claims.claim: In Minister of Home Affairs v NICRO the Constitutional Court of South Africa declared invalid the 2003 Electoral Act provisions that barred prisoners serving sentences of imprisonment without the option of a fine from registering and voting, because the government had put wholly inadequate information before the Court to justify a blanket exclusion, and ordered arrangements so that those prisoners could vote in the April 2004 election.
claims.source: Constitutional Court of South Africa, Minister of Home Affairs v National Institute for Crime Prevention and the Re-integration of Offenders (NICRO) and Others (CCT 03/04) [2004] ZACC 10; 2005 (3) SA 280 (CC); 2004 (5) BCLR 445 (CC), decided 3 March 2004, per Chaskalson CJ, paras. 57, 65-67 and order at para. 80; https://collections.concourt.org.za/handle/20.500.12144/2233
claims.notes: Official full judgment read from the Court's collections repository. Heard 25 February, decided 3 March 2004. Order (para. 80) declares invalid s. 8(2)(f), the phrase 'and not serving a sentence of imprisonment without the option of a fine' in s. 24B(1), and s. 24B(2) of the Electoral Act 73 of 1998, and orders registration and voting arrangements. Para. 57 accepts that denouncing crime could be a legitimate purpose; paras. 65-67 hold that the government must put sufficient information before the Court, that this was 'a blanket exclusion akin to that which failed to pass scrutiny in the first Sauvé case', that the Court had 'wholly inadequate information', and that 'the attempt by the Minister to justify the limitation fails'. Majority Chaskalson CJ with eight concurring; Madala J dissented and would have dismissed the application (para. 128); Ngcobo J would have cured the provisions only by reading in an exception for prisoners whose appeals are pending (paras. 152-153). The case turns on justification and does not hold that every disenfranchisement of prisoners is invalid. The law-report citations are those in SAFLII's case title and were not checked in the reports.

claims.claim: On 5 February 2020 the District Court of The Hague held that the legislation governing SyRI, the Dutch government's risk-indication system for detecting benefit, allowance and tax fraud, contained insufficient safeguards and was insufficiently transparent and verifiable to satisfy the 'necessary in a democratic society' requirement of Article 8(2) ECHR, and declared Section 65 of the SUWI Act and Chapter 5a of the SUWI Decree to have no binding effect.
claims.source: Rechtbank Den Haag (District Court of The Hague), NJCM et al. v. State of the Netherlands, case C/09/550982 / HA ZA 18-388, judgment of 5 February 2020, ECLI:NL:RBDHA:2020:865 (Dutch original); English translation ECLI:NL:RBDHA:2020:1878; paras. 6.7, 6.72, 6.86, 6.95 and dictum 7.2; https://uitspraken.rechtspraak.nl/details?id=ECLI:NL:RBDHA:2020:865
claims.notes: Both the Dutch original and the court's English translation were read through the rechtspraak.nl open-data service. Para. 6.7: the legislation 'does not strike the “fair balance” required under the ECHR'; para. 6.86: 'insufficiently transparent and verifiable'; para. 6.95: insufficient safeguards regarding risk indicators and the risk model; dictum 7.2 (Dutch: 'onverbindend ... wegens strijdigheid met artikel 8 lid 2 EVRM') declares Section 65 SUWI Act and Chapter 5a SUWI Decree non-binding as against the admissible claimant organisations and those whose interests they represent. The plan's description ('contrary to ECHR Article 8') is correct but should say Article 8(2). Limits: the court expressly left undiscussed whether the legislation was sufficiently accessible and foreseeable (6.72); it held that SyRI was not an unsuitable or a priori disproportionate instrument (6.77) and that the legislative choice met the general necessity requirement (6.78), faulting the safeguards instead; some claimants were inadmissible (7.1) and all other claims were dismissed (7.5). This is a first-instance civil judgment.

claims.claim: On 24 August 2017 a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court of India declared, in the Order of the Court signed by all nine judges, that the right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution, overruling M.P. Sharma and, to that extent, Kharak Singh.
claims.source: Supreme Court of India, Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) and Another v. Union of India and Others, Writ Petition (Civil) No. 494 of 2012, judgment of 24 August 2017, Order of the Court paras. 1-2 (pp. 546-547 of the Court's PDF); reported as (2017) 10 SCC 1; https://api.sci.gov.in/supremecourt/2012/35071/35071_2012_Judgement_24-Aug-2017.pdf
claims.notes: Read the Supreme Court's own 547-page PDF of the judgment. The Order of the Court records that Chandrachud J delivered the judgment for Khehar CJI, Agrawal, Nazeer and himself, and that Chelameswar, Bobde, Sapre, Nariman and Kaul JJ delivered separate judgments; para. 2 disposes of the reference in the terms stated in the claim. Limits: this answered a reference on whether privacy is a fundamental right; it did not decide the validity of Aadhaar, which was decided in the separate judgment of 26 September 2018. The tests for permissible restrictions (legality, legitimate aim, proportionality) appear in individual opinions, not in the Order of the Court, and were not pinpointed here. The SCC citation was seen only in secondary sources.

claims.claim: Eubanks investigates how data mining, policy algorithms and predictive risk models affect poor and working-class people in the United States, arguing that the most invasive and punitive automated systems are aimed at the poor.
claims.source: Virginia Eubanks, Automating Inequality: How High-Tech Tools Profile, Police, and Punish the Poor (New York: St. Martin's Press, 2018), 272 pp., ISBN 978-1-250-07431-7, LCCN 2017036194; https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250074317/automatinginequality/
claims.notes: Bibliographic details from the Open Library edition record, which is built from library MARC records (publisher St. Martin's Press, 2018, 272 pages, LCCN 2017036194, OCLC 1013516195) and quotes the publisher's description: automated systems 'control which neighborhoods get policed, which families attain needed resources, and who is investigated for fraud', 'the most invasive and punitive systems are aimed at the poor', and the book 'systematically investigates the impacts of data mining, policy algorithms, and predictive risk models on poor and working-class people in America'. The publisher's own page renders only with JavaScript and could not be read. The book text was not read and no page is verified. Its three case studies (Indiana's automated welfare eligibility, Los Angeles' coordinated entry system for homeless people, and Allegheny County's child-welfare screening model) are described in secondary sources only; the publisher's description mentions Indiana and a Pennsylvania family. Some reviews cite a later Picador paperback.

claims.claim: Article 22(1) GDPR gives a data subject the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them; Article 22(2) allows exceptions for contract necessity, authorisation by Union or Member State law with suitable safeguards, and explicit consent, and in the contract and consent cases Article 22(3) requires at least the right to obtain human intervention, to express one's point of view and to contest the decision.
claims.source: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 (General Data Protection Regulation), OJ L 119, 4.5.2016, p. 1, Article 22; https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj
claims.notes: Article 22 ('Automated individual decision-making, including profiling') read verbatim in the Official Journal text from the EU Publications Office (cellar XHTML for CELEX 32016R0679); EUR-Lex returned a bot challenge. Paragraphs 1-4 checked. Limits: the right covers only decisions 'based solely' on automated processing with legal or similarly significant effects; the 22(3) safeguards attach expressly to the contract and consent exceptions, while under 22(2)(b) the authorising law must itself lay down suitable safeguards; 22(4) restricts use of special-category data. Later corrigenda and case law on Article 22 were not checked.

claims.claim: Article 48 of the Weimar Constitution allowed the Reich President, where public security and order were seriously disturbed or endangered, to take the measures necessary to restore them, if necessary with armed force, and for that purpose to suspend temporarily, in whole or in part, the fundamental rights in Articles 114, 115, 117, 118, 123, 124 and 153; the President had to inform the Reichstag without delay, and the measures were to be revoked if the Reichstag demanded it.
claims.source: Die Verfassung des Deutschen Reichs ('Weimarer Reichsverfassung') of 11 August 1919, Reichsgesetzblatt 1919, p. 1383, Article 48(2)-(3); German text at documentArchiv.de, http://www.documentarchiv.de/wr/wrv.html
claims.notes: German text of Article 48 read on documentArchiv.de, which gives the source as Reichsgesetzblatt 1919, S. 1383; the English wording of the claim is my paraphrase of Art. 48(2) and (3). Art. 48(1) also allowed the President to compel a Land to perform its duties with armed force; Art. 48(4) allowed Land governments provisional measures; Art. 48(5) said details would be set by a Reich statute. An English translation hosted by German History in Documents and Images could not be retrieved (expired TLS certificate), so none is cited. How Article 48 was used in practice (decree government from 1930, the February 1933 decree) is not established by this entry and would need its own historical source.

claims.claim: Ackerman proposes a 'supermajoritarian escalator' for emergency powers: the executive may act alone only until the legislature can convene, the emergency then lapses without majority approval, majority approval sustains it for two or three months, and continuation then requires escalating supermajorities of sixty percent for the next two months, seventy for the next, and eighty thereafter.
claims.source: Bruce Ackerman, 'The Emergency Constitution', Yale Law Journal 113 (March 2004): 1029-1091, at 1047-1049; https://yalelawjournal.org/essay/the-emergency-constitution (PDF https://yalelawjournal.org/pdf/289_jz567rmk.pdf)
claims.notes: Full text read from the Yale Law Journal's PDF (printed pagination 1029-1091). P. 1047: unilateral executive action 'only for the briefest period'; 'one week' if the legislature is in session, 'two weeks at most' if not; then 'an escalating cascade of supermajorities: sixty percent for the next two months; seventy for the next; eighty thereafter'. Pp. 1048-1049 give the rationale (preventing normalisation, minority veto over electoral manipulation, milder use of powers); n. 47 proposes de-escalation on the same schedule for a new emergency. P. 1055 describes South Africa's two-step rule (majority, then 60 percent renewals) as 'the first supermajoritarian escalator'. The issue number was not confirmed (the journal's page gives March 2004). It is a normative proposal framed around terrorist attacks, not a description of an enacted system; Ackerman calls it a nonstarter as a formal US amendment and suggests a framework statute instead.

claims.claim: Gross and Ní Aoláin present a systematic theory of emergency powers that uses three models of the law's response to crisis to evaluate states' legal options, drawing on historical and comparative material from the Roman republic to the initial responses to the July 2005 London attacks.
claims.source: Oren Gross and Fionnuala Ní Aoláin, Law in Times of Crisis: Emergency Powers in Theory and Practice, Cambridge Studies in International and Comparative Law 46 (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2006), ISBN 978-0-521-83351-6 (hbk), 978-0-521-54123-7 (pbk); doi:10.1017/CBO9780511493997
claims.notes: Checked the Cambridge Core book page (print publication 30 October 2006; series number 46; ASIL book prize noted) and its description ('Three models of emergency powers are used to offer a conceptualization of emergency regimes'). Chapter titles and ranges from Crossref: 'Models of accommodation' (pp. 17-85), 'Law for all seasons' (pp. 86-109), 'Models of extra-legality' (pp. 110-170), 'Five degrees of separation' (pp. 171-244), 'International human rights and emergencies' (pp. 247-325), 'Emergencies and humanitarian law' (pp. 326-364), 'Terrorism, emergencies, and international responses to contemporary threats' (pp. 365-421). Identifying the three models with these chapter titles is my inference from the titles; the book text was not read. The plan named no specific point, so none is claimed.

claims.claim: A Campbell systematic review of ten randomised trials (1,879 offenders; 734 interviewed victims), in which offenders and victims agreed to meet before random assignment, found that face-to-face restorative justice conferences caused a modest reduction in repeat convictions or arrests over two years (standardised mean difference d = -0.155, p = .001; nine of ten results in the predicted direction) and higher victim satisfaction with the handling of their cases (d = 0.327, p < .05).
claims.source: Heather Strang, Lawrence W. Sherman, Evan Mayo-Wilson, Daniel Woods and Barak Ariel, 'Restorative Justice Conferencing (RJC) Using Face-to-Face Meetings of Offenders and Victims: Effects on Offender Recidivism and Victim Satisfaction. A Systematic Review', Campbell Systematic Reviews 9(1) (2013), 2013:12, executive summary pp. 4-5; doi:10.4073/csr.2013.12
claims.notes: Full text read from a copy on the Cambridge Institute of Criminology site (https://www.crim.cam.ac.uk/system/files/documents/rj_strang_review.pdf). That copy's front matter misprints the series number and DOI (it shows '2013:10', 'DOI: 10.4073/csr.2013.10' and 'Campbell Systematic Reviews 2013:9'); Crossref confirms that 10.4073/csr.2013.12 is this review and that 10.4073/csr.2013.10 is a different review (mentoring). Findings checked in the executive summary (pp. 4-5): intention-to-treat analysis; d = -.155 (p = .001) on two-year repeat convictions or arrests; victim satisfaction 'uniformly positive (d = .327; p<.05)'; cost-effectiveness in the seven UK trials of 8 times overall and up to 14 times in London. The authors' own abstract calls the offending effect 'a modest but highly cost-effective reduction'. Limits the book must keep: results apply to cases where both offender and victim consent; one of the ten trials reported a backfiring effect; the authors disclose (p. 6) that three of them ran two of the trials, two operationally directed seven others, and Sherman wrote the grant proposals and initial designs for all ten.

claims.claim: Using an original cross-national historical dataset, Elkins, Ginsburg and Melton study why some national constitutions endure while others do not, concluding that although constitutions are imperilled by social and political crises, certain aspects of constitutional design can substantially lower the risk of a constitution's 'death'.
claims.source: Zachary Elkins, Tom Ginsburg and James Melton, The Endurance of National Constitutions (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2009), ISBN 978-0-521-51550-4 (hbk), 978-0-521-73132-4 (pbk); doi:10.1017/CBO9780511817595; ch. 5 'What Makes Constitutions Endure?' (pp. 65-92), ch. 7 'An Epidemiological Analysis of Constitutional Mortality' (pp. 122-146)
claims.notes: Checked the Cambridge Core book page (print publication 12 October 2009) and its description, which also says the authors scrutinise whether endurance is desirable at all; chapter titles and ranges from Crossref. The book text was not read and no page is verified. Do not take a lifespan figure from this entry: the publisher's description says 'only half live more than nine years', while secondary summaries found in search cite a nineteen-year median or predicted life expectancy (linked to Jefferson's proposal); the two were not reconciled against the book.

claims.claim: The Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture obliges each State Party to set up, designate or maintain one or several independent national preventive mechanisms (Articles 3 and 17), to guarantee their functional independence and resources (Article 18), to grant them powers to examine the treatment of people deprived of their liberty, make recommendations and comment on legislation (Article 19), and to give them access to all places of detention, private interviews and the liberty to choose where to visit and whom to interview (Article 20).
claims.source: Optional Protocol to the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, adopted by UN General Assembly resolution 57/199 of 18 December 2002 (annex), UN Doc. A/RES/57/199; entered into force 22 June 2006; 2375 UNTS 237; Articles 3 and 17-23; https://documents.un.org/api/symbol/access?s=A/RES/57/199&l=en&t=pdf
claims.notes: Protocol text read in the official resolution document A/RES/57/199 (77th plenary meeting, 18 December 2002); entry into force (22 June 2006 under art. 28(1)), UNTS reference (vol. 2375, p. 237) and registration checked on the UN Treaty Collection status page (https://treaties.un.org/Pages/ViewDetails.aspx?src=TREATY&mtdsg_no=IV-9-b&chapter=4&clang=_en), which listed 96 parties on 24 September 2026. Further NPM provisions: Art. 18(4) requires 'due consideration' to the Paris Principles; Art. 21(1) forbids sanctions against anyone for communicating information to the mechanism; Art. 22 requires authorities to examine its recommendations and enter into dialogue; Art. 23 requires publication of its annual reports.
