Limits: binding only on States Parties; Art. 24 allows a declaration postponing Part IV obligations for up to three years (extendable by two); NPMs recommend and do not issue binding orders. OHCHR's page refused automated access.

claims.claim: The Paris Principles, annexed to UN General Assembly resolution 48/134 of 20 December 1993, state that a national human rights institution should have as broad a mandate as possible, set out in a constitutional or legislative text; a pluralist composition; adequate funding so that it has its own staff and premises and is independent of the government; and members appointed by an official act for a specified duration.
claims.source: UN General Assembly resolution 48/134, 'National institutions for the promotion and protection of human rights', adopted 20 December 1993 (85th plenary meeting), UN Doc. A/RES/48/134 (4 March 1994), annex 'Principles relating to the status of national institutions', 'Competence and responsibilities' para. 2 and 'Composition and guarantees of independence and pluralism' paras. 1-3; https://documents.un.org/api/symbol/access?s=A/RES/48/134&l=en&t=pdf
claims.notes: Full resolution and annex read in the official UN document. Competence para. 2: 'as broad a mandate as possible, which shall be clearly set forth in a constitutional or legislative text'; Composition para. 1 (pluralist representation, government representatives in an advisory capacity only), para. 2 (adequate funding 'to be independent of the Government'), para. 3 (appointment 'by an official act which shall establish the specific duration of the mandate'). Limits: the resolution only 'welcomes' the Principles (op. para. 11) and encourages states to have regard to them while 'recognizing that it is the right of each State to choose the framework that is best suited' (op. para. 12); the Principles are a non-binding standard. Complaint-handling powers appear only as optional 'additional principles' for quasi-jurisdictional commissions. OHCHR's page refused automated access.

claims.claim: Sergot and colleagues translated much of the British Nationality Act 1981 into a Prolog-style logic program so that its consequences could be derived mechanically; they treated the Act's negations as negation as failure, which they said is justified only under a closed-world assumption, and noted that the Act's default rule for abandoned infants is nonmonotonic and that its counterfactual conditions could not be expressed directly in the logic.
claims.source: M. J. Sergot, F. Sadri, R. A. Kowalski, F. Kriwaczek, P. Hammond and H. T. Cory, 'The British Nationality Act as a Logic Program', Communications of the ACM 29(5) (May 1986): 370-386, at 379 (negation as failure) and 381-382 (abandoned infants; counterfactual conditionals); doi:10.1145/5689.5920
claims.notes: Full text read from Kowalski's author-hosted scan (https://www.doc.ic.ac.uk/~rak/papers/British%20Nationality%20Act.pdf); the ACM Digital Library refused automated access; bibliographic data checked against Crossref. Pinpoints use the printed pagination. P. 379: 'not[Q] holds when all ways of showing Q fail'; 'justified whenever we can make a “Closed World” Assumption'; 'inappropriate in those circumstances where it is unreasonable to make a Closed World Assumption'. Pp. 381-382: the abandoned-infant default (Section 1(2)) 'is nonmonotonic' - the child's citizenship conclusion would have to be withdrawn if the parents were later identified and did not qualify - and 'extended Horn clause logic is not adequate for dealing with counterfactual conditionals', which the authors handled by writing additional alternative rules. The paper presents an experiment, not a deployed decision system; it also discusses vague concepts such as 'being of good character', which it did not formalise.

claims.claim: Catala is a programming language designed for a systematic translation of statutory law into executable code, built to express the general-case and exception structure of statutes; its authors proved core compilation steps correct with the F* proof assistant and, in formalising French family-benefit rules, found a bug in the official implementation.
claims.source: Denis Merigoux, Nicolas Chataing and Jonathan Protzenko, 'Catala: A Programming Language for the Law', Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 5 (ICFP) (August 2021): 1-29; doi:10.1145/3473582; open access, also arXiv:2103.03198
claims.notes: Abstract and introduction read in the arXiv version (v2, 2 July 2021); volume, issue (ICFP), 29-page length and publication date (19 August 2021) checked on Crossref; the ACM Digital Library refused automated access. A search result gives the article number as 77, but it was not seen on the publisher's page, so it is left out of the citation. The abstract says the language targets areas where law 'leaves little room for interpretation' ('algorithms in disguise'), and the paper also evaluates section 121 of the US federal income tax code. The bug claim is the authors' own report ('we uncover a bug in the official implementation of the French benefits'); the bug itself was not examined here.

claims.claim: An OECD Observatory of Public Sector Innovation working paper describes 'Rules as Code' as governments creating an official machine-consumable version of rules alongside the human-readable form, and warns that technocratic fixes can become the default without due consideration of whether they are appropriate and legitimate as well as workable.
claims.source: James Mohun and Alex Roberts, 'Cracking the Code: Rulemaking for Humans and Machines', OECD Working Papers on Public Governance No. 42 (Paris: OECD Publishing, October 2020), pp. 2 and 13; doi:10.1787/3afe6ba5-en
claims.notes: Full PDF read from the OECD content server (https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2020/10/dechiffrer-le-code_d56cab77/3afe6ba5-en.pdf); the cover confirms the series and number 42 and the authors; Crossref gives 12 October 2020. P. 2 (foreword): Rules as Code 'proposes that governments create an official version of rules (e.g. laws and regulations) in a machine-consumable form' that 'would ... complement the existing, human-readable form'; the paper is 'the third in a series of ‘innovation primers’'. P. 13: 'There is a real risk for decisions to be made with the intent of optimising or improving what is, without regard to broader democratic and governance concerns. ... Technocratic fixes can easily and accidentally become the new default, bypassing due consideration as to whether they were right (appropriate and legitimate) as well as workable (feasible and effective).' It is an advocacy primer for practitioners, not an evaluation of outcomes; the country case studies it contains were not checked.

claims.claim: Apt, Blair and Walker defined stratified logic programs, in which no cycle of predicate dependencies passes through negation, and showed that such a program has a canonical model, built stratum by stratum, that is minimal and supported and does not depend on which stratification is chosen.
claims.source: Krzysztof R. Apt, Howard A. Blair and Adrian Walker, 'Towards a Theory of Declarative Knowledge', in Jack Minker (ed.), Foundations of Deductive Databases and Logic Programming (Morgan Kaufmann, 1988), pp. 89-148, ISBN 978-0-934613-40-8; doi:10.1016/B978-0-934613-40-8.50006-3
claims.notes: Bibliographic details (title, authors, book, 1988, pp. 89-148, ISBN) checked on Crossref; Minker as editor is from secondary citations. The chapter text itself could not be read (publisher site refused access). The content claim is verified only through the first author's own later summary: K. R. Apt and J.-M. Pugin, 'Management of Stratified Databases' (CWI report, https://ir.cwi.nl/pub/10594/10594D.pdf), section 2, which states the ABW definition ('stratified if no cycle in its dependency graph contains a negative arc') and the ABW theorem that the model 'does not depend on the stratification', is a minimal model, and is supported. That report cites an earlier version in the 1986 Washington workshop proceedings (pp. 546-629) and notes that Van Gelder proposed the same class independently, so priority should not be attributed to these authors alone. No page within the chapter is verified.

claims.claim: Denning modelled secure information flow using a lattice of security classes, arguing that the lattice structure, justified by the semantics of information flow, gives concise formulations of the security requirements of existing systems, a unifying view of systems that restrict information flow, and a basis for automatically certifying that a program's information flows are secure.
